Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 47, to repeal The War Charities Act, 1917.
He said: The War Charities Act was passed in 1917 entirely as a war measure. It provided that all associations collecting moneys for works of charity during the war should be licensed, and that a register should be kept in connection with these organizations; it was also provided that returns should be made to the Department of the Secretary of State every six months in regard to the work done, showing what moneys had been collected and what disposition had been made of them. During the war 846 of such associations were licensed, and, of these, since the close of the war 671 have been dropped from the register, being no longer in existence. There are 143 associations now under license as chapters of the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire, and these are practically all the organizations at present under the licensing system. It has been deemed advisable to repeal the act, as it is felt that the system of licensing such associations is no longer necessary and is only a burden on the women working in these organizations. The officials of the department have advised me that there is no longer any necessity for this particular statute.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks in this debate I cannot help referring to the changed attitude in certain sections of this House during the last two or three sessions. If the pictures that have been painted of the calamity that has overtaken Canada and the glowing scenes that have been depicted of conditions prevailing in the United States and France are to be taken as a test of patriotism, then I think the Progressives are entirely exonerated from reproach for any unpatriotic speeches that have been made here at any time. Our Conservative friends have certainly painted a very gloomy picture of existing conditions in the Dominion; on the other hand, the government and its supporters have endeavoured to convince us that members of the official opposition were entirely wrong and that everything was running along satisfactorily. Now, I do not like to believe that conditions are as bad as they are pictured by our Conservative friends, and at the same time I am sorry that I cannot believe they are as rosy and as satisfactory as pictured by the government and its supporters. Knowing that agriculture is the basic industry of the Dominion I feel perfectly

The Budget-Mr. Milne

satisfied that other industries cannot be more prosperous than this basic industry. I know the conditions of our agricultural sections, and therefore I am forced to the conclusion that things are not as good as we would like to see them. Undoubtedly many of our citizens are leaving their country for the United States, and our tax burdens are too heavy; but our main trouble is that we cannot sell our commodities at a profit.
The causes for these unsatisfactory conditions are not all to be laid at the feet of the present government. No doubt world conditions have had a considerable influence in causing the depression which we are now experiencing. On the other hand, it must not be forgotten that in the past there has been a good deal of blind optimism in running our national affairs, and in addition for the last thirty or forty years there has been considerable unsound financing. By blind optimism I mean that our railways were constructed fifty years ahead of our requirements, and many of our public buildings have been erected in an extravagant manner and. equally far ahead of our needs. These huge expenditures that were never warranted are to-day imposing an extremely heavy burden on our citizens, a burden which will have to be borne for generations to come. We have heard a good deal about our huge national debt of 82,400,000,000. This debt has increased since 1911 by five hundred per cent. A good deal of the increase has been attributed to our war expenditure and the cost of demobilization. If we deduct the moneys paid out on this account, we find that we still have an increase since 1911 of over 135 per cent. The expenses of government have increased from $122,681,000 in 1911 to $344,221,000 in 1923, or about 173 per cent. While this mountain of debt has been piling up what provision have we been making to meet its payment? It is true our population has increased from 7,206,643 in 1911 to 9,082,000 odd in 1924, or about 25 per cent. Since 1867 our national debt has been reduced only nine times, the reductions totalling less than $80,000,000. There has been no attempt to establish a sinking fund to meet maturing bonds and to take care of depreciation, or anything of that nature. We have followed since confederation the insane policy of borrowing money to pay the interest on our debt. We know very well that if a business concern adopted such an unsound practice it would be only a very short time before it would be bankrupt.

While this insane financial policy has been pursued, what has been happening to our natural resources? Our farms have become depleted of their fertility; we have plant diseases, insect pests, weeds and many other things established in our soil; and these are going to increase our cost of production tremendously. W'hat is happening to our forests? Large areas have been wiped out entirely. I refer especially to the forest areas of the western provinces. The country has suffered the loss in order that certain influential individuals might become immensely wealthy. What has this depletion brought in its train? I could show hon. members areas in the western provinces through which flowed streams that had their source in the forests and watered our prairies for miles and miles. To-day those streams run only for a veiy short time in the spring, thereby depriving many districts of a regular water supply.

I was speaking about, the streams having dried out due to the forest being cleared away in some of our prairie sections. Besides, we are informed-and we believe it to be true-that the presence of forests has an imiportant effect upon the extent of our rainfall1. Through the wiping away of our forest areas in the prairie sections our rainfall has decreased, and that is one of the things the prairie provinces need in the very worst way.
What has been happening in our mines? We are informed that certain coal mines have been drawn on to such an extent that it is necessary to go several miles under the sea to secure the coal, thereby increasing the cost of getting it to the head of the mine. I may say just here that I am decidedly opposed to the increased duty on coal. I am not an admirer of the dole system, but I would rather dole out assistance to the miners if I know it is going right to them than to dole it out to a corporation or company which has absolute control of the whole situation, there

The Budget-Mr. Milne
being no assurance that the workmen of our country will reap the benefit of the protection afforded.

speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware
that there are a large number of independent coal companies operating in this country?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I believe there are, but what I say to one I say to all. What has been happening to the fisheries? A good many of our lakes throughout the Dominion are fished out. We used to hear of tremendous catches of salmon in the British Columbia streams, but to-day, I understand, many of the canneries that formerly operated there have had to shut down owing to the want of fish. It is essential that large sums of money be spent in the very near future to replenish our supply of fish in order to keep this industry going.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why keep the fishery industry going if you are not willing to keep the coal industry going? The coal companies to which I refer have been working from one to three days a week for the last year and a half. Is the fishing industry to receive assistance and the coal industry to receive none?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a very pertinent
question, I suppose, especially when a man is interested in coal mines. You cannot make coal; but no departure from policy is involved in the suggestion that the streams and lakes of our country be replenished with fish, the policy is regarded as a sound one and there is no question in my mind that it will have to be carried on to a greater extent than it has been in the past.
In any reference I make to our resources being depleted, I do not mean to intimate that they are practically exhausted or anything like nearly wiped out. We still have unlimited natural resources, but the resources that were easily accessible, Mr. Speaker, are practically gone, and the production costs of all these basic industries have been greatly increased. The sorry part of it is that instead of making some reservation while these easily accessible resources were being exploited, nothing was done in that direction and our liabilities were increasing all the time while the resources were being depleted.
It seems to me we have been wallowing around in financial difficulties long enough and that we should turn our faces the other way and head for some solid ground. All the conditions I speak of have been brought about while we have been following the old policy of protection. There has been very little difference between the tariff policies in
161i
force in this country as far back as I have been able to get information. From 1915, ut to the last few years the highest average dutj on our total import was 26.1 per cent; to-daj it is about 22.3 per cent. As a matter of fac* a few years ago it was down as low as 20.5; in the last two or three years there seems to have been a slight increase. But I do not consider that these slight fluctuations are due to any change in policy; the policy, so far as we can ascertain, has been practically the same. When one party was in office the other was advocating lower duties, but when those in opposition got into power the other party promptly started off on the same tack. My observation has convinced me that both the Liberals and the Conservatives are protectionist parties. Some try to get under the flag of low tariff, but they have a hard time to establish themselves there and an even harder time to convince the people that they are sincere.
Let me deal for a few moments with agriculture and agricultural conditions-and I do so because I have been familiar with those conditions all my life. In this respect I may depart from the general method that is followed in the east, because from what I can gather it would seem that most people in this part of the country like to talk about agricultural conditions when they know very little about them. Agriculture is one of the most important industries of our country. It is our basic industry-and you do not have to go very far these days before you get conclusive proof of that. During the Easter recess I was visiting around the country a little, and every business man I spoke to about business conditions would say, "Oh, if the west gets a good crop this year, things will foe all right; we shall be on the royal road to success." I have heard that, I would not like to say how many tames, but at least a dozen times during the last six months. That convinces me more than ever that agriculture really is of vital importance to the country. Our friends in the government do not seem to lay much stress on agriculture this year, that is, if we are to assume that their sympathy is indicated by the proposals in the budget, but some of the officials in the government service apparently realize its importance. I will read an extract from Seasonable Hints, No. 31, March, 1925:
Canada's prosperity depends largely on agriculture, and in turn agricultural prosperity depends on our ability to satisfy local markets and produce a large surplus of superior quality for export. Unless this surplus is produced at a cost per unit sufficiently low to compete with other exporting countries, then our export trade, in fact our agricultural prospe-:*v. is curtailed if not doomed.
252*
The Budget-Mr. Milne

I say that when our agriculture is doomed there is not .much hope for Canada's prosperity.
Agriculture leads in our products exported. The total exports of agricultural products, including raw, partly manufactured, and manufactured, amount to $527,807,628; products of forest origin, $273,603,598; products of mineral origin, $170,686,286; of marine origin, $30,988,812. I think that is a sufficient reason why agriculture should receive consideration, and I propose to deal with it for a little while.
What are the farmers of Canada doing? The value of their total field crops has increased from $899,834,000 odd in 1923 to $995,234,000 odd in 1924. Our 'butter production has increased from approximately
126.834.000	pounds in 1923, to 182,287,000 pounds in 1924. There has been a slight decrease in the amount of cheese produced. Then as to the total value of our live stock -and I might say that I did1 not try to get the numbers, because to give the numbers in each, particular class of live stock would have meant giving a lengthy list of figures -the total value of our live stock in 1923 amounted to $613,260,000, and in 1924 to $641,144,000. That shows an increase in the value of our live stock, and at the same time the price per animal was somewhat less than in 1923. Our poultry also shows a substantial increase.
I want to be pardoned for referring to Manitoba specifically, but I do this for the reason that the western provinces are continually-being accused of "wheat mining"; that is the term that is invariably used, especially in eastern Canada. I will give you figures to give you an idea of what Manitoba produces. In 1924 her total field crops were valued at approximately $136,000,000. Her total wheat crop was valued at $55,296,000. That shows the proportion of the wheat crop to the total field crop. Other field crops that were produced in Manitoba were fodder corn to the amount of $2,070,000; potatoes, $2,063,000; hay and clover, $5,320,000; turnips and mangels, $540,620; alfalfa, $208,000. Other cereals produced were: oats, approximately $33,250,000; barley, $28,500,000; rye, $6,000,000; flax, $6,500,000.
Manitoba has increased her number of cattle holdings from 691,000 odd in 1923 to
710.000	odd in 1924; sheep have increased from 93,000 to 95,000; swine from 291,000 to 425,000; poultry from 3,289,000 to 3.693,000 odd. Her butter production has increased from 10,730,000 to 12,632,000 pounds; her cheese from 231,000 pounds to 500,000 pounds;

her honey production from 66,047 pounds in 1920 to 1,302,000 pounds in 1924.

speechtext:
I could not say. I have given the House these figures to show that Manitoba is not a " wheat mining " province, as it is generally considered to be. The farmers of Manitoba are producing live stock and dairy products, and are developing practically every branch of agriculture that can be followed in that country, and with the exception of fruit I think they have nearly as wide a range of production as any other province in the Dominion.
Now, do the farmers of Canada know their business, or are they really working at something they do not know anything about? We would be inclined to think from what we hear sometimes that we did not know very much about our business, but I want to put on Hansard the number of prizes that Canada has won for her live stock at the International Fair in the last three years. In 1922 Canada won at the International Live Stock Show at Chicago 30 first prizes, 28 seconds, and 26 thirds; in 1923, 42 firsts, 40 seconds, and 32 thirds; in 1924, 68 firsts, 47 seconds, and 35 thirds. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, do the Canadian farmers know their business? I think the figures I have given will answer the question definitely; our Canadian farmers are producing and their products are of a high quality. But they are not doing this without considerable effort. There are many toilworn hands on the farm; there are many stooped shoulders that have been accomplishing these things, shoulders that will never straighten. There are many women on our Canadian

The Budget-Mr. Milne
farms that I pity. I would rather not say what I am about to say, but I believe that unless these things are known we shall never be able to solve our problems. Here are the conditions that exist. I can take hon. members to many farms where the women milk daily seven, or eight cows, feed calves, and keep a flock of from a hundred to a hundred and fifty chickens. Besides doing these things they are raising a family and looking after the home. Now, what are these women getting in return? The farmer's wife works night and morning, Sunday and Monday throughout the year. But if she wants to get a power washing machine to lighten the labour in the house she is taxed 30 per cent. I believe the rate is 25 or 35 per cent. If she wants to exchange her butter or eggs for a pair of boots or some woollen underclothes for the children she is taxed 25 to 30 per cent. But, besides this, after that woman has gathered her five-gallon can of cream and taken it to the dairy, the government planks a twojcent tax on the paltry little cheque of probably S2.50 or $3 which she receives for her cream. I think when we come down and consider the facts as they are to-day in our country we find conditions that are really disgraceful. The farm woman's small cream cheque of two or three dollars is taxed, but a cheque for three or four thousand dollars is not so heavily taxed speaking relatively. I certainly think that this stamp of two cents on a cheque for $2 or $2.50 is-

speechtext:
Yes, very nearly the last
straw. And what is she offered in compensation for that? Cheaper grape fruit for breakfast. In a nutshell that is what the hard working farmers are getting to-day from this budget -an additional tax of two cents on their cream cheques and a reduction on grape fruit. But perhaps I had better make that statement clear. I imagine there are some people living in the east who use grape fruit every morning for breakfast, but it is not a common article of diet for the farmer's breakfast; I do not believe there is one fanner out of five hundred who ever eats grape fruit at his morning meal.

speechtext: Porridge.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His breakfast consists
mainly of oatmeal. Now the farmers are doing their share and are willing to continue doing so; there is not a respectable farmer in the whole country but is willing to do his share. There are exceptions to every rule, but generally speaking that may be said of
the farmers of the country. Now, you may tell me that the farmers in western Canada, and even the farmers in old Ontario, have made money in farming and consequently my argument absolutely falls to the ground. As to that I want to say something about the changed conditions in farming, and I am not going to deal with Ontario specially, because Ontario went through the condition I have in mind a good many years ago and the situation there now is entirely different from what it is in the west. Perhaps my description is applicable to sections of Ontario as well, but I am going to apply it more particularly to the west because I am better acquainted with conditions there. In the west twenty years ago we had cheap land, we had free homesteads and' we could buy land at from $2 to $5 an acre. To-day in the west we have to pay from $20 to $50 an acre for our land. Twenty years ago we had big yields; there was no difficulty in getting, for example, forty bushels of wheat to the acre, that was quite a common thing; and if we did not get thirty-five bushels to the acre we thought Providence had been hard on us. What do we get to-day? Fifteen or sixteen bushels to the acre. That falling off is caused, as I mentioned before, by various plant diseases, for example rust. We cannot estimate how rust has diminished the value of our grain crop. We have plant diseases, we have plant insects, and we have weeds. These things were unknown twenty years ago. Then too at that time we had low taxes. I can remember when our municipal tax amounted to $5 on the old homestead. What is it today? It amounts to a neat $100. I know of quarter sections in western Canada where the farmers are paying $130 a quarter section and1 where there are probably only forty or fifty acres under cultivation out of one. hundred and sixty. In those days only a small capital was needed to enable the farmer to carry on; today a huge capital is necessary and he must have recourse to borrowing. Most of the farmers are compelled to borrow, and they have to pay from 8 to 10 per cent interest on the loans they get. At that time also fuel was cheap. There were few sections of Manitoba where we could not get our fuel from the woods in a day's drive. To-day we have to buy coal, and to relieve that situation an increased tax of fifty cents a ton has been placed on coal. Furthermore, at that time we had cheap building material. The farmers could haul logs from the woods and build their outbuildings and-even, as a good many did-their homes, log houses which were very comfortable and very good in their day This facility
The budget- Mr. Milne

is not available to-day; you have to go to the lumber yard and buy lumber at 850 and 860 a thousand in order to get your home established. Then, taking the cattle industry into consideration, years ago we had all kinds of pastures. We could go out into the meadows and cut around as much hay as we thought we could put up, and we would have plenty of hay to feed our stock. The cattle were turned out in the spring, and roamed over perhaps a section or two near by-free pasture. What have we got to-day? We have to confine our cattle to our own land which is probably worth $30 or $40 an acre, and we have to provide hay off our own farms. These are the changed conditions that we have to face to-day; they are entirely different from what they were twenty years ago. I will admit that under the conditions which formerly prevailed the farmers were able to pay the extra burden of taxation that was thrust on	them and perhaps did not
feel it. But to-day the	farmers are
suffering from a tremendously increased cost of production and are groaning under the load. I do not mean to say that the present government is responsible for these conditions, but I say that these conditions cannot be remedied without an effort. While I appreciate the work of our press I desire to say that as long as the hand that controls the pen is directed by others, the press is not going to help us very much in solving our problems. I do not want to say anything about other organizations that are in existence. We find these organizations more in the industrial section of Canada than in the west, but if we are going to solve our problems we want the help of everybody. The people have got to help themselves so far as they can. We cannot expect better conditions on our farms and in our agricultural districts unless we have a diligent and careful people, and I maintain that generally speaking we have. We must be ready to adopt better methods of farming; we must be ready to co-operate in every possible way to promote the community or Dominion interests. Unless we can do that we cannot expect prosperity. No family can get along if one member of the family takes all the cream for his porridge. Dad will look after that; he will spread the cream around But if Dad takes all the cream for himself, what will happen? The youngsters get out as soon as they can. That is the condition existing in Canada to-day. Unless the provinces of the country are prepared to deal justly with one another, we cannot expect good results; but the fellow who is getting
[Mr. Milne.l
the skimmed milk is going to press for justice. I claim the government, instead of following a fiscal policy that will encourage special privilege should be doing just the very opposite, they should prevent such a thing as that occurring. I am satisfied that the tariff has had a lot to do with the condition that exists in our country to-day. We cannot hope to increase the price of our products, because the price is set in competition with the world; it is hopeless to assume that we can do that, we cannot do it by any system of taxation or anything else that I know of. The only alternative we have is to lower our cost of production, and in order to do that we have to look for cheaper production costs, and I maintain that the tariff is one of the main things by which to bring about that result. If we had cheaper implements of production and cheaper necessities of life, it would materially assist in cheaper production.
The credit machinery of our country never was adopted for the agriculturist. It is just about as applicable to the farming industry of our country as a clover huller would be to husk or shell corn. I say that a three or four months' credit was never adequate for the agricultural people, and the day for the mortgages maturing in three or five years is past and gone so far as agriculture 4 p.m. is concerned1. I am not going to deal with the credit phase of the question very much because I do hope that the government will take some action this session. Last year we were living in hopes all session; this year we are still living in hopes. I merely mention the matter to impress on the government the necessity of taking some steps in this direction. Many farmers in our country have given mortgages bearing eight, nine or ten per cent. Very often you will meet a farmer, who will tell you, "Well, I have been able to pay the interest on my mortgage this year, but have not been able to pay any principal". I claim that the interest he is paying at the present time should amortize that whole debt in twenty-five or thirty years. In that event he would have some encouragement, whereas at the present time he goes on paying interest and at the end of twenty or thirty years his debt is just as great as ever. Something must be done, otherwiio many farmers will become insolvent and leave the country. We were looking for some remedy last year; I believe the Banking and Commerce committee recommended that the Bankruptcy Act be amended, and I would cerlainly advocate that that action be taken as early this session

The Budget-Mr. Milne
as possible. We have thousands of farmers leaving our country and our Dominion simply to get rid of their debts. The creditors might just as well make some arrangement and free these men of their debts, because they will never get anything out of them any other way. Cheaper credits would naturally reduce our cost of production.
Transportation is another big problem and requires immediate attention. When we consider the amount that is taken out of our product in getting it to the ultimate market, we realize how important it is, especially to western farmers, who are located far inland. We have a national railway which was left on our doorstep by private enterprise. I say by all means transfer some of the capital of the National Railways to our national debt or to some other account. I do not know what you would call the "other" account unless you call it the "political bungling" or "campaign" account. I am pretty well convinced that if the government had been true to the people of this country an account of this kind would have been opened long ago. The load that is tied around the neck of the Canadian National Railways has very little to do with the value that is in the National Railways, and I say by all means get rid of that. Until we can get rid of it, we will have to pay interest on the bonds, no doubt. But why burden the National Railway in its management when no private corporation could carry on with that load? If the road had gone through the ordinary- court of bankruptcy we would have had the debt added to our national debt but it would have been off the railway. I say therefore that when transportation is of such vital importance we cannot afford to strangle our carrying system or to allow it to be crushed under any unjust or unfair load.
There is a suggestion that the National Railways should be taken over by the Canadian Pacific, and that is something to which I would be absolutely opposed; I would oppose any such bargain. I do not think it would be in the best interests of this Dominion to have a monopolistic corporation of such magnitude - operating a public utility such as our railways. Perhaps the ideal condition exists to-day from the standpoint of stimulating an efficient management; we have one road privately owned and one road publicly owned, and satisfactory results should accrue from such a condition, if some regulating agency will prevent duplication of service and extravagance of equipment. We cannot allow wasteful competition to continue. I think that there should be some control by
means of which the duplication of train service might be eliminated, and I should also like to see such a measure of control as would cut out some of the extravagance that now obtains in connection with some of our palatial office buildings as well as in the matter of dining car service, hotel service, and Pullman car service. The companies will tell us that the Pullman, dining car and hotel services are run at a loss, and I see no reason why we should continue to carry these conveniences at a loss. If the people who demand this class of accommodation really want it they should pay for it; there is no justice in making the citizen who rides in a day coach and eats from a lunch box pay for the exclusive service which is provided in the Pullman and dining cars and in the hotels. I would advocate action, and immediate action. Last year it was rumoured that something would be done to get the heads of the railways together. Well, they have been together and have parted again, and so far as I know and the Dominion knows we are no further ahead now than we were before in the matter of reducing useless com-pefjtion. Frankly, I do not believe that the heads of the railways would care to have any interference in their affairs; they have a big job and they have a complete staff to do the work, and I do not think they are apt to invite us to interfere with them. But I claim that we should interfere to the extent of regulating things to some degree. If we cannot carry on the two systems under separate management, efficiently by some means of regulation, then by all means let us bring them under one head and make the joint system a publicly owned affair. We cannot continue under existing conditions to lose $50,000,000 a year, when we might be saving at least $100,000,000 a year, according to figures quoted in the House yesterday.
I shall now touch briefly upon the soldier settlement problem, which is of vital interest to the agriculturists of western Canada. I mention western Canada -again because I am more familiar with conditions there than I am with conditions in the east, the same thing might apply in this connection to the newer parts of Ontario and other provinces. Here is the condition of affairs. When the soldiers were established on the land it was necessary to build schools and construct roads; and other things that go to make up a community had to be done. In the province of Manitoba, over twenty-five per cent of these farms have been vacated, and I know certain municipalities in which as high as sixty per cent of
The Budget-Mr. Milne

such lands have 'been abandoned. What load does that throw on the rest of the people who are left there? We have to maintain these school systems and carry on all the community work, and we must keep up the roads that go past the idle farms. This is an absolute burden on the people who are left. The burden becomes almost unbearable. I certainly think that the municipal taxes should be paid by the government on vacated lands. There is an objection to that; it is held that if this were done in one place it would have to be done elsewhere as well. So far as that is concerned, I notice an item in the Auditor General's report which strikes me as being almost parallel with this, that is to say, in the matter of road construction. I understand that in Peterborough the city wanted the street repaired past some of the public buildings there, and the government here appropriated $1,163 for the purpose of carrying out the work. It is held that there was a precedent for this grant, although the Auditor General questioned that claim. Let me ask this question: Is the . city of Peterborough any more entitled to a road past that government property than the people in my municipality are entitled to a road past a quarter section there?
I have endeavoured to show in my remarks that instead of trying to increase the price of the farmers' products we should try to decrease the cost of production, and that this could be brought about by a lower tariff on the implements of production and on the necessaries of life. Cheaper credits and cheaper transportation if possible, would also assist materially in cheapening production. There are other things that have to be considered, and I want to give everyone credit where any credit is due. I am glad that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is in his seat, because I am going to say that in my opinion the Department of Agriculture and its officials are doing a really valuable work from the point of view of investigation. I do not approve of all that is done on the experimental farms; a good deal of the money spent in this direction could be utilized to better advantage in other ways. The work that has been carried on by the plant and animal pathologists is I think excellent, and we cannot do too much to develop it. We have been so far devoting all our energies to increased production, which is all right; but we should not forget the importance of distribution and marketing. It costs more than half the price of our agricultural products to distribute them to the ultimate consumer; that is, the railway companies, the commission men, the merchants and the retailers get more than the
[Mr. Milne.)
producer. I believe that we should have an economic expert to study the problem of distribution, a system might be evolved by which a considerable saving could be effected. Up to the present time it seems to be nobody's business to bring about economy of distribution; everybody steps in and takes a slice wherever he can, thus adding to the ultimate selling price. I think some of the work that is being done to-day by the Department of Agriculture might well be dropped in favour of a study of a more economic system of distribution. And this study should not be confined to the products of the farm; I think the economic distribution of manufactured goods should be included. It is rather startling to compare the manufacturers' price with the retail price. A short time ago I met the agent for a company that makes trousers, and I was surprised to note the difference between the prices at which he was selling his goods as compared with prices the consumer pays. Therefore I think the manufacturer could well afford to make a careful study of the economic distribution of his products.
I do not propose to discuss the amendment to the budget. To my mind, it is like the chip in the Scotchman's porridge-it does not amount to much. What I would urge most earnestly is this-if we expect conditions to improve in this country we must stop throwing mud at each other, and seek a common basis to solve our national problems.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Montmorency) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker,
the period preceding a new budget is always attended by a certain expectant anxiety. Some desire the enforcement of certain restrictions which will protect them against competition; others want greater trade facilities and lower prices on everything necessary to their own industries; every hon. member strives to obtain for- those he represents all that he possibly can to make life pleasant for them. It is the duty of the government to listen to all the representations made, to lend an ear to the legitimate claims of the members of the House of Commons who represent the constituents of the various ridings and then to bring before the House the measures that it considers in the best interests of a majority of the. population of the country. Hence, the budget, whatever its nature, cannot appeal alike to everyone.
Last year the government made certain changes in the tariff which chiefly affected the implements of production necessary to the development of the natural resources of the country. The benefit of these changes accrued

The Budget-Mr. Casgrain
largely to the agricultural community; this was in the nature of an encouragement. One may say that the budget of last year raised the morale of the farming class. The Tories were dissatisfied ; they claimed that the government went too far in reducing the tariff and that the downward revision was contrary to the best interests of the country. This year the government has not touched the tariff; but the Tories are still not pleased and we even hear that a goodly number of the Progressive members who represent a considerable part of the west, are not altogether satisfied either. As regards the Tories particularly, the government has merely followed the advice emanating from that quarter last year, that is, to call a halt in the downward revision of the tariff which the government had begun, to protect the interests of the farmers. This year we have almost completely attained the tariff stability of which there was so much question two years ago, which the opposition demanded then and is still demanding now. I believe it was the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) who said recently in Montreal: "No matter what we do, we shall never be able to satisfy the Tories". I may add that when the Last Judgment comes, when we are about to receive our eternal reward, there will still be critics and malcontents and I feel quite sure that we shall find the Tories among them.
Representing, as I do, a constituency where the chief activities are farming and fishing it is once more my duty this year, as it was last, to support and congratulate the government and more particularly the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the budget brought down in the House. The export duty on electric power is most timely and is in perfect accord with the wise policy of the Quebec provincial government. The decrease in the duties on tackle and other material necessary to our fishermen of the Atlantic and the Pacific and of the lower St. Lawrence is sure to be a great help to this interesting class of our population. The duty on soft coal will benefit our friends of the Maritime provinces without undue interference with the industries in other sections of the country.
There is a new departure in the budget of this year: the Acting Minister of Finance has announced the appointment of a commission to study the tariff. I fully believe that such a commission may be very useful; but may I be allowed to express my humble opinion that the commission's powers should be purely advisory and that it should nowise decide the tariff policy of the government; this to my mind is the absolutely exclusive prerogative
of the representatives of the people in the House of Commons. I therefore accept the second Robb budget, without the slightest reservation, as coming from a wise, prudent, honest and practical man of affairs. It is a budget which gives a reasonable measure of justice to all classes of society. For the second time the hon. minister has had the honour and the pleasure to present to the people of Canada a balanced budget, that is one which shows a surplus of revenue over expenditure, a feature unknown to this country for more than ten years.
Since the beginning of this debate most of the hon. gentlemen who sit immediately to your left, Mr. Speaker, the remnants of the Tory party, have done all they possibly could to paint the economic state of the country in the darkest colours. Were we to believe them, the country is at the end of its tether; the country is ruined! They are the worst calamity howlers one could meet. They are defeatists of the very worst kind and were it not that I mi^ht be accused of exaggerating, I would even say that the attitude they take before the House and before the country, spreading bad news the way they do, is not the attitude of real patriots and true Canadians, irrespective of what may be their race or creed. If a man should have faith in his country, there is assuredly nothing comforting in the attitude taken in this House by the members of the Tory opposition.
Now let us see if what they claim be true. If we look at the newspapers, especially at the financial page, we find1 rather that the country is doing pretty wel after having been through the financial crisis brought on by the war and its aftermath which were so disastrous to our country.

And further in the same article:
The firm intend shortly to extend their Fergus plant, and will spend many thousands of dollars this year in an extensive advertising campaign.
Therefore the people have confidence.
In the morning Journal of March 24, 1925, Sir George Paish, an authority on economics, stated:

hopes we entertained. Although there is a reasonable surplus on the yearly operations, we must nevertheless each year, disburse millions to help meeting the commitments of all the merged railways, and of which the government guaranteed the payments in becoming owners.
Let me, while on the subject, draw your attention to a strange fact and which, in my opinion, is an injustice towards the province of Quebec. It is, that although the province of Quebec, has never guaranteed any of the National Railways' bonds, not more than those of the Canadian Northern originally owned by Mackenzie and Mann or others, it pays, to-day, a large share of them, through the revenues which the Dominion government levies, in taxes direct or otherwise, from the province of Quebec and the French Canadian tax-payer of that province; and this to the benefit of the province of Ontario, and especially the western provinces, which, years ago, through an unwise policy, entirely pledged themselves by guaranteeing the bonds which they thought they could pay in the future, but which they never were able to meet, and that the Canadian government rendered themselves responsible for, when purchasing the National railways, merged in 1919. Quebec, per capita, has far less railways, than,-and1 not as good a service as,-any of the other provinces of Canada. However, when it comes to being stalled, Quebec is never forgotten. If it becomes necessary to do away with the service of a train, to dispense with a station agent during certain periods of the year, Quebec catches it like the others and as much as the other provinces. If it becomes necessary to extend a platform, to construct a side line necessary for the development and progress in a rural district, Quebec is always refused. Under the plea of economy, the development of certain parts of our province is impeded and prevented. If it is a question of giving a better service to certain parts, as for instance the peninsula of Gaspe, which my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil), has had the honour of representing for a number of years, the excuse is given that it is impossible to do more at present; is it found necessary to build a branch line or a new line needed, as in my district, from Murray Bay to Chicoutimi, it is impossible to do so now because of the deficits which we have to meet. In the district just mentioned, there is space to open up for settlement two or three new parishes, these cannot be established owing to the fact that we must economize so as not to increase the debt of our railways and to make both ends meet. This also prevents, in 
many cases, the members of the province of Quebec from obtaining recognition of certain claims that we have been putting forth for a number of years, and it also prevents us from obtaining the improvement of certain essential services for the development of our districts, for instance, the establishment of a boat service between Murray Bay, Tadoussac and intermediary ports, in Saguenay county, which I have the honour to represent in this House. I state that, when to pay these enormous deficits of our railways which threaten to perpetuate themselves, when, so as not to increase the national debt, we are obliged 'to refuse such works,,, which fare necessary to certain districts, it is more than time to think of doing something to solve this great problem of our railways. It has become, to-day, Sir, the most important question. The government that wall finally solve that problem will secure the universal and everlasting gratitude of the Canadian people.
Many proposals have been submitted. Again, yesterday, I was listening with pleasure to the chairman of the committee on railways, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who was giving his views and telling us which, in his opinion, were the three proposals that could be resorted to. I have no technical knowledge as to how railways should be administered. I could not say which of the proposals he advocated yesterday would be the best, but I shall say that the people of this country are looking forward to one thing: the adoption of either of these proposals.
. Only after we have succeeded in dealing properly with this important problem, will the people of this country be satisfied and happy. Some suggested a merger with the Canadian Pacific. I do not know that this would be the best way out, but that company, I believe, whose able management was of such great advantage to this Dominion, could perhaps, to a certain extent, administer this country's railways, provided, however, that the interests of the Canadian people were safeguarded. Sir, there is another question on which I would like to say a few words; this question has been discussed in this House last year and is to come up again this year. It is about a grant to the Quebec Bridge company for the carrying out of improvements which are contemplated on a large scale. Last year a certain amount was voted for preliminary work to be undertaken. The reason given for not voting a larger amount, was because the final plans and estimates were not ready. This year, I believe, everything is ready. As a member

The Budget-Mr. Casgrain
of this House representing a riding, which forms part of the Quebec district, I am in duty bound to ask the government this year to do all in their power to develop the Quebec harbour. The rights of Quebec district should be on a par with those of any other section of the province of Quebec and of any of the other provinces in this Dominion. With the Quebec harbour properly equipped, properly fitted and extended so as to accommodate the large ocean going steamers, it should bring to this country instead of expenses and deficits, a substantial amount of revenue, while such improvements and equipment could not in any way detract from the trade that goes to the port of Montreal. There is, I believe, on the St. Lawrence river, in the province of Quebec, room for two great national harbours, that of Quebec and that of Montreal.
Another point that has been dealt with this y ear perhaps oftener this year than in the past; it was discussed at length by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Hammell) and later, by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Robinson); both these gentlemen suggested that the government should allow a greater amount for the development of the tourist trade in Canada. Coming from a district which a great number of tourists visit each year and to which a great many persons come each year from other parts of Canada, from the States and from every country in the world, I feel that I should join those hon. members and ask the government to advertise more fredly so as to reveal the natural beauties of Charlevoix, Montmorency and Saguenay counties and more particularly the district of Murray Bay where the distinguished Speaker of the House of Commons, the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, spends the summer each year. Some years ago I urged upon the National Railways to carry on a more active campaign to boom this district. I hope that this year, with reduced deficits, the government will be free to vote a handsome amount for publicity work in favour of that district. Last year and in the preceding years, the question of amending the income tax act was referred to. That act, I believe, as it stands to-day, is responsible for a great deal of trouble and handicap for those who honestly and regularly pay their debt tc the country. As it stands, this act offers a way out to those who are anxious to avoid paying the tax. It might well be modified; the government could do away with a few troublesome clauses of the act and, by so doing, increase the amount collected heretofore. Mr. Speaker, to revert to what I said at the outset the Tories complain of the fact that
the expenses of the country were not reduced, that they were increased and that we do nothing to better the conditions that exist in this country in this respect. I have before me the budget for the year ending on the 31st of March, 1926, and I notice a decrease of $6,933,279.38 in the estimates for the year; last year brought also a reduction in the amount expended and so did the preceding year.
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart) speaking on this question last night, told us that the government always brought down large estimates, and supplementary estimates just as large. He was not telling the whole truth because the government have reduced expenditure as much as they could; they have kept down construction .and public works, and if any had to suffer, it is certainly the members of some rural districts which, in many cases, were obliged to wait until the following or another year, to Obtain what they had requested. Fortunately their electors, who are intelligent .and full of common sense, understood that the government, under the circumstances, could not do more. Therefore, the Tory party is very ill advised to preach a greater economy.
I was listening with pleasure, yesterday, to the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) telling us that he had a great admiration for our public employees, but that the civil service is too overcrowded at present. If the civil service is overcrowded, it is due to the fact that, under the Conservative government, from 1911 to 1921, the departments were packed as much as possible; and moreover, the government, in 1918, 1919 and 1920, seeing election time approaching, had a spurt of energy and brought from the United States certain representatives of the Griffinhagen & Young Co., whose services were retained at enormous fees. These persons were paid the sum of $510,747.83 to carry out the classification of the civil service. Result: when this government came to power, there were as many employees as before the arrival of these Americans, and the government was forced in the first and second year of its administration, to dismiss at least 4,000. In the amount which I just mentioned aibovq, spent for the classification of the civil service under the Tory regime, there is an amount of $162,475.26 which w.as spent for the reorganization ,of the staff of the National Printing Bureau, with the result that three or four hundred French Canadians were dismissed. That was about the only result obtained. The Tories wished to practise economy but only the kind we call penny wise and pound foolish. In fact, today, almost all the work, instead of being done
The Budget-Mr. Casgrain

at the Government Printing Bureau, is awarded outside by contract, and all the departments receive allocations to have the required printing done outside.
There is another subject, Sir, upon which I wish to draw your attention-although tihe thing may not be of any consequence-it is the campaign which the Conservative party have been waging for some time in the province of Quebec. If we criticize the Tories, if we put to the fore all we have to reproach them, and if we praise the government, we are taunted with being prejudiced and acting in a spirit of partisanship. The other day, while travelling to Montreal, I read with pleasure, in a newspaper, which I can call an independent paper Le Droit of Ottawa, an article which if jrou will allow me to read to the House, is as follows:
A Conservative campaign. Strange attitude-The Conservative policy during the war-The heritage bequeathed to the Liberals-Mr. Meighen, imperialist. Mr. RodoLphe Monty must have been inspired when he stated the other day: "We must not examine political questions from the viewpoint of parties, but from the national viewpoint." Himself and the other Conservative speakers unfortunately did not put this excellent advice into practice, when, last Sunday, they placed at the door of this present government all the wrongs, all the political blunders made by the governments -which have succeeded to one another for the last twenty-five years.
They behaved themselves like real partisans, warmed up by the approach of general elections, and wishing to sow among the people suspicion, prejudice, and blame capable of harming the political opponent.
The present government is not perfect. Nobody thinks dt is, not even those composing it. That it is open to criticism, there is nothing astonishing: otherwise it would not be human.
But what takes the wind out of our sails, is that it is the Conservatives who reproach the government for the unstability of the tariff, the treking of the Canadians towards the United States, the upholding of the British preference, the increase in taxation, the raising of our debt, the banishment of the French language, et cetera.
Let us distinguish between a public man who carries on constructive criticism, and the one who through envy or hatred, is always bent in destroying and refuses to give his opponent any merit.
It is always the privilege of one who has erred to acknowledge his mistake and try to make amends for it. But what are we to think of a person, having erred, trying to throw the blame on his neighbour's shoulders? That is of what the Conservative speakers were guilty last Sunday.
Conservatives must have a tremendous amount of cheek or their memory must be very poor to broach the subject of the national debt, the deficits of our railways, the extravagance in the administration of public funds. One should not make painful allusions.
The present government has to face problems of an economic, social and international order, almost without solution. If we take into consideration the political contingencies and the rooted practice of carrying on the government by opportunism and half measures, it is doing the best it can.
However, we must not forget that if we have a national debt which staggers us, it is due to the late government. They are the ones who forced
fMr. Casgrain.]
Canada into an excessive participation in the war, who nationalized the Canadian Northern system, who thus contracted obligations of which we shall never see the end. By coming into power, in 1921, the Liberals did not come into a very enviable heritage. The governments, for years to come, if they wish to balance their budgets, must seek a thousand expedients and expose themselves to criticism.
Instead of endeavouring to amend their blunders, the Conservatives aggravate them by rendering more difficult the task of the present government. They should, however, be the first to help them for the welfare of the country.
However, they will have much to do to blot out from the minds of the people, the remembrance of their participation in the war of 1914, with its consequences: Such as conscription, the national ill-feeling, the increase of our debt, the high cost of living, et cetera. Mr. Meighen's attitude, since the end of hostilities, and still recently, is not of a nature to lead us fro believe that the Conservatives, in the event of another war, would be more thoughtful of the Canadian interests.

Mr. Speaker, during the discussion on the bud-

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
get the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) made the statement that the manufacturers of logging equipment on the Pacific coast had not suffered to any considerable [DOT] extent as a result of the cuts in the tariff made last year. On that occasion he referred particularly to a firm known as the Vancouver Machinery Depot, Limited1. I find on inquiry that this is not a manufacturing firm but is rather a firm that is dealing in American machinery and in machinery from the Old Country; it is also agent for one eastern Canadian firm. It has nine agencies,
I understand, of which six are American firms, so that quite naturally under those conditions it is in favour of cuts in the tariff.
With regard to the effect of the tariff reductions in these particular commodities, let me say that early in 1924 tenders were called by the Victoria Lumber Company of Chemainus, on Vancouver island, one of the largest logging organizations in the whole Dominion. Bids were entered by Canadian firms, but when it was learned that the tariff reductions had been made on 5 p.m. April 11, 1924, the order was immediately placed with the Diamond Iron Works Company of Minneapolis, and the contract amounted to some-think like $200,000. I have here copy of a wire from the Metal Trades Employers section of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, dated at Vancouver, April 17, 1925, addressed to Hon. J. H. King, Minister of Public Works. It states:
Companies here actually engaged manufacture of logging and saw mill equipment strongly deprecate statements ascribed to you in local press recently as to the effect on industry of tariff reduction, more particularly as your remarks were based on information supplied to you by principal of firm here who are not and do not claim to be manufacturers and who do not even hold sales tax license but who are jobbers principally of Americal equipment, and whose interests naturally dictate the maintenance of the lowest possible tariff basis to facilitate their sale of imported equipment, irrespective of indisputable serious effect of low tariff in curtailing and discouraging efforts bona fide local manufacturers logging and saw mill equipment.
I have also a letter here from the Britannia Wire Rope Company, Limited of Vancouver, manufacturers of toire ropes, wire products and modern logging equipment, dated at Vancouver, April 14, 1925. It says:
Hugh Dalton, Esq.,
Secretary, Canadian Manufacturers Association,
Pender Street, Vancouver, B.C.
Dear Sir,-
As an indication of just how this juggling with the customs tariff by the Mackenize King administration at Ottawa is affecting young industries such as ours struggling to establish itself, the following figures may be of interest.
In our machine and blacksmith shop, whose work is devoted entirely to the logging industry, 31 men were employed in March 1924, at a monthly payroll of $3,046.73. In March 1925 it was the utmost we could do to find employment for 20 men, with a payroll totalling $1,700.32.
Comment is needless. These figures speak for themselves. If, however, there is any further informatior you desire, or any manner in which we may be oi service to you in bringing home just how much th< reduction in tariff is affecting the workers of the community, we shall be only too glad to have you call upoi us.
Yours very truly,
Britannia Wire Rope Co. Ltd.
T. S. Campbell,
General Manager.
No further comment is necessary, I think, under the circumstances.
