I just brought this to the attention of the House so that we might know the truth. That is all we want. We do not want any unfair advantage at all in connection with matters of this kind.
Now with regard to the budget, I am quite sure, Mr. Speaker, that after listening to the discussion of the budget for several weeks as we have done, we feel that after all people living in one part of Canada know very little about the particular conditions under which people live in other parts of Canada distant from where they are located. It ha3 brought to our attention from day to day the absolute necessity for us to know more about the general conditions of the country, so that when we come to discuss matters in this House we can look at them and take them up in more of a national way rather than in a provincial way. I do not know of anything that would be of greater benefit to us than to possess this knowledge and this viewpoint. Some few years ago I proposed dn some remarks I was making here that it would be to the great advantage of this country if, after
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

an election, the members were afforded an opportunity of moving from one end of the country to the other and meeting various organizations, chambers of commerce, boards of trade, and so forth, so as to familiarize themselves as much as possible with the conditions throughout Canada, and: then when gathering in this House they would be in a position to discuss the matters brought up here in a much more intelligent way than they are able to do at present.
If there is one other thing that is of great importance to this country, it is the creation of a national spirit, and the stimulation of a feeling of pride that we are Canadians and proud of our country, as we should be. I think we might certainly take a lesson in that respect from our neighbours to the south in the way they celebrate the fourth of July. If we could fill our Canadians with the same enthusiasm for the first of July that the Americans display on the fourth, so that they would celebrate it in the way in which it should be celebrated, I am sure we would be rendering a great service to this whole country. Somebody interjects "The twelfth of July." Well, that would be extra.
I think I am on perfectly safe ground when I call attention to the fact that we are in need of all the business increases that we can secure in this country. We should develop every possible line which will promise to bring us revenue, at the same time reducing our expenses to the greatest possible extent and practising economy within the country. I propose to-day to call attention to just a few points in connection, with which I think this might be profitably done.
On the 22nd of September, 1922, our American friends introduced what is known as the Fordney tariff. Up to that time the tariff on agricultural products coming into Canada from the United States, and the tariff on the other side of the line on Canadian products going into the United States were practically equal, with a very few exceptions. But when the Fordney tariff was introduced, we find that their tariff on the other side was raised very much, and there has been no compensating raising of the tariff on this side of the line, and this government has permitted those conditions to go on from year to year, bringing down budget after budget, without ever meeting the situation. I think if we want prosperity in this country, one of the first things that we might do would be to bring our tariff on agricultural products up to that of the United States. After all, the diversified farmer in this country is naturally a protectionist, with very few ex-

ceptions indeed. If he is not when he begins, he soon will be when he has met a little of the unfair competition I propose to call attention to to-day.
I was pleased with one phase of the budget, and that was the proposition to create a tariff board. No tariff should be administered in such a way as to enable any person, either a manufacturer or a farmer, to take unfair advantage of the protection afforded to him, and if this tariff board is carefully selected, if the personnel is such that, it will be able to function intelligently and without any political influence, then a real service will be given to the consumers of Canada, to the farmers, and also the manufacturers. After all, all that the farmer asks in connection with the administration of the tariff is absolute fair play, fair play and equalization of the tariff so that it is just as much a protection to him as it is to other parts of the country.
Taking the commodity of eggs, one that is common to all farms where diversified farming is carried' on, I would like to call attention, Mr. Speaker, to the unfair competition that the Canadian farmer suffers from in this direction. In the first place, there is a tariff of 8 cents a dozen on eggs produced in Canada going into the United States, while we charge only 3 cents a dozen on eggs coming the other way. I have been engaged in the poultry business as a side line on my farm out west, and I know a little bit about the cost of production of eggs under varying seasonal conditions. Now the unfair competition that the Canadian producer has to meet is simply this:	During the months of January.
February, and March, we import into this country immense quantities of eggs from the United States. At that very time our Canadian producers are under mid-winter conditions, requiring a better and more expensive poultry house in which to keep their poultry and protect them from the cold, richer and more expensive feeds to keep up the bodily heat, and in addition to that, anyone who has any experience in the poultry business will know that under these mid-winter conditions you do not receive nearly the production from the hens that you do-under early spring conditions. Now while our Canadian farmer is labouring along in the face of those obstacles and those high expenses, the American producer of eggs in the southern states, and particularly in California, is enjoying during these same months excellent spring conditions when the output is very much increased. As you all know, the greater the output per hen the less the cost per dozen eggs, so the American producer has a decided advantage

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
over his northern competitor. Advantage is taken of these conditions by our Canadian buyers who buy eggs to put in cold storage for the winter supply. Knowing they can secure these American eggs during these early months of the year, they are not particular to put into storage as large a quantity as they might otherwise do if they were faced with an 8-cent tariff, and the result is that when hens on this side are producing eggs in quantity and the eggs have reached a low price, these buyers come forward, secure these eggs and place them in storage, being careful and anxious only to have enough to carry them to that period when the American eggs will be coming in. In that way the local producer of eggs is handicapped. If he were protected with an 8-cent tariff, the local buyers would be careful to put in a much larger quantity, and this would have the effect of stiffening the price on the Canadian side.
Now, to show you the importance of this industry, let me say that in 1924 the value of Canadian egg products was 856,822,439, and of poultry products, including poultry meat, in the same year 8106,266,756; or in dozens the Canadian hen produces 238,648,685, while in the United States the production reached the huge quantity of 2,196,194,000 dozen. The Canadian consumption of eggs averages about 26 dozen per year per capita while in the United States the per capita consumption is only about 19.36 dozen. It will be seen from these figures how easy it is, under certain trade conditions, for the United States producer to flood this market. Now let us see what we import from the United States, and also what we export to that country. In 1923-24 we imported from the United States eggs to the value of $1,961,477, and in the same year we exported to that country only $49,458 worth. In 1922-23 we imported from the United States 82,494,650 worth, and we exported during the same year 898,181 worth, showing a very distinct and large balance in favour of the United States. The question that I should like to ask, Mr. Speaker, under these conditions is: Would it not be good sound sane business to increase our tariff to 8 cents a dozen, and to save and conserve for the Canadian producer the great amount of business I have just mentioned?
But the government, not satisfied with the competition met by our poultry producers from the United States, have also allowed them to be brought into competition at a very low tariff with our oriental friends on the other side of the Pacific. During the early months of the year we imported from oriental 162
points 3,500 cases of eggs. Of this number 2,500 cases graded as seconds, which is really the fourth grade of eggs in this country. One thousand of these cases could find no grade whatever; they were of such bad quality they were of no use to Canada and they were sent to New York. In this particular connection I beg to offer a resolution from the Surrey Farmers' Institute, a farmers' institute located on the Fraser river at Clover-dale, British Columbia, which resolution is signed by H. Bose, secretary. With the permission of the House I should like to place this resolution on Hansard.
Whereas there has developed, due to natural conditions, a large poultry industry in the lower part of British Columbia, to such an extent that a very important trade is being established with the prairie and eastern provinces of the Dominion.
And whereas this industry owned and controlled by small farmers is placed at a great disadvantage and being seriously handicapped by reason of the flooded importation of eggs into Canada from both the United States and China which uncontrolled by regulations completely demoralizes the markets.
And whereas the freight rate on grain for export is *22J cents, as against the domestic rate of ,41i cents, a difference of $3.80 a ton.
And whereas the duty on eggs imported into Canada is only three cents per dozen as against that of a duty of eight cents per dozen on eggs exported into the United States.
Now therefore we your petitioners humbly solicit the earnest consideration on the part of yourself and your department to the equalization of the duty, the marking of all foreign eggs with the name of the country of origin, and a uniform freight rate, believing that in so doing a more stable market will be maintained and the public best served.
Our Canadian producers also suffer in another direction, largely owing to climatic conditions. We import early vegetables into this country by the millions. This is a very important industry. Many of those engaged in it require considerable skill, and much hard work is necessary in connection with the business. The men who operate in this particular line are perhaps the most intelligent of those working on the land, and they need adequate protection. Owing to the fact that vegetables produced to the south come on the market so much earlier than Canadian early vegetables the demand for early vegetables has already been pretty well satisfied with the result that the Canadian producers do not reap the high prices they otherwise would secure. In addition to that they are met with the competition from mid-season districts after the first flush of the season is over, when the grower in the United States has obtained already his high prices and is bent on getting rid of his surplus stock. Towards the end of the season these cheaper products are brought into Canada and enter

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

United States and 80,000,000 in Australia, and hon. gentlemen will realize the position.
A great factor in stabilizing the sheep industry in this country would be the placing of the wool market on a good sound foundation. I think that would have a greater effect in stabilizing the sheep industry in Canada than anything else. We have at present a varying price for wool.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I desire to ask the hon.
gentleman simply for information; is it not my hon. friend's opinion that the greatest curse, and hindrance to sheep raising in this country, is the dog nuisance, which brings no revenue to anybody?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, we have dogs troubling us to a great extent out west, but out in my district we have learned to shoot with a forty-five calibre rifle, and we always keep a horse and rifle ready for use at any time, so that if a dog enters your premises he becomes the object of your attention. I may say that out in British Columbia the dog nuisance got so bad that a provincial law was passed allowing a farmer to shoot a dog which happened to be on his premises where sheep were kept, if the dog did not have an attendant with him. Many dogs disappeared after this law was passed, and nobody knew where they wTent. Out in British Columbia we have no objection to a man owning dogs and chasing sheep with them, providing he owns the sheep himself.
We also have trouble with the coyote and in the coyote section out on the prairies and British Columbia we have to care for our sheep under herded conditions. In the open country a man will herd two or three thousand sheep a day, but in British Columbia a man will only handle about a thousand sheep.
I have heard that people will not go into the sheep business on account of the coyote; but by making proper provision, putting up fences and taking other precautions you can protect your sheep against depredations of the coyote. The hon. gentleman has placed his finger on one of the chief dangers that we have to encounter out west. However, I have always thought that there was enough money in the sheep business to stand that loss.
We imported last year about 5,205,926 pounds of wool. We can practically produce now nearly all the kinds of wool that are necessary, with perhaps very few exceptions. However, we should make an attempt to produce at home the very kind we import at the present time.

On the prairies they are now producing the Rambouillet merino wool and they are producing a very much better quality than formerly. On May 27, 1923, when speaking on the budget I called attention to the fact that there was a fifteen per cent tariff on our statute books on combed wool, and that this had never yet been put into effect. I pointed out that year that we were in competition at that time with the bonused combed wool from Australia and from Japan, and nobody can ever hope to compete with the Chinese or Japanese successfully. In this particular instance, again the farmer has been permitted to hustle for himself, as he has in connection with the matter of eggs, and also in connection with early vegetables. I would strongly urge on the government that they put this provision into effect. I should like to put on Hansard a letter I have received from the Dominion Combing Mills, Limited, dealing with this very matter. The letter reads:
Dominion Combing Mills Limited Top Makers
Commission Merchants and Wool Brokers Toronto
April 23rd, 1925.
Hon. S. F. Tolmie,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir:-
1.	Are you aware of the fact that the action of the Department of Customs in not enforcing the Customs Act is equivalent to discrimination against our firm.
2.	Items 555 and 556 of Customs tariff are not being enforced.
3.	The Commissioner of Customs and his staff are aware of this and admit the facts.
4.	This duty was placed on the statute to encourage someone to establish a key industry.
5.	After investigating the matter and being assured there was a duty on wool tops, we established the finest combing mill in the world at Trenton, Ontario, capable of taking care of the entire requirements of all the worsted spinners in Canada.
6. Over 15,000 citizens of Canada are financially interested in the success of this company and all the wool growers in Canada, and numerous other industries, will profit by its success.
7. The failure of the government to enforce and collect the duty as called for, means a loss of over half a million dollars a year in revenue, on wool and wool tops, and a severe hardship to the shareholders in this company.
8.	The officials of the department claim that they cannot enforce this duty without instructions from the Finance Minister.
9.	As one of the law makers of this country, will you please call the attention of the Finance Minister of the unfairness to us in this matter, and use your best influence to have the law properly administered.
Yours sincerely,
A. E. Rea,
President.
The prospects for the production of sheep in the immediate future are very good. We

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
have assurances that there is a shortage of wool in the world at the present time amounting to about 395,000,000 pounds. Every effort should be made to improve the quality of our wool and also of our sheep and meat products. The best way to do this is by the distribution of pure bred sires, but we are met with the obstacle of the tremendous increase in our freight rates and you can understand a man not washing to buy one sheep for the purpose of improving his stock when it will cost him a considerable sum to have that animal shipped to him. He could afford to do that years ago, but now the freight charges render it almost impossible for him to obtain these sires.
I should like to urge as strongly as I can the advisability of co-operating with the provincial government and the Live Stock Associations clubbing together and buying in carload lots pure bred animals, so that they might be shipped to the nearest point for distribution, and sent to their destination either in automobiles or by express. I might suggest also that the distribution of new breeding stock might be carried on in the same way, and I am quite sure that in building up this industry we are working, on perfectly sound ground. I have no doubt that it will add greatly to the value of agriculture in Canada if we can get our people thoroughly interested in sheep.
With regard to the swine industry, the market at the present time can be said to be good, indeed, it is much better than it was a little while ago. And it is interesting to note that hog raising is coming into greater favour than it was a few years ago. When this industry was first introduced it met with a good deal of opposition simply because our farmers did not understand the situation and1 did not appreciate the absolute necessity for placing on the British market such animals as would secure for the producers of Canada the highest possible price. There is no use trying to fool the Englishman about what he will eat; he knows more about that than anybody else in the world. I listened with interest to the discussion that took place with regard to the estimates for live stock when they were under consideration, and it was pointed out that it would be a great favour to some of the producers of hogs in this country if we did not tie them down so closely to weights in the production of the Wiltshire sides which the British market requires. It was proposed that there should be a little latitude, that the farmers might be allowed an extra ten or fifteen pounds of weight in the hogs they raised. That would be all right for the producer but it would not produce the kind
of hog which the Britisher wants; and the price would be immediately cut down.
I think we should hurry up the hog industry; if one thing should be speeded in the whole live stock business it is this particular industry, if we are to secure a sound footing on the British market. If we want to get such a market we must increase the volume of our output. To-day the British market desires not only a steady but a uniform supply and of sufficient volume to keep it interested. Why is there need of haste at the present time? It is necessary for this reason. We find that Russia, a great grain producing country, has regained her feet and she will be in the market shortly looking for a place for her surplus products. Then we must remember that Poland has a hog population of eight to ten million; in that country there will be a production of some five million hogs every year which will be thrown upon the market. In comparison with this, we have altogether in Canada only about.
4,800,000	hogs. And Sweden is also aiming at a place in the British market. So that if we can increase the volume of our hog output and send the right sort of animal, and if by this means we can once get located firmly on the British market, there will be little chance of these other countries dislodging us. But we can only do this by means of education among our farmers and demonstrations that will show exactly what kind of hog is necessary.
I am glad the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is here, because when we were discussing the live stock estimates he was good enough to promise that some day he would have a demonstration carried out either at the experimental farm or at one of the packing houses to indicate exactly what a bacon hog was. That demonstration would show just what kind of animals should be produced and what the British market requires. This is an excellent opportunity for the minister to put that promise into effect. There are a number of men here who are making their living on farms, besides others who are interested generally in farming, and if such a demonstration were carried out there would be missionaries who would carry the information to the four corners of the country. I sincerely hope therefore that the minister will take advantage of the opportunity he has and will see that this is done some time before the close of the session.
There is no reason at all why we should not be in a position to beat our competitors in the British market, even such a competitor as Denmark. By strict attention to business
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

and a careful study of the types required in Great Britain Denmark farmers have been able to establish a market in the United Kingdom second to none. On the average they receive probably the highest prices the year round for their bacon. But we should be able to beat Denmark in this direction for the reason that to-day they are importing over sixty per cent of the grain necessary for the production of these hogs as well as for the production of butter, whereas in Canada we grow our own grain and ship our product in the more concentrated form of bacon and also in the shape of butter. If what I have said is of importance, I would suggest that if we are to speed up production we should take this opportunity of promoting, in the manner I have described in discussing the shipping question, the distribution of breeding stock so as to stimulate and increase the volume of our output at the earliest date.
I come now to the cattle situation. I am glad to note that there has been a steady increase in our exports to Great Britain particularly after thirty years of fighting, on the part of both Liberal and Conservative governments, for the removal of the cattle embargo. In 1922 our exports of cattle to Great Britain numbered 18,475 head; in 1923 it had increased to 56,672; and in 1924 we shipped overseas 79,435 head. In addition to this there has been a slight improvement in prices. A very interesting fact that has developed in connection with the beef industry of the world, and something that was quite unexpected a short time ago, I might here refer to. In 1921 prices dropped over fifty per cent and cattle were produced at a loss in Australia, New Zealand and South America owing to the low market in Great Britain. What caused the change? The surplus in 1924 has entirely disappeared and the outlook at the present time for the cattle producer is better than it has been for some time. It was so bad in the Argentine in 1922 that they destroyed on birth hundreds of thousands of calves; and besides this, the pastoral lands given over to the grazing of cattle have been ploughed up in many instances and now cereals are being produced. The continent of Europe, up until the war, consumed mostly pork; they imported more pork than anything else. Since the war, however, they have learned to eat beef, and fortunately they have learned to use frozen beef. This is all the more fortunate for those producers south of the equator. That the people of Europe are satisfied to take frozen beef is due to the fact that they boil or stew their meat, adding flavourings of various kinds that disguise the taste, so that they do

not notice the difference between frozen and fresh beef, as the Englishman discovered years ago. This trade in Europe has increased to an enormous extent; whereas in 1922 the people there consumed 113,240 tons of frozen beef, they bought 223,000 tons in 1923, and the consumption increased in 1924 to 459,000 tons. This meat has been used by France, Belgium, Spain, Italy, Holland, Czecho-Slovakia, Austria and Germany, and the trade appears to be on a fairly permament footing. This meat, finding another outlet, is not forced on the British market, and the result is that the Britisher will have to pay a slightly increased price for his meats, and 'Canada will benefit in consequence. The consumption of frozen beef on the continent has had an interesting effect on the United States, who are finding that so far as their pork shipments to that part of the world are concerned there has been a reduction of some fifty per cent. Now, our farmers can help themselves to a great extent in the beef industry. In fact I think they should always take the position-if I may be allowed to offer suggestions, having been in the ousiness all my life-they should take the position of helping themselves, of doing their best, under all conditions. While they can look for a certain amount of assistance from the government and from the live stock associations, after all what they do themselves is what actually counts. During certain periods of the year, particularly the months of October, November and December, if you take a trip out through that western prairie country, you will find trainloads of skinny cattle being shipped to market; they are only half fat and many of them are of very poor quality indeed. Improving the breed of our cattle has made very fair progress in past years until to-day it has reached the point-and I think the minister will agree with me-where it is more important to see that the animals are properly fed before they reach the market. The farmer can assist himself to a very great extent by properly fattening his cattle. There is another way whereby he can improve his position, and that is by avoiding crowding all his cattle on the market during the months I have mentioned; he should scatter them over the winter period and on into the spring. If he will do that he will be able to get better prices, wherever that is possible. I know that in certain sections intelligent farmers are buying these half-fat cattle, feeding them and selling them at a very fair profit.
Concerning immigration, which is linked up very closely not only with agriculture but also with our national prosperity, I quite agree with those members who have said it is nonsense

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
to bring settlers into this country on any large scale to compete with those who are already here unless we can assure them a good living. Immigrants, however, are not nearly so easy to secure as they were a few years ago. With our national debt of two and a half billion dollars, with only four people to the square mile, and with 22,000 miles of government owned railway on which there is an annual deficit of from 860,000,000 upwards, you will see how necessary it is that we should fill up our vacant spaces if we are to put our railways on a sound basis and be able to meet our obligations. There are two or three ways in which our railways might be placed on a paying basis. Perhaps one way, the least to be desired, would be for the Canadian National to compete with its great competitor, the Canadian Pacific, in such a way as to obtain from it a sufficient amount of business to attain a paying position. This would be very unfortunate indeed, because I think the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day deserves great credit for what it has accomplished. It is one of the greatest organizations of its kind in the whole world. If one of our great transcontinental systems were to profit at the expense of the other it would be very unfortunate for the whole country. The next way would be to settle our land, fill up the intervening spaces so as to get revenue for the railways from the land adjacent to their lines. This will be necessary even if a certain degree of amalgamation or working arrangement is brought about between the two lines. I am heartily in favour of some sort of agreement that will operate these railways at a lower cost and so reduce the deficit. I think it is a far better plan for us to sit down and try to work out a proposition of this kind than to continue year after year to pay railway deficits.
In connection with immigration, the prairies have received most attention in the past. To-day we hear complaints from various parts of the country, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific as to why immigrants do not come here now as they did before the war. In the first place, intending immigrants are met with heavy fare, very much greater than it used to be. At the present time to bring over a man and his wife and four children from some point in Europe to the prairie sections of this country costs at least $450. In addition to that, the immigrant would require at least $1,000 to make any kind of a start on a farm. If he has this money, whether he lives in the Old Country or on the continent of Europe, but particularly in the latter, he is in a position, under present conditions there, to be "somebody" and perhaps can do just as well at home as by emigrating. Canada can absorb an immense number of agricultural labourers and farmers, but we have reached the point where these men have not got the money to come, even if they desired to. It has been suggested by some that we should adopt the open door policy, that is, allow immigrants to come in unchecked. This in my opinion would be a very unfortunate policy. In the first place, we would fill up the country with a class of people whom we do not desire at all, and we would be seriously increasing our unemployment and adding to our bread line in the winter time, for many of such immigrants would soon become a public charge. Moreover, I think it is only fair to assume that we would simply become the back door to the United States for those immigrants who had enough ginger to move across the line if they were not satisfied to remain here. Now, we would like to secure Scandinavians. I have seen them do remarkably well in the western United States, particularly in the state of Washington, and also in western Canada, where I have an opportunity to observe them. They are hard workers, careful, and usually very thrifty. But Sweden, Norway and Denmark discourage emigration altogether, and do not permit the spreading of propaganda within their borders. The United States has been the source of our immigrants for a number of years, but conditions have changed there considerably, and during the last four years the western states particularly have been pretty well combed by our immigration agents without very great success. After the great boom during the war, when farming paid high prices and when the value of land went up to $150 and $200 an acre, there was the usual crash such as usually follows an experience of that kind, and over one hundred thousand farmers in the western states, particularly in those sections where the single-crop system of farming is carried on, drifted away to the cities. In addition there were a great number of bank failures. Now, many farmers in those sections who would like to come to this country are so heavily mortgaged that they cannot sell out and secure enough capital to move anywhere.
Therefore, under present conditions the British Isles offer the best field for the development of immigration. But even there we find that in many cases they are hard put to it after the war, and for lack of means cannot move out to this country to establish themselves. The British government, recognizing this fact, in 1921 passed legislation
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

speechtext:
The reports from the agricultural experiment stations situated in the provinces I have mentioned indicate that these lands are of a very fertile nature, and that they are quite capable of sustaining the thousands of farmers who wish to engage in diversified farming, being well adapted for dairying, for live stock raising, for poultry raising, and so forth, as well as being able to produce large amounts of fodder for carrying live stock through the winter season. I might point out that in addition to the fertile soil situated in these districts I have mentioned, there is an ample supply of water, plenty of rainfall so as to assure crops every year, ample timber for building fences, houses and bams, plenty of fish and game in many of these districts, and in addition there is an opportunity for the man *who is getting under way, and who possesses only a small capital, to engage in work in the various camps, lumber camps, tie camps, mining camps, fishing camps and so forth, so that part of the year he can put in on his farm and the balance of the time be earning a little ready money if he so desires.
Some one of you may perhaps shake your head at the proposition of a man going on to a bush farm in Canada at this time, but let me just point out that this great country was opened up by the pioneers who went on to the bush farms, and who cleared them up under much more adverse circumstances than are offered to the men who engage in that line of work at this time. In those days their markets were very limited indeed. They were also badly handicapped for transportation. They had1 no railways, and in many cases no roads, and sometimes the roads they had were of very poor quality, but in spite of all these handicaps, being men of spirit, they went on to these farms, raised large families, and they were the predecessors of

some of the most prominent business men in Canada at this time. In those days they disposed of their dressed pork in some eases at 2} cents a pound, eggs at 15 cents a dozen, and butter at a very low price, and they had to take most of it out in trade at the country stores, so they were entirely at the mercy of the storekeeper. The man taking up one of these farms to-day will be in a much more favourable position, inasmuch as his markets are very much better, his means of transportation much better, and in no way can his lot foe compared with that of the earlier settler to whom I have referred. Of course to engage in this line of work we would not want a class of farmer who would farm in the summer time and be a tourist in California during the winter. To begin with, he would have to be a man who would be willing to work, and in the second place the fact that he was the right kind of man and that he was engaged all the year round would keep him much better satisfied than it would the man who is only engaged for a portion of the year. This settlement is most important to the progress of this country, and it is particularly important in connection with placing our railway problem on a satisfactory basis. It is also important to the preservation of confederation, so as to link up the Atlantic with the prairies on the one hand .and the Pacific with the prairies on the other. This is a matter, as I have said, of great importance to this country. The federal government in my opinion should take very keen interest in it and by co-operation with the provincial governments and with the Old Country government-for	the latter are
anxious, as I pointed out to-day, to send settlers to this country-they should be able to accomplish a great deal of valuable work in this direction. When we have solved the problem of bringing the different sections of the country closer together under mutually satisfactory conditions, then we will have solved many of the other questions which we have under consideration at this time. I think in this connection the federal government might go to the extent of largely engaging in the financing of this colonization scheme, and money spent in that direction I think would be money very well spent.
Now, while I have said something about the importance of immigration to this country, let me touch on one other very important point, and that is the preservation of the young Canadians who are bom here. speechtext: I have no statistics at all for Quebec, I am sorry to say.
