speechtext:
Do you conclude that
there are none?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not come to any
conclusion on that point; the fact is I have none here. Now in this particular case Victoria is shown with 45.1, the lowest infantile mortality. That was in 1922, but in 1924 Victoria broke all the records in this particular connection by reducing her infantile mortality
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

to 31.1 per thousand. At the great Child Welfare Conference held in London last year there were no mortality figures, urban or rural, that came within twice this figure shown at Victoria. The point I wish to make plain to the House is, that this result has not been attained by chance. Victoria has a very live medical health officer and he has worked out a plan for an absolutely clean milk supply, or as nearly as possible. In 1922 the infantile' mortality in that city was 45.1. That was reduced to 44.1 in 1923, and in 1924 to 31.1. As a further proof of the quality of the milk supplied in that city let me say that in 1924 not a single infant death was due to digestive trouble. The medical health officer there has had the close co-operation of the Victorian Order of Nurses, an organization that is very well known for the excellent work that it does. Together they carried on a eompaign of education in the care of young babies. The Victorian Order of Nurses educates mothers on pre-natal care with the result that from
1,000	births the death rate of infants bom alive but incapable of sustaining life totalled 34.4 in 1922, 25.4 in 1923, and only 17.8 in 1924, indicating the great value of this work.
.Now I do not believe that the excellent showing made by British Columbia is the result of chance merely. Let me say in that particular province we have carried out tuberculin testing of dairy herds, and have insisted on good sanitation in the dairies for a very much longer period than any other province in the Dominion, with the result that many of the herds have been clear of tuberculosis for very many years. The record that Victoria has shown, however, is but another added attraction to a city that has already become famous for its wonderful climate, its purity of air, its general healthiness and natural beauty, all of which make it one of the most attractive cities in the world. What has been accomplished in the city of Victoria, and in the province of British Columbia, can be accomplished everywhere else. I should like to see the federal government give every possible assistance to this work, particularly to such organizations as the Victorian Order of Nurses, and especially to give assistance to the Minister of Agriculture in securing the needed money to carry on tuberculin testing in Canada so as to make our herds as clean as possible, because I believe there is nothing more important in this country than the saving of our young life.
In the early part of my remarks this afternoon I made the statement that if there was one thing Canada needed more than another it was business-that we should encourage

every possible source of revenue that we can. In this particular connection we have a very important business engaging our attention in this country, one that is growing very rapidly, one that last year was responsible for bringing $136,000,000 into Canada. I refer to the tourist traffic coming to the Dominion during the summer months. As I have said our income from that source in 1924 is estimated at $136,000,000 divided among the provinces as follows:
British Columbia	 $36,000,000
Alberta	 20,000,000
Saskatchewan and Manitoba	 10,000,000
Ontario	 30,000,000
Quebec	   30,000,000
Maritime provinces	 10,000,000
The. national parks are estimated to be responsible for an income of $21,000,000 while the cost for their administration was only
81,250,000.	It is estimated that tourists brought into southern California in 1924 no less than $148,000,000 of business. There is another very striking statement fmade by Californians, and it is to the effect that 75 per cent of the settlers and investors in that state first came to California as tourists, indicating that the tourist traffic is of the very greatest possible value as an advertising medium. In fact it may well be said that many of the tourists to-day will be settlers in the country in a short time. I may say in this connection that it helps to promote a very much better feeling between the two countries which lying side by side, have maintained peaceful relations for a hundred years, and improves our international relations. The federal government, perhaps noting the importance of this work and the magnitude to which it should grow within the next few years, might render I think a certain amount of assistance by advertising on a somewhat large scale at the seasons of the year best suited to attracting tourists to this country.
There is one other important thing the federal government can do, and that is to remove every possible impediment that confronts the tourist when he comes to this country. At the present time it is possible to climb into an automobile in this city and motor to Sault Ste. Marie, go into the United States and enter Canada again at Emerson, Manitoba. From there you can ride to Princeton, British Columbia in the western end of the Similkameen country, and there you can go into the United States and up to Blain, Washington and then back to British Columbia. The government of British Columbia at the present time is constructing a piece of highway over the Fraser canyon

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
and through the beautiful Hell canyon, one of the finest bits of scenery in British Columbia. When this road is completed, as it will be in a very short time, it will be possible to motor from Emerson, Manitoba, not only to Vancouver but further into the prairie country. Now the length of time allotted to an American tourist coming into the country at the present time is thirty days. He has to report out at the end of that time or secure an extension. If he is going to stay in the country longer he is supposed to put up a bond of $25. I have had several communications from the west in which the parties express a strong desire to have this period extended from one to three months, so as to permit the tourist to come in from the east, take time leisurely to cross the country and get out at the west coast, allowing plenty of time to do it. I would strongly urge this matter upon the attention of the government and I hope they will give it close attention.
There is another matter in which the federal government can render a little assistance to the city of Victoria particularly, and such assistance will be very much appreciated indeed. Outside of Victoria, at William Head, we have a quarantine station. Steamers from Australia, from New Zealand and from the Asiatic countries, come up from the straits of Juan de Fuca and report at quarantine before landing at Victoria. They remain there very often two or three hours, tourists have a chance to go ashore, the Victoria people are afforded the opportunity of meeting the tourists and everybody is happy. But occasionally when they land at the ocean docks at Victoria the immigration officers take such a long time to examine the passengers before permitting them to go ashore that perhaps darkness sets in, or the period of the stay of the steamer at that point is so largely taken up that it is not worth while for them to go ashore and look around. We would like the government to send their immigration officer with the pilot to William Head, where the pilot climbs on board the ship; so that the officer could begin his examination there, and when the ship ties up at the dock at Victoria the examination will be pretty well completed, the passengers will be permitted to go ashore at once, and the people of Victoria will have a little longer time to extend their hospitality.
Another subject on which I touch very briefly is this:	In 1873 two or three schooners
went out from Victoria into the north Pacific ocean to begin fishing for fur seal. This business grew at a very rapid rate until a few years later some fifty-nine vessels were
engaged in sealing, and some fifteen hundred people made their living in that occupation. This was an important business and was very profitable. I might point out that the seal rookeries in the Pacific ocean where the first seal breeds were located are confined to the islands off the coast of Russia, and Japan, and Prybiloff island in the Bering sea, the property of the United States. This point is very important. It simply means that the vessels coming out from Victoria at that time and carrying on their work for a number of years established the claim of the British Columbia people to the sealing industry, because we had no rookeries in our own territory. In 1886-87 the United States closed the Bering sea; Great Britain objected and claimed that it was part of the ocean. After a number of conferences and agreements following one after the other, at Paris, at Quebec and at one or two other places, the Canadian sealers, under the various regulations that were put in force at these different conferences, were practically regulated out of their business, with the result that for three years these vessels lay in Victoria harbour tied up, expecting that at some time in the near future	a settlement	of	the question
would be reached and they would be permitted to proceed with their business again.	During those three years when
the ships were tied up, four other Victoria sealers proceeded to sea, and broke all the laws and regulations which had been made, did not respect any treaty and carried on illegal sealing during that period. When the commission sat for the purpose of awarding proper damages to the men whose business had been taken away from them, they awarded damages to these four, law-breaking schooners, but did not give the others anything. That was their reward for enterprise.
In 1911 Great Britain, the United States, Japan and Russia entered into a treaty prohibiting sealing until 1926. Great Britain is to receive fifteen per cent of the value of the skins kept, and up to the present time their income from this source has amounted to $694,54S. When the treaty went into effect in 1911 it was estimated by Professor Elliot, an expert on sealing, that this should bring a revenue of $7,250,000. Either Professor Elliot was very much out in his calculation or something else went wrong. It is necessary to give twelve months' notice before the present treaty can be cancelled, and I have a resolution endorsed by the chamber of commerce of the city of Victoria, and also by the city council of Victoria, asking that
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

the necessary twelve months' notice be given for the cancellation of the treaty, so that the Victoria sealers may resume their business, and with the permission of the House I will place it on Hansard.
It is dated 6th April, 1925, and reads:
Whereas the Pelagic Sealing treaty expires next year;
And whereas, prior to the treaty, sealing, for fur-seal, was an important British Columbia industry, employing large numbers of white men and Indians, and adding materially to the prosperity of the Pacific coast, and it is desirable that the industry shall be renewed;
And further, it is desirable that any industry training and accustoming young men to a hardy, seafaring life shall be encouraged;
Therefore be it resolved that the board of directors of the Victoria chamber of commerce go on record as being opposed to the renewal of the Pelagic Sealing treaty, and that the Dominion government be communicated with and requested not to renew the said treaty; and also request that, in December next, written notice of such termination be served upon the other parties to the treaty, such notice, at the expiration of fourteen years, as provided by the treaty, being twelve months in advance of the expiry date;
And that a copy of this resolution, together with suitable communications requesting support, be forwarded to Victoria's representatives in both the House of Commons and in the Senate.
I sincerely hope that the government will give this resolution very careful consideration and endeavour to look into the matter very thoroughly from all angles. The people of Victoria will be very pleased if the government find in their favour and recommend the cancellation of the treaty.
While I have been speaking on constructive matters very largely since I commenced today, I desire to say that we are drifting along as far as defensive works are concerned. Out on the Pacific coast during the war we had an opportunity of realizing our defenceless position. At that time there was a very live German cruiser squadron cruising around the Pacific ocean, and we did not know at what time we might be attacked. If it had not been for the interference of the British, who secured the services of one of her allies to protect us, ws probably would have suffered severe damage at that time. Now everyone will acknowledge that, although the war is over, the world is certainly not in a very restful condition. We know that countries are arming on all sides. We have competition for trade, many international questions are arising that might cause an outbreak of war at any time, and I feel that it is very foolish to lull ourselves into a feeling of false security, or to follow the example of the ostrich, hide our heads in the sand and imagine we are safe. It is better to face the proposition squarely and devise some plan of whatever nature we may deem best and just.

and then to carry that plan to a successful conclusion.
In the matter of naval defence, it is quite apparent that the great powers are not satisfied that all danger of war is over. I have here a copy of a White paper issued in London on March 4 giving particulars regarding the number of vessels of certain types under the control of different countries; and the ships are very heavily armed. The following is a comparative table of these vessels:
British Empire.. .. United States.. ..
Japan	
France	
Italy	
Cruisers Destroyers Submarines
8	2	49	12	1511	36	599	23	285	26	20
I quote the following despatch:
The admiralty give details of the designs of many of the new foreign ships in the White paper, but discreetly suppress all details about our own vessels.
Thus we learn that there is a probability of the new Japanese cruisers of the Nachi class carrying the stupendous armament of twelve 8-inc.h guns. They will presumably be mounted in four turrets, and the broadside fire of such a cruiser would be 3,000 lbs.- five times as much as that of the pre-Washington cruisers.
The new French cruisers will have an armament of eight 8-inch guns, and the same number is allotted to the new Italian vessels.
This would indicate quite clearly that the great powers are not satisfied that all danger of war is over. Looking at our own condition, we find that we are practically helpless at the present time. We forget that the mere fact of our being disarmed will not save us from attack, and our losses in the event of attack would be simply tremendous. On the Pacific they would destroy our commerce and levy toll on our cities, perhaps destroying the coast cities; and they would ruin the coal mines of Vancouver island and destroy the dry docks and docking facilities generally as well as our elevators. And in the dry summer season they would set fire to hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of timber which could never be replaced. Altogether an attack would set back Canadian prosperity perhaps a hundred years, on the cpast at all events. Our defence provided at the present time to protect us against any possibility of attack consists of two destroyers and four trawlers. These are not considered naval ships anywhere in the world that I know of except ini Mexico, which country does not stand among -the first. These destroyers do not possess the necessary accommodation for training purposes so that training work cannot be carried on besmnd a day's voyage. The trawlers are slow little vessels steaming about nine knots

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
under favourable conditions and in good weather, and they are fortunate if they make four knots in a gale. I understand that they are unable to lower the boats in rough weather and they have no power to tow. And everyone who knows anything about the Pacific knows what the weather is like there in certain seasons. They are also inadequate for life saving purposes, and nothing but the best equipment should be used in this direction. In case of shipwreck with vessels of this kind a serious loss of life might result.
On the east coast the naval equipment is practically the same, except for the fact that they have an opportunity of training with the British navy at certain seasons of the year in the West Indies.
The personnel of the navy in my opinion is first rate in every respect, and most of the men during the war had an opportunity of serving in conjunction with the British navy. You can imagine therefore what their feelings must be, after having participated in the war, to be required to put up with the meagre equipment at hand. They are carrying on , from year to year in the hope that at some time some substantial improvement will be made in our naval establishment. They get no pension and no separation allowance, and I would call this fact to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Pictou) with a view to having these men placed on an equal footing with our other defensive forces. There is the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve and there is also the Royal Volunteer Reserve, both of which are doing well, the officers being interchangeable with the British navy under certain conditions. Now, in considering the naval question we should remember that it requires about four years to train a seaman or seaman-gunner and seven years to train an officer. So that time is a very vital factor. With regard to our defensive measures, that is simply a matter for experts. After talking about all sorts of things in relation to agriculture I would not risk for one moment any suggestion touching the question of naval defence, for I do not know anything about the subject. I wish however to present a resolution passed by the Air Force Club of British Columbia, and with the permission of the House I would place it on Hansard.
The resolution submitted reads:
Whereas in the consideration of Canada's general defence policy, and having in mind also the trend of modern warfare, some thought must be given to the question of countering the use of aircraft by an enemy;
And whereas an air arm of defence, capable of cooperating with the present or future land and sea defence forces of the Dominion, becomes a matter of
necessity;
And whereas financial considerations make the maintenance of an adequate and efficient permanent air force impossible;
Therefore be it resolved that the Department of National Defence of the Dominion of Canada be asked to give due consideration to the suggestions embodied hereinafter and to take appropriate action in the same connection:-
1.	That a Reserve Air Arm be formed to supplement the existing Royal Canadian Air Force.
2.	That the personnel of such a reserve be drawn from the membership of accredited air force clubs in each province.
3.	That the training of such personnel be done at the existing R.C.A.F. stations and under the supervision of officers of the R.C.A.F.
4.	That supplementary equipment be supplied to each R.C.A.F. station to make such training possible, due consideration being given to the physical requirements of each locality.
5.	That priority be given in the supply of facilities for training to the province of British Columbia in view of the fact that owing to climatic conditions training can be carried on at Jericho air station at Vancouver all the year round.
6.	That training be commenced at the earliest possible opportunity at the Jericho air station for members of the Air Force Club of British Columbia under the supervision as No. 3 provides, all active members of the before-mentioned club to be automatically enrolled on the Air Force Reserve (vide No. 1), and all such active members to be instructed or reinstructed, according as to whether they have flown before or not, and brought to a standard of efficiency to be decided on by the senior supervising officer or O.C. station.
It is submitted that by adopting the action outlined above the Dominion of Canada would be assured at all times of having at the least possible cost the maximum of trained air personnel, both available and in a state of efficiency that would make it a force of the greatest value, both when acting as a first line of defence, and also when co-operating with naval and military forces guarding the coast of British Columbia which lies nearest the most probable zone of warfare in which in the future Canada might be defensively engaged.
What is Japan doing? She has the third largest navy in the world, is very efficient, and is establishing several stations on the Pacific. And the United States is rapidly preparing for any emergency. She has provided for naval defence on three sides and for this purpose she requires a very large force. On the Atlantic coast she is strongly fortified, and she has fortifications on the Panama canal and along the southern section of the country. On the Pacific coast as well as on the Hawaiian and Philippine Mands she has also considerable fortifications. And she is establishing naval bases at all these places. In Alaska She has three military posts already and is talking of establishing a naval base at a place called Dutch Harbour, while at Puget Sound she has six powerful fortifications. In addition to that she has a strong naval base at Bremerton, where there is a 700 foot dry dock; and she is building works for the accommodation of the
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

whole north Pacific squadron. At the mouth of the Columbia river she has three strong forces and in California she has fortifications, naval training stations, marine barracks, naval air stations, army air stations, destroyer bases and huge storage capacity for oil, gasoline and lubricants. In Hawaii she has established very powerful forts and is building a strong naval station at Pearl Harbour, which is being fortified with sixteen-inch guns. In the Panama canal she is placing four sixteen-inch guns at each end and in addition to that she will maintain forty seaplanes besides other defensive works.
Apparently therefore the United States is not going to allow itself to be lulled to sleep by any peace conferences; and with the United States and Japan arming, we in Canada must wake up to the possibilities of the future. Canada is much more favourably situated than the United States from the standpoint of defence. In the first place, it would not be of any use for an army to attack us on the north, even on the Hudson bay. And on the north Atlantic, from Labrador to the north shore of the St. Lawrence, as far as Saguenay river, an attack would be futile. Our eastern strategic area would be Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Gaspe. On the Pacific we have a long coast line which, taking into consideration all the islands and indentations into the shore line, would cover some
10,000	miles. There are very few points along that coast where there would be access to railways or where there would be good roads, while parts of the country are so rough that it W'ould be altogether useless for a force to attempt to land. With our long narrow channels and our deep fiords running into the mainland, certain lines of defence could be very effective. The great question in the event of Japan and the United States engaging in war would be the necessity for our maintaining a position of complete neutrality. There would be an opportunity on the long coast line of the Pacific for one of the belligerents to establish a submarine base and we should be immediately involved in a complication unless we could preserve a strict neutrality. We would, it is true, expect the assistance of the British fleet, but the British fleet might take a considerable time to get under way, as it did in the last war, inasmuch as it must extend over the whole globe for the protection of British dominions wherever they exist. So that the delay might be serious if we did not have adequate defensive works to serve us in the meantime. A good, defensive equipment on the Pacific coast would, on account of the nature of the coast and of

the country there, cause any enemy to hesitate for some time before proceeding to attack us. Now, as I have already pointed out, the plans for our defence should be left entirely in the hands of experts, but I would suggest the following procedure under present conditions. We may be involved in war at any time, and in that event we would be absolutely helpless. No one realizes the necessity for economy more than I do, and I would not for one moment propose that we go ahead and build immediately any big defensive works; rather I would propose that we should have a carefully thought out plan of defence, and then decide on certain construction work and proceed gradually, adding a little every year, until we had completed a very effective defence. I would call this to the attention of the government, and particularly of the Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to briefly
express my views on the budget, and to do so in the French language. It has sometimes been a matter of reproach to French Canadian members that they do not make a more frequent use of their native tongue in the debates of the House of Commons. No one more than myself, Sir, wishes to uphold our claims in favour of the rights of the French language. Is it necessary for me to add that, when we express ourselves in another tongue than ours, we do not do so because it eases our task or we think that we can express ourselves more fluently in a language which is foreign to us. However, it may be necessary, in a brief debate, when views are exchanged in the course of the same sitting and the vote must be taken that very evening, it may become necessary, if we wish to acquaint the House with our views as to those very rights connected with the French tongue, to couch our remarks in a language which may be understood by those for whom they are intended.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is why the French
Canadians in this House, often take part in English, in the discussions, and furthermore, because they wish to maintain, in the Parliament of Canada, the influence of the province they represent. Far from rebuking them, I think they should be congratulated on the unavoidable effort they are forced to make to reach this aim. Nevertheless, I am fully aware that, if we go to extremes, there would be danger of not hearing often enough, in this parliament, the lovely accents of the French language; there are other discussions,

The Budget-Mr. Rinjret
such as those that are protracted, when it is, on the contrary desirable that the French language should be heard. I, therefore, think that the discussion on the budget, or the one in answer to the Speech from the Throne are occasions when one may do so without any inconvenience. Quite a number of my colleagues, before I rose, took advantage of this privilege in the course of the present debate, and it is a pleasure for tne to follow suit.
There is, at present, a committee appointed to revise the rules and regulations of the House, and through the partly opened door, we have already heard the rumour that one of the reforms will tend to limit the speeches of members to half an hour. It is my intention, Sir, even before this new regulation is submitted to the House or is adopted, to apply it to myself, and I shall endeavour to express myself as briefly as possible.
I wish, first, to express my astonishment that, in the course of this debate, so little was mentioned about the tariff. In listening to the members of the opposition last year, and even sometimes when they are delivering speeches before the public of this country, the most important question, was that of the tariff. Yet, we 'have heard quite a number of members from the opposite side, we have equally looked into the empty and distressed amendment of the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and we have noticed that no mention whatever is made of the tariff. I am anxious to hear the leader of the opposition to see if he will not take his cue from his lieutenants on this question or whether they only obeyed formal orders from him. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) will fall back, no doubt, on his contention that he has placed on the order paper of the House, a motion which outlines and explains his policy on protection. He has already, on more than one occasion, made use of this subterfuge to avoid being dragged on these grounds by questions or other means. I am inclined to think, Sir, that when the leader of the opposition placed this motion on the order paper at the beginning of the session, it was not with the idea of discussing it, but rather to give himself a pretext not to do so when, as in the present circumstances, he would be called upon to state definitely, both his views and those of his followers, on the budget.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And why? Why did he,
through the intermediary of his lieutenant, move an amendment in which are not included his views on the tariff? He wished to drag behind him,-which is an easy task- the very small phalanx of those who support him in the House; however, he also wished to transmit a message devoid of a tariff proposal to a whole group of agrarian members holding entirely different views from his own, on this question, but who on other grounds may disagree with the government.
The Conservative party last year had forecasted that the King government would entirely demolish the tariff walls. In the city of Montreal, Sirr, they published beforehand the photographs of the factories which, it was said, would close their doors in the course of the year. This year, the opposition is very much disappointed to notice that in the present budget, the government not only does not lower the tariff, as it had been foreseen, but that on certain items the changes are upwards. And, in my opinion, this is an excellent policy, a policy of good common sense. Tariff, to my viewpoint, must not be a question of fast rule. It always amuses me, I wish to be frank, to hear certain members in the House for whom there is but one rule to follow in tariff matters: if you lower the tariff, it is an excellent policy, if you increase the tariff, it is a bad policy. While you have others who, obeying the same impulse, but in an opposite way, take absolutely the same attitude in favour of what they call protectionism. I would further add that the tariff should not be based on local consideration. Very often a member who proclaims himself moderate in tariff matters takes the following attitude: He demands protection for the industries which are in his county, although he is perfectly willing to open the doors for those which happen to be in the neighbouring counties. I do not agree that we should look at the tariff in that light. I think, on the contrary, that tariff is above all a business question, an adjustment to be established among the various interests of the country. The present government was quite justified, last year, in lowering the tariff on farming implements, as it wished by this measure to help the farming class which needed it, and events have shown that this lowering of the tariff has given excellent results.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, I equally state that the present government is quite right, this year, when they increase the tariff on coal; for, in so doing, it adjusts a situation which was extremely complicated and greatly
The Budget-Mr. Rinjret

to the disadvantage of our Canadian coal producers. Once more has the government proved its wisdom.
For my part, I would approve with pleasure a budget introducing, on the one hand, reduction in tariff, where they can be useful to certain classes; however, on the other hand, raising the duties where they are necessary. In other words, I would support a tariff policy which, leaving aside fast rules and theory, only acknowledges the practical interests of the country.
While on the subject, I would like to point out: That a certain group has been led to believe that the -word protection was identical with that of high tariff. I maintain that the only way of protecting industries is not necessarily to raise the tariff. For instance, last year, by decreasing the tariff on the raw material which enters into the manufacture of farm implements, the government was protecting, on the one hand, these industries, in the proportion that it had, on the other hand, exposed them to foreign competition.
The industries of this country are at various stages of industrial development. It has happened to me, in the course of a session of parliament, to receive representations on the part of two industries requesting, as means of protection, measures which were the very counterpart of one another. And why? The former manufacturer, who was located in the county of my good friend from Rouville (Mr. Morin), turned out a finished product; and what he wanted, was a high tariff on the finished article. On the other hand, the other manufacturer received from foreign countries a product which he but finished, therefore, his interest was that we should allow this half finished product to enter free, while the manufacturer who produced the same article wanted it protected by a duty. You cannot, under one tariff, afford equal protection to all industries; if you admit the raw materials free of duty you protect certain industries more effectively than with a uniformly high tariff wall.
Another way you can help industry indirectly is by increasing exports, by obtaining .tariff concessions in the way of decreased duties on our products entering foreign countries. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is undeniably wrong to confuse the term " protection" with the term "high tariff," since quite frequently the effects of the one and of the other are conflicting.
As to the British preference I think we might with advantage study this question. .Were I to find fault, it would be to say that the British preference is too restricted. Just

as I balk at a doctrinaire tariff so with the British preference I would have preferred that instead of being on a straight level it had left some margin for readjustments, had retained some elasticity. I believe it is time to ascertain right now if there be not certain products on which the British preference should be curtailed or done away with entirely. Moreover I would like to see a certain measure of reciprocity granted Canada by England. However, I have read with interest in the newspapers that the present Imperial government in its budget, will restore the famous McKenna duties. Once that is done the 'home government may be in a position to grant us certain favours over foreign products.
I would like now, Sir, to say a word concerning our transportation problems, which are many and varied. This year the government will attempt, through the medium of a subsidized company, to control ocean rates. The question has been referred to a special committee. Those who have followed the proceedings before this committee realize how very complicated the problem is; and for my part I shall certainly have nothing to say on the matter until the committee has finished its work. But I might request the Conservative organs to do as much; while the parliamentary committee is compiling the testimony of those who are best acquainted with the subject, I cannot be expected to evince mudh interest in the forecast of these Conservative organs which have already decided that the evil is non-existent or that the government's plans are worthless. We shall be at leisure to judge matters when we are fully apprised of the whole situation.
The House will be called upon also to make a very important decision with regard to freight rates established under the Crows-nest pass agreement. I shall not go into the history of this agreement which is well known to you, Mr. Speaker. You are well aware, too, how matters stand. At the present time the rates laid down by this agreement are in force, since the suspension was lifted. The case was taken before the Supreme court. The court held that the act creating the Board of Railway Commissioners did not give the board jurisdiction in the matter at hand. The House will have to decide whether or not we should extend this jurisdiction to the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is quite evident that we will have to study this question ini the light of the needs of every district in the country; and on this point, as on the tariff, I am willing to concede that our attitude should not favour one part of the country to the detriment of another. But it

The Budget-Mr. Rin/ret
in a flagrant contradiction that while we give the railway board the authority to fix rates on our Canadian railroads, the board's hands should be tied with respect to one part of the country. It appears to my mind impossible for the board to devise a harmonious schedule of rates for the whole country if, at the very start, jurisdiction is denied it over certain commodities and certain districts. We are desirous of protecting the interests of the whole country; but I trust that the government, with the support of this parliament, will bring down a bill granting the needed authority to the railway board which is essential to its efficiency.
Another transportation problem with which we have to deal every year is that concerned with the government merchant marine. During the last campaign we were very severe on the preceding administration for having built these ships and saddled a tremendous debt and an annual deficit on the taxpayers of this country. I admit in all frankness, Mr. Speaker, that personally I have more sympathy for the present government than for the marine bequeathed to it and I wish that circumstances would reveal some manner of getting rid of this problem. I realize that any definite advice would be premature. We are told that some of these ships co-operate with our National railways; and if the Petersen contract becomes a reality it is possible that some of them may be added to that fleet, although very grave doubts exist on that score.
At any rate, I must congratulate the government for having offered some of those ships for sale and even if there has not been any satisfactory bidders so far to relieve us of part of that burden, I would certainly be ill-advised to reproach them with maintaining inevitably the balance of that fleet.
But there is something far more important than the government merchant marine: I mean the government owned railways, and on that question I wish to express myself very definitely. Nobody will deny that the fair trial which has been made of public ownership has brought about some improvements, unquestionable improvements in our railway service. Everybody will admit it. But the result is quite different as regards the financial improvements of these roads, for as you study that problem, and ae you go through the public accounts you will find at every page of the public ledgers more items than ever relating to the National Railways which show that the deficit and the obligations are still greater than most people would imagine. We took no exception to a fair trial being made- of public ownership, but 163
I think that such trial, if it is to be fair towards the railways must also be fair towards the taxpayers who have to bear the cost. We can already foresee the day when we shall be bound to realize that the experiment cannot be carried on forever.
The other day, when I was present at the committee inquiring into the estimates of the National Railways, I was greatly impressed by two formal statements of Sir Henry Thornton. First, he said that there was not enough traffic in Canada to support two competing roads such as we have at present .and he added that owing to the progress of the motor cars which are now carrying not only passengers but freight, the 'loss thereby sustained by the railways was greater than the gains they were able to make elsewhere. The president of the National Railways further stated that, in his opinion, if the two roads were merged into one system, he thought their profits would be sufficient to pay the interest on all fixed charges. We must face the actual facts. The losses are not operating losses, for we are told that there are profits from that source. It is due to the tremendous amount of interest which we have to pay on obligations and fixed' charges. That is why, if we have done wrong in building or in giving grants for the building of too many roads at a time when nobody could expect that the war would revolutionize our financial system, it was also a mistake, in my opinion, and perhaps a greater mistake to take over these railways, especially so because the government, when they bought the roads, assumed all their obligations, whereas it certainly would have been possible, had they proceeded otherwise, to assume only part of these obligations. Whereas no private concern in the world would have taken over the Canadian Northern or even the Grand Trunk and assumed at the same time the whole of their obligations, the government of the day, that is the government preceding the present administration, bought the roads and said: All these obligations, all these guarantees, all these debts, we are ready to assume and endorse and we will pay each year the interest on these charges. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, when people talk about changing the train schedule and doing away with so many trains on such or such a line, I think that is merely adding a drop of water or rather taking it from the ocean. Naturally, under such conditions, any saving, how small it may be, would be welcome; but is it not evident, at first sight, that it is not the way to secure for the railways not even profits, but a lesser deficit than that which we have at present.

The Budget-Mr. Rinjret

The fixed charges will always exist and we shall always have to meet them. But, Sir Henry Thornton says, if the two railways were merged, leaving only one system, the returns to be derived therefrom could balance the interest charges to be met and then we might be able to make both ends meet. I admit that there, are considerable objections on both sides. If the government or the National Railways are to take over all the railways of this country, it means that we shall go deeper into public-ownership and you know, Mr. Speaker, that it has not been a success anywhere in the world. So far as I am concerned, I would be very sorry, notwithstanding the stand taken 'by some hon. members from this side of the House, to see the government aggravating our situation in that direction. On the other side, if the railways are; absorbed by the great private company operating it at present, I very well see the danger of a monopoly. The fault rests with the topography itself of our country, trade moves from east to west and vice-versa. Perhaps the fault also rests in the way we proceeded, not only in the last twenty years, but since the inception of railway construction in Canada. How different is the American system. There exists in the United States a great number of railway companies. Each state has its own. There exists no transcontinental railway. We do not find in that country this rivalry to extend from ocean to ocean which drove, first, the Canadian Pacific Railway, then, the Grand Trunk Railway and finally the Canadian Northern to build from the eastern centres as far as the Pacific coast. Moreover, the United States forming a perfect quadrangle, the movement of trade spreads in all directions. It is clear that the railway situation is far better and easier than ours.
Therefore, Sir, in view of this intricate situation and the drawbacks which I fully perceive, I am disinclined to definitely come to a conclusion. However, I think that we should, at least make provision for the time when we shall have to put an end to the present situation, when the trial, as fair as it may be, will end by weighing too heavily on the shoulders of the taxpayers; and consider a project of merger. It will, however, be necessary that, by this merger, the government that is the country, should secure reasonable conditions in regard to financial readjustment of those obligations which run up our public debt, and that the new service obtained, be placed under the complete control of the railway commission, so as to guard against the danger of monopoly.

Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the government on the fair and just way in which it has undertaken, since it is in power, to re-establish the proportion which is due to the French-Canadian element in regard to the various positions of this country. And if I do so-it is always a delicate matter to talk upon a question which gives rise so easily to prejudice- if I do so, it is precisely because we have been challenged by the opposition on this question. A very satisfactory answer has been given, by enumerating a great number of positions which have been allotted to our people, or which, in certain cases, have been for the first time, as for instance in the case of the Auditor General, allotted to a French-Canadian.
It is, I repeat it, a very delicate question. We only claim our fair share. Never would the thought enter our head to precipitate a conflict on this question. The Liberal party, on the contrary, has always been a party of moderation and conciliation; it has always been challenged right and left precisely on such questions. However, it would be very unfair not to recognize that, from the bottom to the top of the ladder, the present government has done enormously to re-establish in the realm of influence the share which belonged to the French Canadians of this country.
I might also, myself, recall the splendid way in which we were represented both overseas and in Washington, by FrenclwCanadian ministers. And, were it not that I see two, who do me the honour of listening, at this moment, and were it not for the fear of wounding their modesty, I would dilate at greater length on the subject. There are others. Never, perhaps, at any time in our history, have we been given, in foreign representation, the recognition granted to us by the present government. The same may be said of appointments to the bench, of our share of influence in the government itself, of the important appointments in the civil service: I recall that at one of the first sessions of this parliament, I strongly advocated that the Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) should appoint a French-Canadian deputy minister in his department. The leader of the opposition, who was sitting on the opposite benches, rose then, and, in the satirical tone, which is particular to him, prophesied that we would never obtain such a favour. Nevertheless, a few months later a French Canadian was appointed Assistant Postmaster General. On other occasions, a more favourable proportion, for our people.

The Budget-Mr. Leuris
was re-established. Everything cannot be accomplished in a day; and I would be the first to ask, that in the assertion of our claims, we do not go so far as to precipitate a regrettable conflict or revolution. We lost so much ground under the preceding government that it was impossible to hope that within a few months equilibrium would be restored. However, what astonishes me, to-day, is that, while we are discreetly endeavouring to obtain favours or our rights, which are generously granted to us, it is the representatives of the party who infallibly refused them to us, that rise in their seats to loudly claim justice. And they are the ones who are held up among certain groups as the saviours of our race.
I wish to point out the fact that in many cases, of equal competence, preference was given to French Canadians, because it was deemed proper to restore our fair proportion. We did not even consider the political affiliations of the candidate to whom we granted a promotion, if in obtaining it that could better the situation of our people. I could understand, perhaps, that certain Liberals carried away by their zeal made us a slight reproach on the subject; I could still understand that in certain cases an English speaking member would rise to ask for explanations on some appointments; however, what I cannot understand, is that it is precisely those of the political group who maintain that they have no other aim than to seek the interest of French Canadians, that they are precisely those who reproach us when we obtain favours of that nature. Fortunately, however, the people are not to be deceived. We witnessed in 1910 and 1911 such a campaign. It was equally said, at the time, that the Liberal government were not fair to our people. A number of our people were deceived1, they voted for certain members who were to save our race, and we well know that when they reached this House they did not even save their skin. The Quebec people know where to find their friends. When I say that I am astonished at this campaign, it is but my first impression; no, I am not astonished. Ever since they have come into existence, since that memorable time when, in 1909, that party came to life in broad daylight, they have always taken that attitude towards us. They have never placed any faith in the Liberal party and neither have the}'' ever acknowledged what we have done for our people; they have never ceased criticizing. Whenever we obtain a favour, instead of congratulating us as we deserve, they hasten to point out some other thing upon which, it seems, we have gone wrong;
163i
and far from registering the successive stages of our conquests, they only create difficulties and throw obstacles in our way which very often prevent us from obtaining more. I stated, Sir, at the outset that I would remain within the half hour limit; I hope that I have not gone beyond the time stipulated and that I have complied beforehand with the excellent new regulation that your committee will submit to the House in the course of this session.
Were I to sum up my views, I would first state that I am in favour neither of free trade nor protection, but of a tariff committed to no fixed rule or sentiment, or that is inspired by the true interests of the country. And as to our railways, without going deeply into such an important and intricate question, I state that the time has come to study carefully a merger scheme which would lighten the burden of state ownership; providing that this merger scheme be of a nature to free us from our public debt, of part if not from the whole of the obligations which these railways impose on us; and that we can place the new service under the perfect control of a commission which will see to it that the interests of the taxpayers are fully protected.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my only reason for rising to take part in this debate is to deal with the financial situation of Canada as I see it. But before dealing with the financial statement, I should like to make a few remarks with regard to certain questions that have been raised and brought to my notice during the past few days.
A few days ago I read in the newspapers that a certain gentleman from western Canada had suggested a scheme that would relieve us of a great many of our difficulties and possibly solve our financial problems. I read the brief report of his remarks and afterwards received the full account of what he said. I thought at first he had some new scheme to offer that would afford a remedy for our present difficulties, but after going into it very thoroughly, I find there is very little in it that is new; it is simply the old National Policy intensified and carried to the "nth" degree. I have reference, of course, to the Patterson scheme for Canada. I will first synopsize it and then briefly criticize it. It proposes a protective tariff "high enough to guarantee that goods will be made in Canada." Well, there is not very much new about that. Then, protection for the consumer by ' regulating the price of goods made in Canada. There may be something new in that
The Budget-Mr. Lems

if it is possible to accomplish it. Then, limiting the import of goods to the extent of eighty per cent of their present figure. Now, in attempting to carry out this scheme, the first premise would be fairly easy; and I can readily understand that such a premise would appeal to those whose slogan is, "buy goods made in Canada." It would be easy enough if the right party got into power to make the tariff high enough to guarantee that commodities would be made in Canada. The second premise is a little more difficult; the control of commodity prices when you shut off competition is admittedly difficult. It would be possible to place on the statute book a law to provide that the present prices of any commodities protected by the new legislation should not be exceeded, but who is to say whether the price is justified or not, and who is to enforce the law everywhere in Canada? When you attempt any artificial restriction with or interference in commerce, in nine cases out of ten the consumer suffers. To stop eighty per cent of the present imports into Canada could also be arranged if the tariff was high enough, but what would be the result? At present we sell over
200,000,000 bushels of wheat in the European market, Great Britain being our largest buyer; and we also ship bacon, eggs, cattle, butter, fruit, flour, and so forth, in large quantities to those markets. How will these people pay for the commodities we ship to them in such large quantities if they are prevented from selling to us? It is beyond my comprehension. Even if it were possible for them to pay in gold, what about the return cargo?' How long would the shipowners continue to carry our cargoes at the present prices-and there are many in this House who think the prices are already too high-if the ships had to come back empty? It could not be done. The scheme is absurd, fantastic; the child of a disordered brain; a scheme the results of which would make the present confusion appear as law and order. If we hope to sell in a foreign market we must reciprocate by buying in that market, otherwise the consumer and the primary producer will ultimately suffer.
I know there is a 'great demand in Canada for lower taxation. I have spoken to ministers, to bankers, to business men, to boards of trade and to hundreds of farmers in the west, and they are all very anxious that the government should show some signs of tackling the problem and of instituting some scheme that will ultimately bring about a reduction of our national debt. Yet we are' forced to the conclusion that we must raise

a larger revenue. I have studied the question very carefully and I believe that if the government will get down to real business it can be done. We have to make a start and we should give the people a lead and encourage them. The people of Canada are very much depressed and I know it is difficult to remove that depression. But your difficulties and problems are not solved by putting your hands down to your side; by inactivity; by submission to the powers that be. On the contrary, they can only be solved if we courageously shoulder our burdens and give the people a square deal, and that can only be done by taxing those who enjoy special privileges that are not enjoyed by the masses.
Before passing to the financial question, I would like to congratulate the member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) on his contribution to this debate, and especially his contribution to agriculture. It was full of pregnant suggestions, and there is not a doubt in my mind that if many of them were carried out, the agricultural communities in Canada would be greatly assisted. But we are too often fed up with suggestions. We realize that many of our own men are practical farmers, experienced in every detail of their work and yet under these conditions they are not able to make their farms pay.
The other day there was placed in my hand a paper with reference to Canada's competitors in the various markets of the world. I do not think that our farmers need very much advice on how to farm or as to what system of farming they should cultivate, but what I do believe is this, that the government and the powers that be should assist or at least attempt to provide adequate markets for the great production of our farmers at the present time. Here is one suggestion that I want to make, and it is in regard to butter. Three years ago I was in Moose Jaw at the time of the by-election, and when I returned to the House I made the statement that eggs and butter were selling at a certain price, and a friend of mine diametrically opposite read a certain passage out of the Moose Jaw Times of the same date evidently contradicting what I bad said. I was new to the House at the time or he would not have got away with it; he would not get away with it to-day. I want to point out that at that particular time he was quoting from an editorial, and that editorial was copied from an editorial that had appeared somewhere down in Fort William, so it had absolutely no reference whatever to the situation. Let

The Budget-Mr. Lewis
me read this in regard to Canada's competitors:
Let us look at the possibilities of the British market, as it is the only stead}' market in the world and should be catered to by the Canadian people, as is being done by numerous other countries. It might be interesting at this point to know something of the amount of butter imported by the United Kingdom. We find that the figures for the year 1924 are 592,789,232 pounds. Again, let us look where this butter comes from. We find Denmark at the head of the list with exports of 194.226,032 pounds, or 32.8 per cent of the whole import of Britain. Next in volume is New Zealand with 121,706,704 pounds or 20.5 of the whole. Following in line comes Australia with 70,567,616 pounds.
That is Australia, farther away from the British market than, we are, but it has 11.9 per cent of the whole import.
Next in order is Argentine with 60,340,448 pounds, or 10.2 per cent. Next in order the Irish Free State with 51,666,832 pounds or 8.7 of the whole. Next comes the little land of Finland with 15,071,168 pounds, or 2.5 of the whole. Next is Canada with 14,713,888 pounds, or about 2.5 of the whole.
I shall not go further down the list. There are a few other countries with an even lower amount. What I wish to suggest is this: Here is an opportunity for the Department of Agriculture, the pools and the co-operative societies to get together to see if it is not possible that we in western Canada shall have part of this market for our dairy products. In the recess while I was at home, butter was selling at 20 cents a pound. There is very little money in it at that, and all the local dealers could get for it if they sent it to the city of Moose Jaw was 17 cents. New laid eggs were selling at 15 cents per dozen. Now there is very little use in advocating diversified farming in western Canada because the local market is already glutted, and unless we get some co-operative marketing system, and a definite understanding of what is required for the British trade, it is not much use continuing as we are doing. The British trade, as I have already said, offers a steady market, and I believe it is worth our while to cultivate it. Prom the figures I have read you can readily see that we are only touching the very fringe of it. A dairy commissioner from New Zealand, who wa3 on his way back home from Great Britain via Canada, and whom I met in Central Butte told me that as a result of his year's work the average price in the British market of New Zealand butter was nearly 50 cents or Is. ll^d. per pound.
I do not know what it will cost to take butter from western Canada to Great Britain. I know it costs 3 cents a pound to get it to Montreal. It may cost another 3 cents to take it overseas, and with commission charges
of 4 cents, there would still be a margin left to the western dairy farmer of 40 cents a pound, double the amount that he is getting at the present time. But to capture the British market we shall have to have a uniform standard of quality and also be in a position, I understand, to guarantee a regular supply to that market. It is well worth while, and if ou authorities, provincial and federal, and our co-operative societies would get together in an attempt to get a fair share of the trade of the British people it would solve one of our dairying difficulties at the present time.
Attention has already been called to the proposed extension of the stamp tax to be applied to cream cheques. It has been, mentioned by many of our western members, and I have received letter after letter from various companies in the west and numerous letters from many of the dairy farmers. In view of the reports made by the western members, I think the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), when he makes his reply, should announce to the House that this tax will apply only to cream cheques over $10. As has already been explained, many of these cream cheques are only for $5, and some of them for less. Without stressing any further importance of this infant industry of the west, I would point out that the minister has already many examples of such exemptions on the statute book at the present time. Por instance, cheques over a certain sum, over $2,500, are tax free, even though the cheques may run up into the millions. It is true that a tax is paid up to a definite figure, but once that figure is reached the balance is untaxed. Now if the Acting Minister of Finance listened to the pleading of his wealthy friends or the capitalists, because that tax was changed to meet their wishes, surely it is just as reasonable for him to accede to the wishes of the struggling mass of primary producers. Another example is the tax on automobiles. On automobiles under $1,200 the excise tax is 5 per cent, and on cars over that amount, 10 per cent. This is eminently fair, as we feel that those who can afford to buy a better and a dearer car can afford to pay a higher tax. We also exempt from the income tax incomes less than $2,000. Here we have three specific instances of tax relief or total exemption under certain sums, and I feel that the Acting Minister of Finance would be only following these precedents if he eliminated from the proposed new tax all such methods of payment in the case of sums under $10. speechtext: Referring to the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, I would remind my hon. friend that there is a difference in the figures, because the calendar year and the fiscal year are not the same.

speechtext:
I understand that. I have taken the net deficits and not the loans-just simply the deficit of the railway. The further figures are as follows:
Debt of Dominion, consolidated 1925.. $2,431,487,113 Loans from Dominion government to
Canadian Northern Railway	 560,397,957
Interest accrued 1925	 31,271,043
Total	*3,023,156,113
We have also backed the Canadian National Railways with respect to their bonds sold to the public to the extent of:
Bonds 1925	*913,913,082
Interest 1925	 38,361,704
Total	*952,274,786
The Budget-Mr. Lems

If we add this to the public debt we have an indebtedness of $3,975,540,899, which means a per capita debt of approximately $441.70. Besides all this the Dominion government have made appropriations in cash to the Canadian National Railways amounting to $451,712,484.98. The total assets on which this company is called upon to earn a profit amount to $2,074,255,348 while the Canadian Pacific Railway including its steamship service has assets of only $1,113,756,696.56, or approximately one-half. How can we really expect the management of the Canadian National Railways to make the railways pay under such disadvantage? Even if we adopted the system of my hon. friend who interrupted me a moment ago, an opponent of public ownership, we could hardly expect the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway to make the amalgamated lines pay, unless we first reduced the capital indebtedness of our own lines; and if thi3 were necessary, if the lines were amalgamated in order to give the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway a fair chance, and we had to add the amount of the reduction to our consolidated debt, why not do it now and give the present officials and public ownership a fair chance? It seems to me that before we attempt to incorporate the two lines, we should see if a system of co-operation and strict economy would not be to the best advantage of the people and of the companies. The officials are only human; they are fully aware of the difficulties of the Canadian people and they know we can only stand so much taxation. Why then does this parliament not go on record demanding that the officials of the two railways get together, and not only cut out duplication in passenger lines, but duplication in freight service and in building extensions? Failing this, inform them that the government will legislate in the future to merge the two systems into one Canadian National system.
Now in the face of such a statement I do not think the budget address will bring very much hope to the Canadian people, or inspire them with fresh confidence in the country, or even in the present administration. Instead of reducing our capital debt we go on adding to it year by year, which forces the government to increase our taxation. This taxation is already heavy, and unless we attempt in some measure to decrease it we shall drive people out of the country. It is quite true a large amount of our expenditure is fixed charges, but the reduction of expenses for last year is very

small indeed. It was $5,100,000 this year and the previous year $7,480,542. Our expenditures are still well over the $300,000,000 mark which means that every man and woman in Canada will have to pay a federal tax of $33 for ordinary revenue of this Dominion. The Acting Minister of Finance states that the situation is one of which Canadians may be proud, and he goes on to explain in part the reduction of revenue by stating that as a result of decreasing the burden of taxation the government will receive $52,837,000 less from the people of Canada.
This is a very nice way of handing a lemon to the Canadian people: in other words, we tell them that the loss of revenue is due to decreased taxation. I think we shall have a very difficult task if we attempt to prove to our people in the west that they have had any reduction in taxation. It is true partially that the reduction of revenue was due to the reduction of the sales tax and also to the reduction in the customs tariff last year; but it is also due to the fact that in many places in Canada a great many people did not have the purchasing power to buy even the necessities of life. That is nearer the truth than the former.
It was estimated by the Minister of Finance last year that as a result of the reduction in the sales tax the loss of revenue on the same amount of business transacted would be $20,000,000. The loss of revenue however has been $35,000,000 and this shows that the loss in the purchasing of goods by the Canadian people must have been in the neighbourhood of $300,000,000 on a basis of a sales tax of 5 per cent. The loss in customs duties has been some $14,000,000, which is almost twice what the minister expected last year as a result of the reduction in the customs tariff. This also means that the condition of the Canadian people was worse, in the purchasing of such commodities, to the extent of $70,000,000. So that the loss of revenue to the department as a result of the reduction last year was $28,000,000, the rest being due to business and financial depression in the country.
I do not blame the government for this. I readily realize that it is due to the condition* that have come as the aftermath of the Great War, and it is due also to the depression that now exists in Europe and in other countries of the world. I say I do not blame the government for it. But I have been sitting on a certain committee lately, and when we ask individuals to explain the reason for this decline in business they tell us one and all that it was due not to the tariff or tariff

The Budget-Mr. Lewis
changes but to the financial and business depression that prevails throughout the world ac the present time. I am sorry therefore that the government have apparently fallen into the error of believing that this depression is due to the reduction in the tariff. I regret that they have lost faith so soon in their own pledges. I would urge the government to overhaul their platform, which is similar to our own, except for the fact that although they have had an opportunity to put it into force they have not done so. If the Liberal party have really lost faith in the policy to which they pledged themselves, I think the Progressive party had better put their policy to the test; it would at least have this virtue, that the people of Canada when called upon to vote the next time would know where we stood.
I want to suggest to the government most seriously a scheme whereby we may reduce our national debt. I think that if we look the situation fairly and squarely in the face as business men, anxious in our own hearts to put this country on a paying basis, we shall find that this can be done. I said a moment ago that the total consolidated debt of the whole Dominion was in the neighbourhood of approximately $4.000,000,000; and in spite of the remarks of my hon. friend opposite,
I believe that the Canadian National Railways have at least some assets. We might place them say at $1,500,000,000. On the other hand, as I pointed out just now, we have a loan to the Canadian National Railways, with interest, of $600,000,000. Let us take this $600,000,000 from the railways and put it into our consolidated debt 'and that will bring the total consolidated debt up to $3,000,000,-
000.	That means that if we are going to pay our ordinary interest on the consolidated debt and make provision for reducing it at the rate of say $50,000,000 a year, we must raise in revenue through taxation 10 p.m. between $425,000,000 and $450,000,000 a year. The first duty I would urge upon any government in power would be to see to it that provision was made not only to pay the interest on the debt and to run the government but to introduce a system that would reduce the debt. If we started some system whereby we could devote $50,000,000 a year towards the reduction of the debt, in sixty years we should get it down to zero. It is a large sum, but it must be reduced. It will take Great Britain sixty years to get rid of her debt, and some of the European countries even longer; and I do not see why a young nation like Canada, with immense
natural and great potentialities, should be unduly discouraged. It is a just debt and I feel sure that the people of Canada, if taxation is applied with equity and justice, will be willing to discharge it. To carry out such a system looking to the reduction of our national debt to the zero point in sixty years, under the present administration, with a deficit in connection with the Canadian National Railways and discharged by a population of
9,000,000, it would mean that every man, woman and child would have to pay $50 in federal taxation. But if we were to increase the population to 10,000,000 we should automatically reduce that per capita contribution to $45; while if we increased the population to 15,000.000 in the next ten years-and I see no earthly reason at all why this could not be done under a sane business administration and a sound immigration policy-we should reduce the amount still further to $30 a head. And with the increased immigration, with the increased trade, with the increased commerce the railways themselves would begin to pay; and there is no doubt in my mind that there would be a reduction in the deficit to the extent of $5 a head. If this system were carried out, in ten years we should be on Easy street, and we should have cut taxation in half.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I take it that we are to deduce from all this that the hon. member's idea is that the solution of our trouble depends mostly upon an increase in immigration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not particularly in immigration; it depends upon the raising of our own people too. I think this is an object that is worthy of due consideration. I do not believe that this country can stand much longer any sort of political gerrymandering or angling for patronage or power. With such an ideal as I have suggested we could be on Easy street in a few years. As we have all read in history, Nero fiddled while Rome burned; but that could not be much worse than the spectacle presented here of war scandals being resuscitated and dirty linen washed while the country is fast going into bankruptcy. The moment we put into force such a system we shall make progress. And I have no doubt at all that if the Progressives were returned to power such a system would be carried out; I am sure it would have been put into practice during the past four years, and it would result in elevating the present depressed morale of the Canadian people to a normal, sound, sane, optimism, which is the right-
The Budget-Mr. Lems

ful heritage of a northern energetic, virile people On the other hand, to go on as we are at present would simply breed unrest, dissatisfaction, misery and disunion. Indeed it is already here. It is all very well for people to try to close their ears against it. Last year I addressed dozens and dozens of meetings in the west, meetings composed of business men, members of boards of trade and the general public, and at only one meeting was I not asked what the result would be in the west if we had secession. I am not advocating secession, I am simply endeavouring to show what our people are thinking. They are thinking seriously of these problems, and they are wondering whether secession would not be one form of relief. I do not think it would. I stand for unity, but I also stand for a sane, business administration.

Does the hon. gentleman
believe that the Progressives could give us such an administration?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it would be just as
sane as the immigration policy advocated by my hon. friend a few days ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
