I had in mind the success
of the Progressives in Ontario; that is why I asked my friend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is too small for Montreal

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was not going to say anything about immigration, but since my hon. friend has mentioned it, I may tell him that I do not agree with some of the statements he made regarding immigrants from the British Isles. I have been in western Canada twenty-three years, and during that time I have had the privilege of visiting mission fields eighty and ninety miles away from the railways, and there I have come in contact with many British settlers. I want to say that those settlers are just as good as any that come to this country; and when we have had to help any in a charitable way, it was not the British settlers but those of other nationalities. I do not altogether stand for the open door policy, although I should like to see more people come to Canada. I remember my hon. friend said that Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt and they made a success of it; but it is just as well to remember the kind of cattle scheme that Jacob inaugurated; it is also well to remember that they even had to sell one of the brothers to get the almighty dollar; and further it is well to remember that when one of them was in slavery he managed to get a corner on wheat. So for those reasons we need to be careful how we let these people in.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Progressives could not
teach them anything on that, could they?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps not. Now, the question before us is:	How are we going to raise the
$450,000,000 required to pay our way, in view of the fact that everyone is demanding lower taxation? It is true that there would be a considerable saving on the Canadian National Railways if the amalgamation proposed by some hon. members were to be put into effect. I do not agree with the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), nor do I think many others will agree with him, that we could save $100,000,000 a year by such an amalgamation, but I do believe that a saving of say, $25,000,000 could be effected. That would leave us at least $425,000,000 to raise in order to pay our way. I am not going to criticize the government unduly for extravagance, although I do think that the Minister of Agriculture, mind you, has added just a little too many men to the civil service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose the hon. member ought to know best.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps. I notice that about every two or three days we receive one of these papers, and recently I noticed that five positions were advertised, four being in the Department of Agriculture. I am not saying that possibly these men are not needed, but I think the minister has been a little extravagant in filling positions in his department during the last four years. I also think that when everybody is demanding economy our cabinet ministers should be satisfied with less expensive cars to run around in, driven by liveried chauffeurs, and so on. This may be all very well in a prosperous country, but when there is such urgent need for economy, let us at least cut out some of these expensive frills.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Might I inform my hon. friend that ever since I came to Ottawa I have been using a second hand Tory car?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am afraid that my hon.
friend is an exception to the general rule. Even with the strictest economy we cannot very well get along with the amount I have mentioned. The difficulty of the Acting Minister of Finance is increased by the loss of revenue. However, I am going to suggest a few ways and means whereby I think he could raise $50,000,000 additional revenue, and the taxes necessary for this purpose would have at least this virtue,-that they would fall upon those who are able to pay. Now, there are certain taxes which might be de-

The Budget-Mr. Lewis
scribed as optional, and I am going to make a comparison between these and other taxes which are inescapable. For instance, if a man finds a binder is necessary to run his farm, he has no option, he must buy tihat binder and pay the tariff duty assessed against it. But if the government were to place a 10 per cent tax on tickets for admission to professional hockey or professional baseball games, the man who does not want to pay the tax need not buy a ticket; therefore the tax is optional. You will find in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal, Regina, Saskatoon and other Canadian cities thousands of people who will pay prices ranging from one dollar to two dollars for tickets of admission to professional hockey and professional baseball games. Now, if they are so fond of this kind of professional snort, there is no reason wihy the government should not take a certain amount of that money; indeed I think they ought to. It is just as logical, just as sane as placing a tax upon woollens, boots and shoes and other things that a man who is raising a family must buy. Then I see no earthly reason why the government do not get after the bachelors. When there is drastic need of revenue, you have to take drastic means of raising it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do you know how
many there are?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are a great many. I
would tax all bachelors over twenty-five years of age.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about old maids?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Never mind the old maids.
A man, no matter how patriotic he is in raising a family, is penalized, while the bachelor to a large extent escapes taxation. I think the right hon. Prime Minister is setting a very bad example to the young men of this country. I read a speech delivered by him at a dinner that he attended in the Old Land, in the course of which he spoke of his illustrious grandfather, the "Little Rebel," the man who stands so high in Canadian history. If there is not very soon a change in the right hon. gentleman's condition, he will never have any grandchildren to boast of their illustrious grandfather! Now, to raise a family in this land costs thousands of dollars, and I consider that the husband and wife who are raising a family to-day are our greatest patriots.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And I consider that the
men who shirk that responsibility ought to be taxed so that they may be compelled to
at least pay their share of the cost of government. I have not figured out what would be a fair rate of taxation, but it should be graduated, beginning at age twenty-five and increasing for every year thereafter that the bachelor shirks his responsibilities. I am going to suggest seriously ways and means of raising the revenue.
One source of revenue that the minister has overlooked is the automobile industry, one of the most flourishing industries in Canada. I do not agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that the tariff should be lowered, but it is my opinion that, the excise tax should be increased upon Canadian manufactured cars. The hon. member for Macleod, and also the Acting Minister of Finance himself, spoke of the number of oars owned by Canadian people and pointed out that the price paid for these cars was at least 35 to 40 per cent higher than that paid in the United States. The value of the cars sold in Canada last year, the product of Canadian manufacturers, was 863,541,000, which, plus the tariff, would bring the selling price to the consumer up to 8100,000,000. The imported cars were valued at 811,000,000 and upward, but these would not be included in this new source of revenue. The tariff on these cars was shown to be about 35 per cent, so that the manufacturer in Canada has protection to the extent of one-third of the price of the cars compared with the manufacturer in the United States. The excise tax is from 5 to 10 per cent-5 per cent on cars up to $1,200, and 10 per cent on cars in excess of that value-still giving a protection to the Canadian manufacturer of from 25 to 30 per cent. The sales tax is the same on both United States and Canadian cars. If the minister would raise the excise tax on Canadian manufactured cars from 5 to 10 per cent and from 10 to 20 per cent, allowing the tariff to remain as it is, the cars would still sell at the same price to the consumer, because if the manufacturer raised his price the cars that were bought would be obtained from the United States. Thus the home manufacturer would still be protected, as also would the workmen-of whom we talk so much but for whom we do so little in this parliament-and there would be paid into the public treasury a sum of from $12,000,000 to
815,000,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is on the assumption that just as many cars would be sold?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I am not assuming that there is to be a decrease in the number of cars bought.
The Budget-Mr. Lems

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you raise the price you will decrease the number purchased.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not raising the price at all; I am suggesting that a larger excise tax be imposed. This would still give the Canadian manufacturer the benefit of 20 to 25 per cent protection over all other rivals and I feel sure that no injustice would be done to Canadian industries. The hen. member for Macleod showed quite clearly the other evening that the Canadian manufacturers could stand this extra tax, because they are exporting to all civilized countries in the world, with the possible exception of the United States.
There is another source of revenue that the minister might with a good deal of profit investigate. I have reference to the excise tax on cigars. I mentioned this fact to the minister in my speech on the budget in 1922, when the value of the cigars imported was in the neighbourhood of $14,000,000, and this figure has not since been reduced. I showed at that time that the increase of the excise tax on cigarettes was out of all proportion to the increase on cigars, and that while cigarette? were generally smoked by the working people the expensive cigars were used by those who could well afford to pay. The tax on cigarettes was raised from 75 to 90 per cent, while on cigars it remained as low as 5 per cent. I want that to sink in. This is hardly in accordance with the professions of the Liberal party that they were in favour of the principle of placing the taxes on those who could afford to pay. Later the minister lowered very slightly the excise tax on cigarettes, but the tax on cigars remained the same-65 to 70 per cent lower than on cigarettes. If the duty on cigars was made the same as on cigarettes-and for the life of me I cannot see why there should be any discrimination-it would bring in an additional revenue of over $6,000,000 on the basis of the present consumption. Here is a source of revenue that well could be utilized, without any resort to a nuisance tax such as the tax on cream chequer which is now proposed and which affects every farmer in western Canada; for in the final analysis the consumer and the farmer are always called upon to pay.
Now, I want to say something about the French treaty. As a result of the French treaty, last year we imported into this country nearly $15,000,000 worth of brandies, perfumes, and other luxuries of the kind, these commodities coming in under a preference provided by the treaty. It is a pity that after they 
come here the government cannot place an excise tax upon them; for certainly they are luxuries, and those who use them, those who can afford to buy such things, can pay a little extra, especially when the nation is in such great need of funds.
Another thing that the minister has overlooked is the luxury tax. I know this is a verv delicate subject, but when people satisfy their expensive tastes; when they delight in luxury, it seems to me they should be willing to make some contribution to a much depleted federal treasury. I want to say this for the city of Ottawa:	I have been in many cities in Canada and I believe the ladies of Ottawa are the best dressed of those of any other city in the Dominion. But if they can afford to buy such expensive dresses, if they can afford to buy the expensive fur coats that we see galore on our streets, then it is fair that they should pay something into the public exchequer. In other words, we should be willing to pay a luxury tax. I do not wonder that some of our young people do not wish to stay on the farms. I was speaking to a man the other night and he was sajdng that on the farm we ought to grow everything, ought to card our wool, make dresses, and so on. Yet when you go into the city you see most of the young girls with shoes that cost as much as eleven dollars, but which are not worth two; you see extravagance on every hand-and then you wonder why our young people are not remaining on the farms. I submit that that is a source of revenue that the government should look into. It would bring in millions of dollars, and it is much fairer to tax the people who can buy these luxuries than it is to tax those who can hardly make ends meet.
Another prolific source of revenue that has been overlooked in this country is the radio industry, which has become a very extensive industry indeed. I do not wish to be misunderstood:	I am not desirous of raising the
prices to the radio fans, because the prices they pay are already too high. But the profits that are made on radio equipment are out of ail proportion to those made on other manufactured goods. The bill that was brought in here the other night made the situation quite clear so far as certain tubes used in radio sets were concerned. These tubes have been sold at $6; an hon. member behind me says that they have sold as high as $9. I have bought them at $6; to-day I believe they sell at $4. In the committee, when we were hearing a discussion of these radio matters, a gentleman from the United States who had gone into the question said that it cost just sixty-seven cents to produce these tubes, yet

The Budget-Mr. Spence
they have been sold to the Canadian people at as high as $9. Here is a splendid source of revenue. It was also stated in the committee that we have over 400,000 receiving sets, and a great many of these are not paying a license fee. It was estimated that the Canadian public consumed over one million of these tubes, and in the near future, as radio is extended to every part of the country, the number will go far beyond that. Why, then, not place a tax upon these things if they are going to sell them to the Canadian consumer at four, five and six dollars? I think it is quite time the government took their fair share of the profits on these sales in order to help pay our national debt.
Under the same head of luxuries would come, I think, jewellery. There is a great deal of expensive jewellery worn in this country, and you get a glimpse of it when you come to this parliament. There is no reason in the wide world why, if people can afford to buy these things, they cannot afford to pay a part of our national debt. These are the people the government should get after, and let the workingman alone who has to buy leather mitts, overalls, woollens, and boots and shoes for his family. At the present time the average man and woman cannot afford to raise a family, and we have to resort to a policy of immigration to fill up the vacant spaces which under healthy and normal conditions should be filled with our own children.
As to economy, I know that subject is taboo, but it seems to me that our war debt and our war obligations are decreasing year by year, the administrative expenses are only very slightly less. It is a very difficult thing to economize in a country like Canada, where the administration of the government must extend from the 49th parallel to the Arctic sea and from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Nevertheless, our position is such to-day that trenchant economy is absolutely necessary, and if we are going to pay our debts, we must have this economy and raise the money. So far, I say quite seriously and frankly, no real attempt has been made to pay off our national indebtedness. We heard from the Prime Minister before the last election that the late administration, in spite of all the war profits that had been made, had not paid off one cent of the national debt. That may be true or otherwise, according to the manner of analysing the book-keeping, but it is all very well to criticize the old party for what should have been done eight or nine or ten years ago and was not done. I say that we
in this parliament, and I am taking my own responsibility in the matter, have been here also for four years, and we have received hundreds of thousands of dollars from Great Britain in regard to our war debt. We have also collected millions and millions of dollars of special war revenue in this country, and so far we have not paid off one cent. Is it not time that we should begin to sweep our own house and accept our own responsibility, and give the people of Canada a lead?
I would urge the government to get down to business and take stock of our natural resources and of the possible sources of revenue that I have indicated, sources that would be less burdensome to the masses, and let the government make a serious attempt not only to balance our ordinary expenditures but to pay the whole yearly expenses of the government. We cannot go on ad infinitum increasing our debt without seriously affecting our standing in the financial world. The people are anxiously awaiting signs of statesmanship in this respect from this parliament, not only from the government but from all sides. They are demanding that the expenses shall be kept within the revenue of the government. They are asking that we at least seriously grapple with the problem, instead of weighing in the balance how many votes will this policy gain or lose. If the government will come out definitely and with faith in their pledges and tell us what they really intend to do, I am willing to give them my serious support and make the very best contribution I can in the matter.
Before these budget speeches are concluded,
I would like to hear the Prime Minister make a speech on the budget. I would like to hear him definitely state what he is going to do in regard to the Grain Act this year, which is so important to our western people. I would like him to state definitely what the policy of the government will be in regard to the Crowsnest pass agreement. I would like him to say definitely what he is going to do in regard to rural credits, and in regard to soldier settlement and re-establishment. I would also like him to state definitely what he is going to do in regard to the Hudson Bay railway. If he comes down with a sane, healthy, business programme, I am willing to give him my very best support.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seldom worry the House, and if I worry it for a little while to-night I hope hon. members will be indulgent. I hesitate to take up the time of the House at all, after so many speeches have been made by
The Budget-Mr. Spence

so many hon. members on all sides. My own view is that a vote should have been taken on this question two weeks ago, yet we are still going on in this lackadaisical way without the government apparently exercising any control. I see members getting up and seeing how many pages of Hansard they can fill, simply playing to the gallery. The first thing will happen it will be impossible for any man who has any business to attend to to come to this House at all. As I said last year, you should apply economy to yourself. It is irritating to have to sit and listen to the stuff you hear in the House. There are only two classes of people who Should be in this House-those who have made their pile and need no more, and those who have no visible means of support, but I do not know that then it would be better than it is.
I must confess that I had a speech ready at one time, but now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to have all gone. One member has stolen a piece, another has stolen a piece, and I must now try and do the best I can with what is left.
I had intended to discuss the railway situation, which is the most difficult problem this country has to contend with to-day, but my good friend for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) expressed my views the other night very well. I must compliment him on the splendid address he gave us on the railway affairs of this country. AVhile I do not agree with him in regard to the compromise he suggested, I feel that if he. and I and a few more would get together and make a few compromises, we might solve the railway situation. I do not mean myself particularly, but members of the House, because we are not very far apart after all on this question. Something has got to be done with the railways, but I will not touch on that further, as I do not want to repeat what hon. members have said. I will try and confine my remarks to the administration of this government and to business generally.
We all regret the absence of the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I feel that industry and commerce in this country would not have been in the state of chaos it is in to-day had the Minister of Finance been in his own good health, because I think he would have followed a policy of stability. However, the government are to be congratulated in having an Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) so capable of preparing a budget to suit the government's purpose. It is apparently satisfactory to them all, and may I say that it took some manipulation on the

part of the Acting Minister of Finance to show surpluses where deficits exist.
I must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I am not a politician. My life has been a busy one, trying to eke out a living in the business world. May I say that at no time in the last thirty jmars has it been so difficult to carry on a business as it has been in the last two years, regardless of anything to the contrary that may be said by hon. members opposite. It is to be regretted that such a diversity of opinion should exist among hon. gentlemen on this side and hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the actual financial situation of the country. Is it not possible that the government in reality see eye to eye with hon. gentlemen on this side and is really aware of the true state of affairs? Let me say that a proper system of accounting should be adopted in preparing the financial statement so as to make it impossible for any political party to deceive the Canadian people by not presenting the finances of the country in the proper light. Any auditor of repute who might be called in by any branch of the government service should prepare a reliable statement which would disclose the truth in regard to the financial situation. The country should not be deceived at any time, but I believe that deception is being practised in regard to this matter. I am not a financial critic. I am not qualified like my hon. friend the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) to speak with authority on financial matters. I have done some financing in my time but nothing bearing any resemblance to what is done here. Very often I had to do my financing without any resources behind me; here you have the whole country behind you so you cannot be short of cash.
Why did the government bring down its budget before the end of the present fiscal year? Was it because it did not want to show that a deficit really existed, and what the amount of that deficit was? A statement was issued by the Department of Finance on February 28 for the eleven months up to that time which showed a decrease in revenue of 854,970,000 as compared with the same period of last year. That was a creditable showing, I must say-a decrease in the revenue of this country in that period of time of over 854,000,000. For the month of February alone the decrease amounted to
84.760.000,	a total decrease for the year of
860.000. 000.	Then hon. gentlemen opposite wonder why the country is not prosperous and why business is not good.

The Budget-Mr. Spence
This falling off in revenue would not be a real calamity if there was a corresponding reduction in the expenditure, but there actually was an increase in the public outlay for the same eleven months of $1,558,197, so hon. gentlemen can understand that the country is getting no better fast. The government endeavoured to lead the public to believe that the advance to the Canadian National Railways amounted to $56,000,000, but some time later a supplementary estimate came down for $7,500,000, making the total advance to the national system $63,500,000. That is what I call handing it out easy by piecemeal to the public. No wonder the government is ashamed of the financial statement in connection with the National Railways when it has information with respect to it handed out in that way.
The Conservative party to-day is to be congratulated on its tariff policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: "Hear, hear" is right. Since the Liberals have started to tinker with the tariff they have ruined Canadian industries and caused the depression which exists to-day. The government's action with respect to the tariff has been the cause of the great depression which prevails in this country at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unemployment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Naturally that follows from the injury to our industries brought about by the tariff changes. The government has now called a halt which proves conclusively that the Conservative policy was correct. The changes in the tariff which the Liberals made in 1923 when the duty was lowered on textiles killed the textile industry in this country, and drove the textile workers from Canada to develop the industry in other lands. In 1924, the duties were lowered on farm implements.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the textile industry has been suffering in every country in the world-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know about that; I am only discussing conditions in Canada-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -particularly in England and in the United States?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and my conclusion is that they are very much worse here than they are m any other country. I hope to be able to prove that after a while. This government also lowered the duty on farm implements, thus depriving the country of much needed revenue. When the government saw it had killed the implement business it tried to prop
that industry up again by taking off the sales tax, and removing the duty on raw materials entering Canada. That probably made conditions better for the Massey Harris Company and the International Harvester Company, but the country was deprived of the revenue which it should have got, and we have been making good the loss 'by personal taxes, or something of that kind. The injury to Canadian industries from the tariff changes resulted in the killing of a number of subsidiary companies; I know of one such company in Owen Sound which did a business of making bolts and nuts for the Massey Harris Company and the International Harvester Company. I know of another concern in Welland that had a contract for $50,000 worth of malleable iron with the International Harvester Company, and immediately the duty was taken off agricultural implements that order was cancelled. The Conservative party are now advocating a revision of the tariff on account of the industrial upheaval which resulted from the Great war. Other countries have become selfish and are taking steps through tariffs to protect themselves. We must follow their example if we wish to hold our own. Every other country has a higher tariff to-day than it had befqre the war. Yet Canada is trying to reduce its tariff. We cannot sit idly by and ask our Canadian people to live on starvation wages or permit them to leave Canada in order to seek a living in some other land.
We have heard talk from hon. gentlemen opposite about the elimination of combines, but we harve not seen any action taken yet in that direction. Hours at a time in this House have been occupied in discussing the Petersen contract. I have some knowledge of the transportation business and I have come to the conclusion that it would be impossible to obtain lower ocean freight rates by the method adopted by the present government. It is merely a sop to the farmers of Canada, particularly to the farmers of the west, to make them believe the government is going to reduce the freight rates on their cattle and their Wheat. There is also an attempt to lead the public at large into the belief that the Conservative party are behind a combine and have no consideration for the Canadian farmer. This action on the part of the government is deception pure and simple. Let me say that the Conservative party does not hope to gain any advantage by misleading any element in this country. Our aim is the initiation of sane and sound policies that will be in the interest of Canada and its people. Our policy has always been one of progressiveness.
The Budget-Mr. S-pence

A year or two ago this government undertook to regulate the question -of 'lake and other freight, and we all know the mess it got into. The only result of the government's action wias to drive vessels from the lakes and it cost the farmers of the pnairie -provinces some 84,000,000. Eventually the government had to -coax -these vessels back into the trade again. Now the government is talking of controlling rates on the Atlantic but its policy is nothing but a delusion and a snare in the hope of fooling the farmers again. Every hon. member here believes in low freight rates and would support any honest and tangible policy that would bring that result about. This parliament wlas not asked to vote for -control of ocean -rates; it was asked to vote a grant of $13,000,000 to -the Petersen company without any hope of controlling o-cean rates. We h-ave a merchant marine of our own, and if we could at all control ocean freight nates it ought to be through that merchant marine. Why pay a subsidy to another steamship company to get lower rates on -cattle? If you have any idea of helping the producer or exporter of cattle, why not pay him five or ten dollars a head, and then you would be sure that those you intended to help would receive the benefit themselves. A statement was made by the Prime Minister that the ocean rates had killed industry. That is absolutely wrong. If rates on the ocean are high, they are still too high on the land. The railways themselves have done a great deal to injure the country and to kill business. They did not give a proper service and they did not give any attention to the country's need, particularly in the express business. I will give the House an instance of what the people of Toronto were up against a few years ago when the men who operated the railways were trying to run them. Between Toronto and Hamilton there is a fine fruit growing country, and thousands of crates of strawberries were shipped from every station along the line. There is a large business in that commodity between Toronto, Hamilton and St. Catharines. The train came down at eleven o'clock each day and picked up from 800 to 1,000 crates of strawberries. Some days when the conductor was in a bad humour, when there would be a large number of crates lying on the platform, on a hot day, he would say, "Go on, let them lie there". Possibly the engineer would be in the same kind of humour and would say the same thing. We appealed to the railways, and they replied that the passengers were always kicking about the service. This course drove the business from the hands of the railways to the motor trucks. Hundreds

of trucks of berries would be carried in that way between Toronto, Hamilton and St. Catharines and other places. It is no wonder the business of the railways suffered. However, I do not blame it so much on the people who had the money in the railways as on the people who were running the railways. In any event the rates at the present time cannot be compared with the rates some years ago, particularly before the war. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) gave a splendid illustration ot how impossible it would be to have freight rates on the ocean as low as they used to be. He told the House particularly of the cost of the boats to begin with, and of the wages paid to the captain, the steward, and first and second mates, all the way down the line, each one drawing twice or three times as much as he was receiving before the war. That is the reason why it would be impossible to get freight rates down to the pre-war figure. No one would expect the men of the merchant marine to work for such a small pittance as they used to get, while men on the land received 100 to 150 per cent more than they received previously. I think the -men o-f the merchant marine deserve -the best of treatment, on account of their conduct during the war. Their loyalty to Great Britain should never be forgotten. I have had great respect for these men ever since the war, and I hope each and every one of us will remember, when we are paying our freight rates, that we should not begrudge the men of the merchant marine a reasonable and fair salary.
To my mind the subsidizing of a fleet of boats similar to the Petersen steamers would never have any effect on the Atlantic. We might just as well set two countries at war, one with a dreadnaught and the other with a row boat. You know which would come out on top. If the United States Shipping Board with 300 vessels in operation and 900 in reserve could not offset a combine on the Atlantic what could ten boats the size of -the Petersen fleet be expected to do?
The present government are absolutely opposed to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. They are prejudiced against it, and they are not getting the best results. When I first heard the merchant marine ridiculed by hon. gentlemen on the government side,
I advocated, as I do now, the inauguration of a service with the merchant marine between Canada and Mediterranean ports. I pointed out to them the commodities we could get from those ports, the number of boats which could be kept running and the amount of -tonnage. I also advocated putting on the merch-

The Budge'-Mr Spence
ant marine between the West Indies, which is a British possession, and Canada and building up a trade 'between the two countries. But nothing has been done. If we had established a proper and regular service between Mediterranean ports and the West Indies today we would be carrying thousands of tons of freight to the Canadian National Railways and keeping the merchant marine going at the same time. But there would be no use in doing that unless we had proper refrigerating service and a heated dock at either St. John or Halifax. There is no necessity for a heated dock at Montreal, because we cannot get up there in the winter-time, but it would be absolutely necessary to build a heated dock at S't. John or Halifax, and in that way we would develop our country and develop the British possessions, and good results would be obtained. I understand that it may be the intention to withdraw the Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats from the West Indies. I may say that that would be a terrible disaster for the West Indies, and we would be putting the business in the hands of the United Fruit Company of Boston, which is the greatest known monopoly in the world. The West Indies could1 never succeed if the business got in the hands of the United Fruit Company. We should develop a large business with the West Indies. We can create a large market for wheat, and we could extend that market to all classes of Canadian manufacture. I understand there is a great demand there for shoes and other commodities which we produce. May I say that the WTest Indies must have our support, or it will be lost to us entirely. The Americans are keeping their eyes on it very closely, and something might happen in that regard. It is up to the government to make a statement as to a permanent policy regarding steamship service, equipment, refrigeration to Canadian ports and heated docks at St. John or Halifax. We should be able to dispose of a million dollars worth of produce in the West Indies. All the people of Canada are thinking along the lines which I am now proposing. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Harris) received a letter, I think from a gentleman in North Bay, and it deals with the question of the government giving steamship service to the West Indies. This is an important question and I wish the government would1 give attention to it. The letter says:
So that they could obtain remunerative prices, and many thousands of acres will again be brought back to a productive state as a result if refrigeration is provided. Pineapples, bananas, grapefruit, oranges, lemons, and so forth. Cocoanuts and every kind of tropical fruit can be produced.
If all that he suggests can be produced in the West Indies, and we have any interest in that country, let us do all we can to give a proper service between our own ports and the West Indies.
The letter continues:
I should say that if the government agrees to put on a refrigerator service (and I cannot imagine such madness as that they will refuse to do this), their fruit buying agencies in the colonies must be arranged at once, so as to put an end to the present monopoly.
That is a letter that came from a gentleman in North Bay who I presume is interested in the West Indies. I happened to get it this morning from my hon. friend from East York. From the information that is available, money is now being lost under present rates. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) the other night said that the tramp steamers were a very important factor in the reduction of the cost of ocean transportation. He is right; but the difficulty with the tramp steamer is that she travels only when she can get a cargo and therefore does not give the service; and what the people want is regular service. This the tramp steamers cannot provide. There is not nearly so much stuff shipped to England, Germany and other European countries to-day as was sent over before the war. The people in the British Isles, in Germany, France and other European countries have not the money to purchase to the same extent as they did before, and what money they have is depreciated. I remember that before the war everything that was produced in this country in the line of fruits would be shipped to France, Germany and England, particularly apples, evaporated or dried; and even the cores of the apples were baled and shipped to Germany, coming back here in the shape of wine, or brandy or champagne or something of that kind. To-day our producers are suffering because of the lack of demand for the poorer class of apples which we could dispose of under normal conditions in the European countries. As a result, business on the Atlantic has suffered and that is why the rates are a little higher than they should be.
Generally speaking, a low tariff is worthless. The home market is the best for all our producers. My hon. friends to my left do not think so, but I will not deal with that point just now. Our need in this country is an increased home consumption. Our population is being depleted in the industrial centres; our workers are leaving for lack of employment; and even people with incomes large enough to live on comfortably in normal times are being forced to get out, because our taxes are so numerous and heavy. There

The Budget-Mr. Spence

can be no question that the home market is decidedly the best for our truck farmers and fruit growers. Take the tract of land for about 100 miles between Toronto and Niagara Falls, and you will find that the people there grow nothing but fruit and garden truck. Now, if unemployment gets any worse and our people continue to leave the country, and if such cities
11 p.m. as Hamilton and Toronto are drained of their working population, then there will be no hope for the truck farmer and the fruit grower. Their market is entirely in the city at home, because they have no chance of getting into the American market. The Americans produce all their own fruit and vegetables, so that there is no other market for the Canadian truck farmer and fruit grower than the market in this country. This is unquestionably true of Ontario, and it applies also to the good old province of Quebec. There may have been a time when there were large farmers in Quebec, but the farms in that province have been cut up so that every farmer there operates now on a small scale. And as in the case of the Toronto farmer, the truck farmer and fruit grower of the province of Quebec must look to the industrial centres to find an outlet for his product. If therefore our population continues to drift, to the United States these farmers will be wiped out. We all know that the United States is a great producing country, and this can readily be understood when we consider that the climatic conditions there are so very much more favourable to truck farming and fruit growing than they are in this or any other country. In Florida, Louisiana, Texas, Tennessee and North and South Carolina they get from two to three crops a year under these ideal conditions while our farmers in this country spend all their time trying to grow one-crop.
Now, as a result of the low prices that are obtained for fruit and garden truck in thi3 country the prices of our farms are going down; the value of farm lands is being depreciated. Men who have acquired farms in the last five or six years are finding it difficult to eke out a living in Ontario in those places surrounding Toronto, Hamilton and other cities. I know several of them who are going through this experience. And'the same thing is true of the farms adjacent to Montreal. These farmers are finding it exceedingly difficult to meet the interest on the money they agreed to pay for their farms, and they are not getting the protection they deserve. I do not know whether a higher tariff on

vegetables coming into this country this spring would bring about the results we should like to attain, but I might give you an illustration of the condition that exists. Even this year this country was filled with new carrots around the month of December, something that never happened before. We got carload after carload of new carrots in bushel baskets from the state of California in the month of December, and as a result of that new supply coming in the farmers around Toronto lost on nearly the whole of their crop. The reason is not far to seek; so long as the public can get the new stuff they will not buy any of the old vegetables. If we had had a tariff commission that knew something about the business conditions of the country they would have advised the government to put on an embargo for a couple of months to enable the Canadian producers to dispose of their output. Millions of dollars' worth of produce from the United States is being sold to-day on the streets of Montreal and Toronto, although the men who buy it do not make a dollar. The man who buys this stuff is in competition with the other fellow and so long as his competitor buys it he feels that he must do likewise. And while the streets of our cities are loaded with the American produce our own garden truck is rotting. The home market to-day is in a deplorable condition. Two months ago new potatoes sold at $12 a barrel, No. 2 American, while Ontario first-class was selling at from 70 to 75 cents a bag. Yet there was a demand for the new potatoes. A barrel of that old stuff would be worth $1.50 while a barrel of the new potatoes would fetch $12. At the present time a barrel of the new potatoes sells for $6 and the old potatoes around $1 a barrel; yet the people demand the new potatoes. And so long as we have people with champagne tastes this will be the case. We need a tariff commission to advise the government as to what should be done in circumstances of this kind.
Some of my hon. friends to my left and some opposite are changing their minds with regard to the tariff. Some of them are advocating a duty on certain commodities produced in their own ridings. I do not want to mention any names, but I have heard gentlemen this year advocating a tariff who denounced protection last year. We are glad they are coming our way, because the policy of the Liberal party has been tried and found wanting and I see no reason why hon. gentlemen to my left and protectionists in front of me should not support the policy of the Conservative party, a policy devised to protect the interests of all.

The Budget-Mr. Spence
Let me say that there will be a demand yet for protection on the prairies, as I told my hon. friends a year or two ago. I congratulated them on the development of their industries in Alberta and in Manitoba. As soon as they get away from mining the country, growing nothing but wheat, and go in for mixed farming they will foe making the same howl for protection as they have made here for free trade during the last two or three years, and then they will give the Conservative party the credit which is its due.
The business administration of this government has not been altogether up to date. I doubt very much if any government ever gives a real, business administration, but this is about the worst I have yet seen. They have been bargaining and making treaties, and in the treaty arranged with France I do not think our negotiators got the best of the bargain, and I am satisfied that the government are disappointed with the result. What followed the ratification of the treaty? We bought $5,000,000 worth more from France and we sold them $3,000,000 worth less. I cannot see what benefit that was to Canada. The imports included wines, silks, satins, and so on, on which we should have collected a revenue. These are luxuries, and those who can afford to buy them can afford to pay duty on them. After all, that is what is ruining this country to-day-the lack of revenue and too much taxation. We hear that another treaty is in course of negotiation with Australia. Whether it will go through or not we do not know. I am not going to enumerate the ' articles on which Australia extends to Canada the preferential treatment, but among the commodities on which we offer Australia a preference rate are meats. Now, that is one of the the things that we export, we have an over supply, and so long as that is the case I am not going to support the treaty with Australia. Then there is a preference given on eggs, cheese, butter, onions and other articles. It is my opinion. I do not know whether it is Shared by my party, that we have lots of those things in this country. To encourage their importation tends to kill our producers, the tillers of the soilv and they are the men we have to protect. I am just as anxious to protect the man who tills the soil as I am to support the manufacturer- in fact I have lost a certain amount of respect for the manufacturer. Then dried fruits, raisins and currants, are dealt with, and to these I have no objection. But I do object to our giving Australia preferential rates on vegetables. This country is so full of veget-1644
ables that we could supply Australia and England combined. All this tends to ruin our men who produce this stuff. So far as I am concerned, I hope there will be no more such treaties negotiated with any country; I think our motto should be "Canada first."
I wish the government would give the country an economical business administration instead of a political administration. I hate to say that they have been endeavouring to humbug the people, but that is really the only way I can express it. They have been manipulating our trade figures to show that there is a national prosperity that really does not exist. The right hon. Prime Minister spent two hours one night trying to tell the House and the country how much better off we are this year than we were last. Any hon. member need only ask himself and his relatives and friends how much more money they have in their pockets now than they had last year to realize the hollowness of such claims. That is what I call humbugging the people-the Prime Minister of this Dominion standing on the floor of this House trying to tell the people they are better off to-day than they were two or three years ago! He could not convince anyone of that. He also boasted that our exports were so much greater than our imports. But we all know why. We have been exporting raw material, such as wheat, copper and pulp-wood; that is the reason why our exports are so much in excess of our imports. The principal reduction in our imports was in bituminous coal, steel and other raw material, which proves that our industries were shut down and did not need either coal or raw materials. An argument of that kind is absolutely nonsensical.
Last year I spoke about government by commissions and committees, and I remarked that the House was run like a six-ring circus. You can add another ring to that this year, if you like. This session committees are the fashion as usual. The government are trying to make the country believe that they are absolutely fair in everything they do, and especially when they adopt the recommendations of any of these committees. But every hon. member knows what might be expected from a committee composed of eight members of the Liberal party, four members of the Progressive party-which is worse than the Liberal party-and three lone members of the old Conservative party. You can imagine what kind of a deal we are likely to get out of that sort of committee. The government can say to an anxious public and to

The Budget-Mr. Spence

any interested corporations: " That committee has not reported yet. Just wait a little while. They may recommend so and so." The government can promise anything and everything to keep themselves in power, and that is the only policy they have got.
Last year I pointed out that the Minister of Agriculture (-Mr. Motherwell)-is he there?

Some -time ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) had an advertisement -published, entitled "Canada is coming back."

We spent last year $21,402 for an agricultural investigation, and nothing at all came out of it. An investigation into ocean rates is being held, supposedly arising out of the report of that committee, though I thought it was because of W. T. R. Preston's report. Then we come to our friend Mr. Preston, who received $10,698, salary and expenses, in connection with various activities on behalf of the government. The Great Lakes freight investigation cost $2,291; the secretaryship of the grain commission, $5,310; allowance for house in England, $150, and so on. Now, this is something I do not -approve of; I do not think it is necessary. Then, we had another commission known as the pulpwood commission. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) asked what was the total cost to the country of the pulpwood commission and the reply came from the Acting Minister of Finance that it wras the tidy sum of $75,672.51. The question was also asked, what was the cost of the grain inquiry and what were the estimated outstanding accounts, to which the minister replied that from June 30, 1923 to March 31, 1924, the cost had been $107,612 and from April 1, 1924 to February 5. 1925, $59,994.88, a total of $166,606. Mr. Speaker, if a man had to work hard for this money himself I do not think he would spend it in that way.
Then, ini 1924-25, W. T. R. Preston was paid $12,000 and $9,000. My own opinion is that there should be fewer committees and commissions and that the government should take the responsibility and do this work themselves. Let me assure the government that from what I am -able to gather the people are going to take a more active interest in the next election than they have taken in elections in the past. Their friends and relations are being forced to leave -their native -land, many to seek a living in the United States, and these people are now ready to stand behind the good old Conservative party, which is always relied utpon to restore confidence and to bring things back to normal conditions.
Somebody on the government side of the House said the other day that two hundred new industries had been started in northern Ontario. Well, if that is so, it is a case of two hundred men individually starting ou-t in industry themselves in order to -provide little

The Budget-Mr'. Spence
jobs which they were unable to get in any other way.
A great deal has been said with regard to the desirability of our manufacturing our pulp-wood rather than shipping it out in the form of raw material. The Ontario government are to be congratulated on what they have don? in this respect; they prohibited the exportation of pulpwood from crown reserves, with the result that employment has been given to many hundreds of people. Why should we in Ontario or in the Dominion of Canada send out, our pulpwood and our men to develop an industry in Tonawanda, near Buffalo? To-day that place is booming as a result of those activities. It is clear that a great deal of this material should be manufactured into the finished product in Canada before it is exported. We cut 4,350,000 cords of pulpwood last year and nearly all of that went out in the form of raw material.
It is well known that we have valuable resources of copper in this country, but nearly all the copper we produced went to the United States, and the result is that the English and German business is going to that country instead of coming to Canada. Canada sold only 7 per cent of this product to these countries. That is an unfortunate state of affairs. Of iron ore we imported $128,000,000 worth. If our iron ore industry was developed as it should be, there would be no necessity of our buying a dollar's worth of this material in the United States. Reports of the best geologists in this country tell us that there is any amount of iron ore in the Hudson bay region which will test at 55 to 60; and I understand there is a movement on foot on the part of the Ontario government to have it brought down to Moose Factory for transport over the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway in the near future. I hope that will be done.
I noticed by the budget that the duty was taken off West Indian grape fruit-that is, grape fruit from Jamaica. I approve of that but there is no use taking the duty off grape fruit unless a proper steamship service and refrigerator accommodation are provided to take care of the imported products when brought to the ports of Halifax and St. John. I was talking to an importer of grape fruit the other day in Toronto, whose brother is now in Jamaica. He said he appreciated the removal of the duty from grape fruit, but the trouble was that the Canadian ports were not provided with the facilities for handling this product. My opinion is that there is too much duty at present on the Florida grape fruit. The Union government put a duty of a cent a pound on grape fruit from Florida. I advocate a
specific duty. I do not like the ad valorem duty, because there is always some difference between the buj^er and the customs officials as to how many pounds a box of grape fruit contains. There is always a tendency on the part of the buyer to try to show the Customs department how little the box contains, while the Customs department try to show how much it weighs. The best system is to put on a specific duty of so much per box. The specific duty does not penalize the man who ships a good, thin-skinned, juicy grape fruit as against the man who ships a thick-skinned, pithy grape fruit with very little juice in it. The man who ships the inferior stuff pays 65 cents a box, while the man who ships the first class fruit is required to pay 75 cents a box. I would therefore advise the government to reduce the duty on grape fruit from Florida to at least not more than fifty cents per box, making it a specific rather than an ad valorem duty.
We have another grievance. Last year we had an over supply of onions in Canada. In the district of Leamington and Windsor we had more onions produced last year than this country could consume. There is a duty of 30 per cent on onions coming into Canada and a dollar a bag, or a cent a pound, on onions going into the United States. Had our duty been the same as that of the United States, we would have cleaned all the onions out of this country, with no loss to the producer of onions. So instead of having a 30 per cent duty on onions coming into Canada, let us have a duty of one cent a pound, the same as the United States, and give our own people a chance in this country.
We have strawberries coming in here with a duty of two cents a pound. That is another problem that it is difficult to contend with, for our customs officials have to weigh several boxes in a carload of strawberries. I would advise the government to make the duty so much per box, instead of so much per pound, because there is always trouble over how many ounces each box weighs. Instead of a duty of two cents a pound, which makes three cents a box, I would make the duty on American strawberries five cents a quart box. and two or three cents a pint.
I have always opposed special taxation, the sales tax, the stamp tax, and all that sort of thing. What I would suggest as an alternative is this. To-day the price of oranges, bananas and pineapples has gone up so high that a duty of 25 cents per box would make little difference; it would add nothing to the resale price. Bananas are coming in here
The Budget-Mr. Spence

plentifully at the very time of the year when our own Canadian strawberries, cherries and peaches are coming in,, and they are the biggest menace that our growers have from any foreign market. Bananas are in the hands of the greatest monopoly in the world. I remember many years ago w*hen bananas would not be worth three or three and a half cents a pound. To-day you cannot buy them by the carload for less than 7-i cents a pound, and many times they have to keep them and let them rot there rather than sell cheap. That is the result of a lack of the steamboat service that we should be giving these countries.
My opinion is that the simplest and easiest and cheapest way of getting the money to run our country is by the tariff as far as possible. It is not so irritating; people do not know they are paying it. They get their medicine regularly in small doses. The customs officials are always on the job, and there is no reason why they Should not be kept busy. To-day this government is establishing tax collection offices at different places and employing extra help, which always eats up a great percentage of the money collected. You could eliminate entirely the tax offices if you collected all the money you require by means of duties.
I am in favour of doing anything that will help the prairie provinces or the Maritime provinces, and if Nova Scotia is as badly off as hon. members say I have no objection to the individual fisherman getting the duty lowered on equipment for their boats. I am in favour of the duty on slack coal, but I am also in favour of protecting the man who finds that duty adds largely to the overhead of his business. I will give you an instance. I know of a nursery business whose overhead has been increased by $7,000 or $8,000 by that extra duty of 34 cents on soft coal. Now something should be done to help an industry that that duty hurts. I refer to the Dale's Nursery at Brampton, one of the biggest nurseries in Canada. To-day we have only a 17 per cent duty on cut flowers coming into Canada, while the United States have a duty of 45 to 46 per cent on cut flowers from Canada going in there. What should be done is to help this nursery or any similar organization by increasing the duty on the goods it raises coming into this country when it is affected by this duty on coal to the amount of $7,500 or $8,000 additional overhead.

speechtext:
We have too many methods of taxation and they are too rigid. I am absolutely opposed to the sales tax. The income tax I have no grievance with because anyone who makes sufficient income should pay an income tax. I am sorry to say that the income tax I will have to pay this year will be very low as compared with some years ago. I will be very glad to pay income tax. However, the income tax is not administered just as it should be. Let me give you an instance of how the department treated a perfect gentleman, a man I know very well, who made a mistake. He was executor of a certain will in Toronto, and he was three days late in making his return to the Income Tax department. He was fined $50, although he had paid the tax within the time limit. That was about the time the Hon. Mr. Fielding took sick, and I tried to intercede for this gentleman. That is what makes men like that, men of the highest type, get sore on governments because the system is applied so rigorously. I know another case in our own business. In this case the party was using horses and wagons for livery purposes. They were changing from horses to motor delivery, and in the statement they made to the Income Tax department they put down $600 for old wagons and one horse and some harness and

The Budget- -ifr. Spence
things like that. The next year all the party got for their horses and the whole outfit was not $600, but $150. Do yo.u suppose the tax department allowed them anything for that? They said: No, we will allow you 25 per cent depreciation. The man showed them the actual receipts of the sale, but the officials insisted on his coming back and paying income tax on $337.50 that they had no right to get whatever. A system that is unfair in that way is a bad one, and makes bad friends for any government.
The stamp tax I think is absolutely against the ordinary man. The man who issues cheques from $2 up to $200 is penalized, while the man who issues cheques for $50,000 is always protected. We have so many classes of taxation to-day, federal, provincial and municipal, that they are becoming very burdensome. It is very difficult for the ordinary business man to understand these taxation laws; they are not sufficiently simple in form. I know an instance where several parties who were going out collecting money decided that it would be proper to put a two cent stamp on every receipt over $10. These people were going out and collecting say $10 and putting a stamp on each $10 paid on account. Others were not putting on any stamp at all; they thought it was not necessary unless the whole amount was paid to affix a stamp to the receipt. I saw an account which came back to one of the hon. members of this House some time ago and it was marked "Received your cheque. No need to send a receipt." So you see these laws cannot be enforced. From what I know of the mercantile world the government must be collecting much less income tax every year. There are so many old established firms being driven out of business that it could not be otherwise. The hon. member for East York suggested the other day that we had too many representatives in parliament. I concur in what he said in that regard.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"Hear, hear" is right. The unit of representation should be increased. W*e have too much government for our population. I believe in representative government, but we have enough representatives in this House for a population 20,000.000 greater. I want to say there is too much time wasted in discussing radical proposals and economic conditions, and it costs the country too much money. We have township, county and city councils in addition to our federal and provincial legislatures. We are governed to death and in making this statement I am not
giving you my own views; I am repeating the views of the man on the street. The people are sick and tired of too much government; what we should have is a less number of representatives in this House.
Now as to immigration, I agree practically with what one hon. member said the other day. We spent millions on immigration and have induced 350,000 immigrants to come to Canada, but we lost 450.000 of our own Canadian people in the same time. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are importing muscle and exporting brains to develop the industries of the United States. I would spend very little on immigration. I would allow every healthy individual from the British Isles or northern Europe, and a quota from other countries, to come to Canada, and they should all become Canadians or else stay out. We do not want any race of people that we cannot readily assimilate and make good Canadians of. We have immigration agents here and immigration agents there, but the class of immigrants we have been getting for the last few years are a detriment to any country. There never was a time when we had as good an opportunity to increase the population of Canada by the inclusion of good English, Irish and Scotch immigrants as during the present year. There were a number of people coming out from the British Isles and naturally they all wanted to get to the United States because they had heard so much of the great prosperity of that country. When they were refused admission to the United States by reason of the quota having been exceeded they stopped in some of the larger cities of Canada; and had there been a possibility of getting employment in Canada my opinion is the population of this country would have been increased by several hundred young immigrants from the British Isles. A number of them hailing from that part of the Old Country where I was raised, came to me to know if I could assist them. Many of those immigrants made their way illegally to the United States; I believe quite as many entered the United States illegally as were legally admitted.
I may say that I advocated the appointment of a tariff commission in the sessions of 1922 or 1923, and I am still of the same opinion. I suggested that there should be a tariff commission to advise the government, but I would not want the government to accept the views of such a commission if at all illogical. Neither would I have the government appoint a body of this kind merely as a figurehead or an ornament. Competent men are needed in an advisory capacity of
The Budget-Mr. Spence

this kind. My reason for first advocating the appointment of this commission was this: When the present government was elected it was supposed to be a low tariff party and I was afraid it might carry out the platform of the Liberal convention of 1019. Accordingly I wanted to head the government off but it did not keep its promises.
