subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would have the effect of not allowing you to ruin the country. The tariff commission should be composed of men of outstanding ability, men of the highest integrity; they should be men who had been trained in the commercial world, in the fields of industry and commerce, on the farm or in the factory. I would make one suggestion, however, to the hon. members of the government who are listening to me, and that is that Mr. W. T. R. Preston should not be the chairman of the proposed tariff commission. That would be a political commission and these henchmen would always be on the job.
I listened with a great deal of interest the other day to what the hon. member for Prince, (Mr. MacLean) said about discrimination in freight rates in this country. He said that a certain Mr. Armstrong had quoted certain rates, and when I heard the statements of the hon. gentleman I thought I would endeavour to find out whether they were true. He informed the House that the rate on potatoes from Kentville to Sydney, 312 miles, was 53 cents while the rate from Toronto to Winnipeg, 1,232 was 55 cents. Now I happen to know something about rates. The Saturday following when I went home I observed a bill in my own warehouse showing the prepaid freight on a car of carrots to Winnipeg, and the rate was 80i cents. This year on account of the scarce crop in the ivest and the big volume in Ontario the Canadian National Railways made a sacrifice and cut the rate to 66 cents on a 4,500 car. What I wish to say is that hon. members should not make statements of such a character unless they know them to be true, otherwise they are simply creating trouble.
The hon. member in question also talked about the Minister of Trade and Commerce developing a market for Canadian potatoes in the Old Country. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that when a commodity is scarce you can always find a market for it without going to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A few years ago when this country

had a dearth of potatoes the men in the
business did not have to go to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to find out where they could get a supply. They discovered there were lots of potatoes in Ireland, England and Scotland, and they brought potatoes here from those countries. I do not therefore see any particular reason why the Minister of Trade and Commerce should be given credit for developing a market in the Old Country. If the minister had succeeded in getting Britain to remove the embargo from potatoes he would have done something for which he could hlave claimed credit. The hon. member to whom I have referred' said, the Maritime provinces had no market for their .products in Ontario; they had to go to the United States in order to sell their fish and potatoes. Now I may say that we get 7,000,000 pounds of fish from Nova Scotia in the vicinity of Toronto alone, and that city is filled1 with seed! potatoes from Prinice Edward Island. It is not fair either to say that there is no market in Ontario for apples from British Columbia or Nova Scotia. Let me say that I 'have seen thousands of barrels of Nova Scotia apples in the city of Toronto alone. If Nova Scotia would become up-to-date, and if they would use a decent looking barrel or get a good box and pack them nicely, I would guarantee that Toronto would) 'take 100,000 boxes a year. It is their own fault they are not getting the trade. The difficulty has been dishonest packing and old-fashioned, antiquated ideas. They are using nails four inches long instead of inch and a quarter. You would) think the boxes came out of Noah's ark.
The hon, member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) was howling about everything. He was opposed to the duty on coal. He did not like to see one of his sister provinces getting something to help her along. I must congratulate my hon. friends to my left this year. I never heard so little howling in my life. Last year it wias a continual 'howl, but .this year it is different. I think they have been told to be good boys and keep quiet or we will go to the country. They are breaking up internally, and I am going to leave them to their fate. Individually there is not a better class of boys than the hon. members sitting to my left, but collectively their policy is absolutely ruinous to every .part of Canada except their own district. I am informed on good authority that when hon. members talk in this House about secession, they are not expressing the views of the western people, and I am convinced that there is nothing whatever in this talk about the feeling in the west with regard

The Budget-Mr. Spence
to secession. I wanit to part good friends with hon. gentleman to my left and if we should have an election (this year I am -satisfied the present repreeenitation from the west will not bo here again. I may travel out west this coming winter, and I hope to meat them and be friendly with them. I know for a positive fact that, although other Progressives may come here, very few of my hon. friends will be here and I desire to ipart with them the very best of friends. There is a fuelling that there is going to be an. election, and I am honing it will be very soon.
Hon. members have been talking about there being more unemployment in the United States in proportion to population than in Canada. I think the hon. member for Cham-bly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) said that the Associated Press made the statement that in New York alone there were over
300,000	unemployed. He also said that in the New England textiles there was misery and unemployment and stated that it was a better year for the Massey Harris and International Harvester companies. I do not care what the statistics, the hon. member or the Associated Press state I say it was not a better year for the Massey Harris people. They are located within two thousand yards of my riding, and I can remember the time when they employed from four thousand to four thousand five hundred men, with the exception of a short time in the fall of the year, and to-day there are not a thousand people in their employ, and at the present time I know some of the stock holders have very little to live on and there is no dividend. Why any hon. gentleman rises in this House and says they are doing better this year than previously, I cannot understand. I would not believe it. Then there is the Abel Company right in my riding. This company used to employ 1,500 men. They are now the Rumley people of Chicago, and there are only four or five men distributing goods obtained from their plant in Chicago, and Canada is holding the bag in the distribution.
Then another statement my hon. friend made was that a change had taken place in regard to certain lines of boots and shoes. I was talking to a friend the other day who knew the facts, and I regret to say that his report is that the Ames Holden people are going to shut down their factory in Montreal. I have a report from one of our commissioners in New York which proves the statements I have made to be correct and that the statements made by the hon. gentleman and by the Associated Press are incorrect.
This report is by Commissioner Frederick Hudd and reads:
Industry continues at a comparatively satisfactory level of activity and the maintenance of production and distribution point to a favourable business outlook. There is no decrease in production in the basic industries. Pig iron production in February was the highest on record for any February and there was an increase in steel ingot production. In the automobile industry, production has expanded and it is estimated that 277,600 cars were produced in February as compared with 240.912 in January, while at the beginning of March the industry was more active than in February.
The Guaranty Survey appraises the present business situation in the following terms:-
The continuance of a large physical volume of trade is evidenced tby the seasonal record in freight car loading during the first ten weeks of the year. The average daily number of loadings last month was greater than in the preceding month or in February a year ago. Moreover, current reports of retail dealers indicate an active movement of goods into consumers hands. The business of mail order houses and tencent chain stores was about 11 per cent larger.
Factory employment in the state of New-York has increased. This is especially the case in the textile industry. There has been increased employment in the iron and steel and textile industries.
Then here is the money and the exchange situation:
The Money Situation
The discount rate of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York rose from 3 per cent to 3J per cent at the end of February. Payments through banks for the first quarter are above the corresponding figures for last year. Exchange of cheques at the principal clearing houses of the United States in March rose to a total of $41,946,379,288-an increase of 12 per cent over February and of 14.4 per cent over March, 1924. This total exceeded that of any other March on record and March, 1920. by $608,119,597. Clearings in New York city aggregated $23,349,010,749, which was 10.9 per cent over February and 18.8 per cent larger than March, 1924. The exchange of cheques outside New York city totalled $18.597.368 539. an advance of 13.4 per cent over February and of 9.4 per cent over March, 1924.
The Exchange Situation
Our decrease in clearing house returns in eastern Canada was $553,000,000-1924.
I got this out of Commercial Intelligence issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce April 18, 1925.
The policy of protection to my mind multiplies employment. It will attract capital which will be adding to industry and constantly improving conditions in the factory, accumulating assets.
To-day even-body is discouraged; there is no stability and every investor feels himself to be under suspended sentence. There is too much money in victory bonds. I went into this subject last year, and advised borrowing cheaper money in New York. We have barrels of money in Canada now to put into industry, but no one will take a chance and never will as long as the present government
257S
The Budget-Mr. SpenC'

are in power unless they swallow our policy. I say to hon. members of the government: throw up your hands and give Canada a chance; go to the country and ask the endorsa-tion of the people.
The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Thurston) made a statement in this House on the 20th April, that in twenty-five years there would be no Conservative party. Let me say to the hon. member that in five years there will be nothing left but the Conservative party, and the hon. member himself will be out of it in less than five months, with some good Tory representing his riding. I always back up my statements if anyone challenges them.
It seems to me that the government are really forcing the people to consider annexation, and we all know that people will do anything rather than starve. This government's policy is one of wait and see, and they will do anything at all to keep in power. And they got into power through misrepresentation; there is absolutely no doubt about that. They tried to put the blame on the Conservative party for everything that happened in the war, and they pitted the minds of the good people of the province of Quebec against my hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) and the Conservative party. But their luck will change, the chickens will come home to roost. The government's time is nearly at an end, and their doom is certain the moment they appeal to the country. My hon. leader has been accused of making pessimistic speeches. Well, we are all more or less pessimistic, according to the meaning we attach to that word, when we see things as they are and point them out with a view to remedying them. So far as any charge of pessimism is concerned, my leader is altogether misrepresented. I wonder whether hon. gentlemen know just what the word pessimism really means. Do you think that it is right that the country should not know the true state of affairs? Why should the people be deceived? So far as I can see, there is no reason whatever why there should not be a proper statement of the financial condition of the country submitted to the people at large so that they might know just how we stand. Suppose you were at sea on a great ocean liner and a storm arose; what would you expect the captain to do if he had the interests of his passengers at heart? Would it not be the part of wisdom for him to nail down the hatches and so save both passengers and ship? Would it be pessimistic for him to see danger ahead and try to avert at? Let me tell the members of the government that we are trying to save the ship of state.

That ship is listed southward and unless some remedy is applied immediately it will list to a dangerously greater extent before long.
I want to read from a letter I have received from the French Ivory Products Limited, a manufacturing concern in my constituency. Hon. members will see what the state of things really is when they hear this.
Toronto, April 1st, 1925.
Dear Sir,-
Our business consists of the manufacture of toiletware such as mirrors, brushes, hair receivers, puff boxes, jewel boxes, combs, etc., from French ivory (celluloid). This industry has been developed during the last ten years from a very small beginning until to-day it is quite a considerable business and able to cope with legitimate import competition, such as English, where rates of wages, while lower than Canadian, are nearer our standards than are the wage rates of other countries such as Germany and Japan.
Realizing that the bulk of our lines sell most freely in the fall, when merchants stock up for the holiday trade, thus necessitating much short time in our factory during the early part of the year, we set about developing our comb lines which are an all year round seller, and this finally grew into a very large proportion of our business. (One of these lines we were able to supply the government in large quantities during the War). This development has enabled us to keep our workmen more steadily employed throughout the year.
Recently this comb business, which we have built up primarily to keep our wheels turning, and our men employed during the early part of the year, has been imperilled by German competition. We have had to reduce our staff and cut our working hours, with a result that our wage bill has been cut practically in half. During the last year some of our employees have gone to the States owing to the fact that we could not keep them employed.
The prices at which German and Japanese combs can be sold in Canada are below our production cost and yet we have every reason to believe that the ridiculously low prices at which these combs are being bought in Germany gives the agents and jobbers and dealers profit before the public get any benefit of it.
We know the prices at which these combs can be bought in Germany and the large profit that is possible on them, as we were offered an agency. We turned this down as we preferred to manufacture rather than throw our workmen out of employment and try to sell German manufactured goods. We find, however, that the Germans secured other Canadian agents.
Since the war the government have enacted several commendable pieces of legislation in an endeavour to guard against this unfair and undesirable competition, but at present none of these are in force and Germany is now a real menace to our industry.
Only last week our Toronto traveller called on several of the largest jobbers in our line and found them all solidly sold on the German line on account of the prices.
As an illustration we will take a pocket comb with case. This costs in Germany $4.50 per gross. Our nearest comb uses $4.28 worth of material alone which is only charged in at scrap value as the comb is made from small pieces. To the $4.28 must be added our labor, factory expense and commercial overhead.
A similar English comb sells wholesale in England at a little over $18 per gross.
As this is only one illustration which might be multiplied, it is not difficult to see what will happen to the Canadian comb business if some steps are not taken

The Budget-Mr. Spsrte
at once to protect the Canadian workmen against unfair German working conditions.
We would respectfully urge upon you the importance and necessity of immediate amending legislation which will provide greater protection based on Canadian values and Canadian wages and would appreciate your support of any legislation along these lines.
I have another letter along the same lines but I will not read it. But it all goes to show how the country is suffering from this cheap foreign labour in countries where they work ten to fifteen hours a day in competition with our workmen.

speechtext:
hon. member for Chambly and Ver-cheres tlhe other evening endeavoured to stir up a little strife-it .may have been unintentional-on the expenditures incurred in connection with the war. Now if any wrong was done, and I do not admit that there was, the Liberal party were equally guilty; whatever was done at that time was done under the administration of the Union 12 m. government. The hon. member quoted the cost of sending unnecessary men to France. But who knows whether we sent unnecessary men or not? It is possible that the men were not all fit for the firing line, but there were many other uses to which men who were not sufficiently sound for the trenches could be put in the rear in connection with transportation and so on. He also condemned the government of that day for having wasted $247,000,000 on the Ross rifles and other equipment. That is a ridiculous statement, for the hon. member knows that the Ross rifles were in use before the Union government got into power. Then he referred to the waste of $80,000,000 on the Canadian merchant marine, all of which he attributed to the Conservative party; and he talked about $10,000,000 expended on useless Canadian Northern Railway stock. The hon. member knows that the Canadian Northern had to be taken over, so that his remarks in that direction are not pertinent- Then he spoke about the loss of revenue in tax free bonds. But if he knows anything he knows that our bond market was in very poor shape at that time; England was in the war and America was not sympathetic, and we had to give some encouragement to the people here to buy the bonds. That is why these bonds were sold at 5-'. per cent. The hon. member puts down the loss at $110,000,000. Now. we had to give some encouragement in order to sell those bonds at all, because as I have said, we had no bond' market and were in a difficult position. Statements of that kind should not be made on the floor of the House; they simply promote strife between the good people of Ontario and the good people of
Quebec. There is no necessity for such discussion; the war is over, and we may as well have peace; there is no use for us to be continually fighting. Those of us who are comparatively new members have been more or less disgusted with the way in which certain hon. members quarrel across the floor. We are here to legislate for the present and the future, and we should care very little for .the past. Sometimes I get weary listening to hon. members resurrecting things that happened years ago. If it comes to extravagance, no government has sinned more than the present, unless it was the Drury government in Ontario, whose members spent money like drunken sailors. You all know what Ontario did to them. So people in glass houses should not throw stones. A few evenings ago the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) delved into ancient history, to thirty-two years ago, respecting a commissioner whom we sent to the World's Fair in Chicago., for the purpose, I presume, of entertaining distinguished guests, and the hon. member gave us details of hotel bills and so on, in an attempt to justify the expenditure last year on the trip of himself and1 two other gentlemen to the Wembley exhibition. I am not criticizing that expenditure, the sum apenit by the boys at Wembley was not very large; but .maybe there was no necessity for sending them to London at the country's expense. However, the criticism of that expenditure by certain hon. members in no way justified the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond referring to a member long since dead, and I do not think he added any dignity to our proceedings by his counter attack. Matters of this kind should not be brought up in the House for they always create more or less trouble.
The government are continually blowing about how Canada is coming through, and they are spending barrels of money advertising how it may be done. I want to tell them how to bring Canada through without spending so much money-just give the people a chance at an early general election, and they will provide the remedy. I believe this government is a menace to Canada, I believe they are actually willing to trade off any part of it for any emolument. They are sacrificing the industries of this country in pandering to the few Progressives to my left in order to continue themselves in power. That is simply their whole consideration. I hope that in the very near future, if they do not soon make up their minds to go to the country and secure the verdict of the people on their administration of the past four years, they will at least

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) on his very short speech-extending over two hours. If there is one man in the House who has criticized members in this corner for long speeches I think it is the hon. member. I do not intend to detain the House at any great length at this late hour, but I desire to touch very briefly on some of the things mentioned by the hon. gentleman. In speaking of the home market he emphasized the fact that the truck gardeners near our cities must depend entirely on that home market. Then why should he need protection? Who is to oppose him in that home market? There cannot be any opposition if he is depending entirely on that market. Who is sending in anything to compete with him? If that applies to the Canadian truck farmer, it will also apply to the American.
We were very sorry to hear the hon. gentleman bid us good-bye. We expected that Tory Toronto would still remain true to the hon. member, and that he would be back again next session, but we regret to hear that he does not expect to be a member of the next House of Commons.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I dislike to prolong this debate, but I do not wish to give a silent vote on this budget or on the amendment. I do not intend to support the latter, for the following reason. I was elected on a platform entirely opposed to the proposition contained in the amendment. As I understand the speech of the hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), I cannot see how any man in this country to-day could support his amendment. He takes into consideration our imports today and places them at $892,000,000, and of : bis total he would bar out $700,000,000, as representing goods which could be manufactured in Canada. Apparently he would bar out everything with the exception of a few raw products, such as silk, wool, coal, crude rubber and so forth. The net result would be that our only imports from Great Britain would be coal. This means that the Conservative party intend to cut off entirely any tiade with Great Britain, with the exception of coal, and yet expect her to furnish a market for our own products. Britain is not in a position to pay in gold for what she buys from us to-day, although the Baldwin government have just declared that the country will return to a gold basis at once. Therefore she must exchange her goods in payment for what

she buys from us. Now, if Canada will not exchange goods with Britain, Britain will look somewhere else for a market. There is this further objection to the purpose of the amendment. If we are shipping goods to Britain, and are taking nothing back in return, we must bear an overhead expense greater than if we were bringing back return cargoes. No doubt this is the considered policy on which the official opposition intends tc appeal to the country. 1 would go a little further. We have been fed on protection for fifty years, and Canada is in her present position in spite of - I think I am within bounds in using that ph'-ase-in spite of our tariff policy, or the old National Policy. Our friends to the right speak as though they considered nothing of any importance in this country today but the industrial structure-the development of factories and financial institutions. They do not take into consideration the fact that the producers of this country are of some importance. The production of the necessaries of life is an essential function, but the necessaries of life are not all manufactured goods. The real measure of the prosperity of a country is the amount of happiness and prosperity that is found in the average home. In this country to-day that prosperity is not prevalent throughout the rural districts, and for that reason I am going to oppose the amendment proposed by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). As I said before, I was elected on a free trade platform, and I am going to read one or two planks from the platform on which the present government was elected:
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.
That the British preference be increased to 50 per cent of the general tariff.
Part of their resolution has been carried out. Concessions were made last year so far as agricultural implements were concerned which resulted in a saving to the farmer, as one hon. member has put it, of 83 cents on a 150 acre farm. Now, we acknowledge that we have received some benefit from that, but I do not believe we should come here and advocate something for ourselves alone; we are in favour of giving the poorer or the labouring people of this country some benefits. The tariff platform as laid down and adopted by the Liberal Convention of 1919 called for what I have just read. But I would like to go a little further and make reference to the fact that the platform received its blessing

The Budget-Mr. Elliott (Dundas)
from the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr Motherwell). Let me read some statements taken from his speech on that occasion:
Whatever conclusions are arrived at here in regard to the platform, the leadership, or anything else, when we go forth to our respective homes we must stand by these conclusions to the last ditch. There is no use of coming here, harmonizing our differences and then going away and everybody having a platform and a leader of his own. Do the best you can to impress your views upon the great body of this convention and, having done that, stand by the net result.
Further he states:
There is another thing I would suggest and that is that no platform, no matter how good it is, will carry itself into effect.
And further:
It is necessary that we should have full confidence in our own platform and leader if we are to instill similar confidence in other people. We must if necessary sound forth a clarion note, even from the housetops, and then people will stop and listen because they will see, that we, ourselves are in earnest.

I am going to quote from the remarks of another hon. member on this occasion the present Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau).
He said:
If we are to have a great nation, it is not the platform of the party that comes first; there is no use in having a platform if you have not the men with the heart to put that platform into practice. First, we must be united. Let us be Canadians; let us be Liberals; and we shall have a great country, progressive, prosperous and happy.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the last plank in that tariff platform that I read has never been touched. Now, I do not want to pick out one or two members of the present government and throw ail the responsibility on them. Our friends here to the right are talking of an election, but I think they want an election least of any in this House, because with the policy they have to go to the country on, they will never come back. I am going to read now from the speech of Mr. Duncan Marshall, who I understand, is at present engaged as Liberal Organizer throughout this country:	He said:
The Dominion government should take from off the backs of the farmers of Canada the burden of the protective tariff. If governments will do these two things for the farmers of our country then the farmers will take care of themselves.
He said further:
We are willing to go as far as anybody will go along the lines of free trade; personally, I should be glad to burn every custom house between Canada and the United States.
I would like to ask whether this man is preaching the same doctrine to-day. If he is, what right have the people to pay any attention to him?
The statement has been made from the right hand corner of this House that the people of the province of Ontario are all for protection. The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) made the following statement the other night:
I think that the average man in Ontario, whether farmer or manufacturer or labourer, is a protectionist on principle, and the man in the west should have some sympathy for their viewpoint, which is just as honest as the free traders'.
In the last election in 1921 there were twenty-four Progressives elected in Ontario, and they were elected on a low tariff platform. There were also elected from Ontario twenty Liberals who subscribed to the tariff policy which I have just read. I submit that these men have not been true to the promises they made to the people of Ontario. I intend to vote against the present budget for the very reason that it does not conform to the platform which I advocated and which I promised the people I would try to carry into effect.

speechtext:
If the tariff
commission that is appointed is an absolutely independent and efficient tariff commission- I do not mean a tariff commission that will be sent broadcast all over this country such as we have had in previous years-but a commission formed of experts in the different departments, and we have men in the departments here who are quite capable of handling any question pertaining to trade in any line in this country, and if the people who are engaged in any industry come to that commission and show why they should have protection, I will be willing to see that our industries are not pushed off the map; but go further I will not.
I have some more choice gems here. I have one here from the Minister of Public Works for New Brunswick. The question has been raised here to-night as to how the revenue should be raised. The hon. member for Parkdale said that his policy was to increase the tariff. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) the other day, in a very clever speech, showed that the tariff at the present time was between the two extremes for the purpose of raising almost as much revenue as it was possible to raise. Everybody knows that if the tariff is raised to an extreme point it performs the same function as an embargo, and that if you carry it down to the bottom you get less revenue. This question of raising the revenue came up at the Liberal convention, and the Hon. Peter J. Veniot, Minister of Public Works for New Brunswick, answered the question how they would raise the revenue in this way:
There are some who contend that the lowering of the tariff will injure the industries of the Dominion. There are some that contend that the lowering of the tariff will reduce the revenue of our country, and that having regard to the conditions brought about by the war and to the fact that Canada is in need of a large revenue, it would be disastrous to reduce our tariff at the present time. There are even some Liberals who hold that view, and to those especially allow me to say a word. Allow me to take them back in imagination to 1896, the time of the introduction of the Fielding tariff. Notwithstanding what our Conservative friends may say as to there being very little difference between the Fielding tariff and the National

Policy, we know that there was a considerable reduction in the tariff of 1896 as compared with that of previous years.
That is a question. He goes on:
Notwithstanding that reduction, ladies and gentlemen, the revenues of Canada increased by leaps and bounds; so much so that when the Liberals were defeated in 1911 the revenues of Canada had soared to such a figure that the like had never been known before in the history of our country.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the Liberal solution of the problem of raising the revenue. I have a number of other extracts that I am not going to weary the House by reading at this late hoiir. I have brought these in for the purpose of explaining why I was going to vote against the budget. I believe the mandate that was given to the present government was to lower the tariff, and had the tariff been lowered the people in this comer I believe would have supported it. It has been said that this present budget is a stand-patter, but I think it is a rock-a-bye, for it goes backward and forward. For that very reason I am not going to submerge my own personal convictions on the question of the tariff by supporting any budget that is not along the lines laid down in this platform. I do not care what the consequences are, and if it means an election should the Progressives in this corner stand out against the budget, the sooner we have it the better, and let the people decide whether the pledges given to them by this present government have been put into effect.
The discussion of this budget, although it has been long, has been very amusing and educative as well. I am going to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) the other day in this House. Someone from the official opposition asked him if he had advocated a low tariff during his campaign. His answer was that he did not know where they advocated low tariff, but it was not in his riding. Now that goes to prove that in the present House there are some who did not believe in the platform which their party adopted in 1919, and it would be very easy for me to name some more of them.
Many statements were made the other day by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), who spent considerable time explaining the system of bookkeeping that this government followed in bringing down the budget. I venture to say this, that the present budget would be similar to the Speech from the Throne in that it would be prepared and placed in the hands of the Acting Minister of Finance by the officials in the de

partment, who would probably be the same as under the late government, and I expect that

The Budget-Mr. Elliott fDundas)
their system of drawing up the budget would be the same that was followed in previous years. But I would like to draw attention to this:	The man in the street does not care a
rip what system of bookkeeping the government follows so long as they pay their way.
The sum and substance of the budget, as far as I can see, is this: When we take every expenditure into consideration, including the advances or loans to the railways, we find there is a deficit, which means that that deficit is added on to our national debt which means :n turn that the taxpayer of this country has to provide more interest in other years. That, to my mind, is of greater importance to the people of this country than the system of bookkeeping that is followed by the government.
Another thing that came up in the House the other day was the disclosures, if I might use the word, made by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). 1 need not recall, because you will all remember, the charges he laid against the official opposition of profiteering that went on during the war, of the money wasted in building the merchant marine after the war was over, and a number of other things I need not go into. But those things are over. I am not saying that the Conservative government of that time was guilty of chicanery or anything like that, but I do say this: As the time is not far distant when we are going to have another war. if ive are to judge by what we see in the papers from day to day, the duty of the government at the present time is to bring down measures which will prevent anything of that kind taking place again in the future. That is the lesson we should learn from the speech of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres. The one regrettable feature in connection with that expenditure is this: If it was reckless, it is passed on to the men who fought to save this country, and they will be carrying that burden till their dying day. That is one of the hardships which those people have to suffer. Surely if it is in our power to prevent such a thing as that happening again we should not hesitate to do so.
There is one more matter I wish to discuss before bringing my remarks to a close-a question that has been brought before the House in many different ways-and that is the condition existing at the present time in Cape Breton. The situation there has been referred to as a strike. I do not think the word "strike" is appropriate; I think it should be regarded as a "crisis." I do not wish to cast any discredit on the corporation that is operating there, but it looks to the public at large
in this country as if that corporation cannot carry on. If such is the case there is a duty devolving upon this government, and that is to provide for those people in Cape Breton who are starving. I am not trying to introduce this matter in a political sense at all; I do not care who is right, whether it is the employees or the corporation, but what I do say is this: That we should not in a country as rich as Canada allow women and children to exist in the conditions which prevail in the Glace Bay district to-day. No matter what the cause of the controversy may be, I say it is a blot on the name of Canada to allow those conditions to exist. If we go back only a few years when the war was on we found thousands of those miners enlisting. When this country was in need those people responded to Canada's call. To-day they are in need and what is this country doing in their behalf? We have heard different sides of this question presented in the House. But I had the pleasure to-day of listening to the superintendent of relief conditions in that district, and I understand that he is to address the members qf this House to-morrow afternoon. I think there is enough human-itarianism among hon. members to go and give that man a hearing. I venture to say that after hearing his statements hon. gentlemen will adopt an attitude towards that community very different from what they do today. We have been told by the Prime Minister, and I do not dissent from his statement, that technical questions prevent him from stepping in and taking some measures for the relief of the miners and their families. But technical questions did not prevent this country from granting relief at the time of the earthquake in Japan, at the time of the Halifax catastrophe, of the earthquake in San Francisco and many other emergencies. Now surely if the Canadian government was justified in spending money of the Canadian people in relieving distress outside our own boundaries-as was the case in two of these emergencies at least-are they not more justified in meeting the necessities of our own people in a case such as the present?
I listened very attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault). In his closing observations he appealed for national unity. I think his appeal should be listened to by everybody in this country. If Canada needs anything it needs unity because we have in the Dominion people of different races and different religions. I think if hon. members would study intelligently all the troubles and problems of the people of Canada, no matter
The Budget-Mr. Lovie

in what district they may be found, national unity would be achieved very much more quickly than is likely to be the case from the way we are proceeding.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the hour is late I recall the fact that in the budget debate last year I had the good fortune to secure the floor at a quarter past three in the afternoon, so I am not going to indulge in any kicking about the lateness of the hour on the present occasion. In taking part in the budget debate of 1925 I had hoped to be able to assure the House that I would not take up very much time, but I am afraid I shall have to speak at some length as there are quite a few points I wish to touch upon.
I wish to say at the outset that the present budget lends itself to criticism on the ground that it is not following up and extending the admirable policy so worthily started by its predecessor the 1924 budget. The budget of last year was accepted by the country as a whole not so much for what it actually contained as for What it portended. The people of Canada thought that a start was being made towards relieving them from the crushing burden of taxation which hangs so heavily on the shoulders of each and every one. An editorial in the Manitoba Free Press at the time the budget was presented last year, announced that that budget gave general satisfaction all over the west, although the reduction in duties was practically confined to agricultural implements, a slight reduction in the sales tax, and a few exceptions. The budget of 1925 offers no reduction in taxation. It is generally called in this House a stand-pat budget, and as such will not be received with veiy much favour by the country in general. Another reason why I at least will reject the present budget is that it is a protectionist budget and as such does not sound the much heralded "death knell of protection" of which we heard so much last year. To listen to arguments in this House one is forced to the conclusion that in advocating the wiping out of a protective tariff one is advocating the wiping out of customs duties entirely. That is not so. What the Progressive party stand for, and what they are fighting for, is to 'have the protective feature wiped out of the tariff entirely. Now, the question will be asked immediately "Where is Canada's revenue to come from?" and I believe it has been asked even this evening. That question, Mr. Speaker, is very easily answered. A protective tariff does not raise revenue; it was never intended that it should. The objective

of a protective tariff, brought to its logical conclusion, is to prevent importations. Therefore no duty can be paid where there is no importation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where does the hon. gentleman draw the line between a protective tariff and a tariff for revenue ouij'? Surely a tariff for revenue ipso facto is a protective tariff?
Mr, LOVIE:	I .think I will answer that
question of the hon. gentleman as I go along in my address.
Canada at present raises $344,000,000 of revenue annually, of which only $108,000,000 or about 31 per cent is raised from customs. Of course in wiping out the protective feature of the tariff one is not doing away with (the customs house as a means of raising revenue, there could still be duties on tea, coffee, silks and so on which are not produced at home, and excise tax on wines, spirits, tobacco and so on which are prodtuicedi at home to a limited extent, and which should all bear their share of a revenue producing tax. The income tax and the sales tax, two methods of taxation, started since the war period, are responsible for raising a large share of the revenue of Canada, and were the plan adopted that I have outlined I have no doubt that the increased volume of business transacted would make the income tax and the sales tax more and more available as a revenue producer. There is no doubt, in fact it is a foregone conclusion, that the fetters of protection duties once removed Canadian trade and prosperity would advance with leaps and bounds. On one point all in Canada are in perfect accord: A remedy for existing conditions must be found and applied quickly. As to what the specific remedy will be there is difference of opinion. Our Conservative friends-there are not many of them here to-night but those that are here are on the job-are constantly advocating that a protective 'tariff high enough to protect the industries of this country and to keep out competition is all that is necessary bo promote trade and give prosperity to alii and sundry. They claim that raising the tariff will stimulate industries at home, prevent the importation of products that 'can be manufactured in Canada, do away with the unemployment problem, stop the exodius bo the United States, and in short, cure all the ills from which we are suffering at the present time. This to my mind is a fallacy of the worst kind. The party in this House that advocates high and still higher protection points with pride to the United States as a, shining example of the benefits of a protective tariff. On this point I should just like to read an extract which

The Budget-Mr. Louie
came to my notice about half an hour ago.
It is taken from the Treherne Times, a paper published in my own 'Constituency:
April 23, 1925: Henry Ford is credited with the following:	We in America can live within ourselves.
We can even raise rubber. We can place a tariff wall about ourselves high enough to keep out the goods of other countries if we so desire. But I for one do not favour that narrow provincial policy. I am for free trade unrestricted and unhampered among the nations of the world. The free, natural unhampered and unrestricted trade between the forty-eight states of the United States is a perfect demonstration of the line that world trade should follow. And sr.ch a course will be followed when we come to know 1 hut all tinkering and monkeying with natural free trade hurts and restricts all legitimate business and industry.
Such world trade based on labour and fair exchange of goods and no favours does not need armies and navies for its protection. It needs only the go-.dwill and confidence of friendly neighbours, who have been helped and not hurt by its development.
And of course Henry Ford's ability is well known and no comment need be made on that article. The party in this House who advocate high and still higher protection point with p: ide to the United States as a shining example of the benefits of a protective tariff and entirely overlook the fact that the United States is the largest free trade area in the world, that on account of her diversity of products and industries, on account of the north being able to trade with the south, and the south with the north, the east with the west and the west with the east, protection has done that great country less harm than it would have in a more restricted area. In short, the United States has prospered, not because of protection, but in spite of it; but we in Canada from our geographical position cannot claim the same results from a protective policy, such as we have had for the past.
To those m this House who are recommending a still higher protectionist policy than we have at present, as a cure-all for the financial sickness of Canada at the present time, I would like to quote for their benefit part of a speech delivered by Richard Cobden in London on September 28, 1843. Richard Cobden was reciting the condition of the people in Great Britain prior to the breaking of the back of monopoly there by the repeal of the corn lawrs, and these are his words. Conditions in Great Britain seemed to have been on a par with what we in Canada have at the present time, namely, starvation in the midst of plenty.
I quote these words to show what conditions were in Great Britain on September 28, 1843.
I do not think I will take time to quote the speech, but I have it here if anyone doubts it.
I may say that the conclusion reached by Mr. Cobden was not the conclusion reached by the Conservative party of to-day as to the 165

nature of the remedy to be employed, but history has demonstrated that Richard Cobden was right in the conclusions which he reached and in the remedies which he advocated for the cure of the economic ills of Great Britain. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) has mentioned in this budget debate that all Great Britain's prosperity was achieved prior to the repeal of the corn laws in 1846. The hon. member has gone back quite a few years for his comparison, but I am able to go back just as far. I might say that I for one worked with and alongside farmers in Scotland who farmed both before and after the repeal of the com laws, and these men were able to tell, and did tell from actual experience, how much conditions had improved for the agriculturist and the working man and incidentally for the whole population after the repeal of the com laws. I do not want hon. members to take my word, but I will quote Cobden's speech in 1884 as to conditions in Great Britain. He gives the conditions in Scotland, England and Wales all separately, and I will take a short quotation from what he said about the Scotch labourer and farmer because I know those conditions better. He said:
Yet I find the following description of the diet of these labourers in a Scotch paper:
"In East Lothian, the bread used by hinds and other agricultural labourers is a mixture of barley, peas and beans, ground into meal; and you will understand its appearance when we inform you that it is very like the rape and oil cakes used for feeding cattle and manuring the fields; and it is very indigestible. coarse food."
He says also:
In this country (Forfarshire), the mode of engaging farm-servants is from Whitsunday to Whitsunday; in some cases the period of engagement is only for half a year. The present average rate of wages is eleven pounds per annum, or a fraction more than four shillings per week, with the addition of two pecks or sixteen pounds of oatmeal, and seven Scotch pints of milk weekly. thus:-

These are the conditions as they were in Scotland before the repeal of the com laws and it is practically the starvation that was brought about that put the protective tariff out of business.
Conditions in Scotland such as Cobden describes prevailed prior to 1846 but do not obtain to-day. These dark days are left be-

25S6
The Budget-Mr. Lome

hind never to return. The putting of the trade of Great Britain on a free trade basis with a revenue tariff on certain articles not produced at home, and an excise tax on certain articles produced at home, has shown the world a method of conducting the financial affairs of a country which is both sure and stable, as it gives fair play to all and special privileges to none, and the record of Great Britain since the signing of the Armistice in the payment of war obligations, and in the reduction of her war debt, has shown that her method of financing is efficient, effective and stable.
The secret of the success of Great Britain is that she trades with the whole world on an equal basis. During the whole period from 1846 to 1914, manufacturers in the United Kingdom had to meet the competition of every country in the world that must find overseas markets for the output of its factories. This competition British manufacturers had to meet, and did meet with success, without a vestige of tariff protection at ports in the United Kingdom. In 1912, only two years before the war, the total value of the import, export and re-export trade of the United Kingdom, was $1,343,602,000. It exceeded the foreign trade of Germany by nearly 40 iper cent; it exceeded the overseas trade of the United States by 70 per cent, and it exceeded that of France by 125 per cent. Our fiscal policy, said the Economist of London, in 1912, approximated that of free trade, while the fiscal policies of our three principal rivals, Germany, the United States and France, was that of high tariffs and trusts. The moral appears to be obvious. If the people of Canada will not trust the Conservative party to apply the so-called cure of high protection to economic ills from which they are suffering, how about the policy of the Liberal party? I will take a few quotations from an editorial in the Manitoba Free Press of May 17, 1924, headed, "A Turning Point in Political History." This editorial will describe the feeling of the majority of people in western Canada in choicer and more concise language, than I can command. It says in part.
The Liberals were protectionists, where they needed to be to get elected, and believers in a revenue tariff where that view was popular; with the result that the parliamentary representation, in place of being a compact body, was a combination of two wings, one protectionist, the other low tariff with a nondescript centre, prepared to be governed entirely by consideration of expediency.
Now, we may ask ourselves the question, what is wrong with Canada and Canadian conditions. That she is sick, no one will deny, and it is no use doctoring the effect. Let us get to the cause if we can. Canada has unlimited natural resources but at present

they are undeveloped. They consist of agricultural lands, mines and fisheries. Of these four sources of wealth which Canada has in practically unlimited quantities agriculture is the greatest. There are in Canada
440,000,000 acres of arable land of which 110,000,000 acres are occupied, only 60,000,000 acres being under cultivation. On what is under cultivation we raised in 1923 over 400,000,000 bushels of wheat, of which 80 per cent had to find a market outside Canada. The export market also ruled the price of the balance sold on the home market, so that the farmers received for their wheat what it was worth in the open market of the world, less storage and transportation charges. The farmer in the disposal of his surplus product has to come into competition with the cheap labour and low standards of living of other countries, as well as depreciated currency and other incidentals. He is prepared for that competition; he accepts it as part of the day's work. But he has to face something far harder at home in his own country, and that is the problem of the high cost of agricultural implements and machinery, excessive' transportation charges both by rail and water, high interest charges on borrowed money, high taxation, and1 a high cost of all articles he has to purchase; while the cost of the necessaries of life is enhanced by the protective tariff and the cost of the distribution system as well. The great problem in Canada, then, at the present time is how to make agriculture profitable. Not only is agriculture unprofitable in the three prairie provinces, but the conditions are even worse. Let me quote from an Ontario newspaper the following:
The Kincardine (Bruce County) Review tells how for years past the Western Ontario United Boards of Trade, representing organizations in Perth, Essex, Brant', Huron, Waterloo, Kent, Grey, Lambton, Elgin, Wellington, Oxford, Middlesex, Bruce and Norfolk, have been collecting information from the 157 township clerks in these counties. They now find that agriculture is on the decline in the area they have beer studying.
It is found that in these fourteen counties 212 60' acres are known to be for sale; farms actually vacant not including those abandoned as useless for agricultural purposes, come to 75,000 acres; there is reported to be 100,000 acres more, land in pasture than is necessary.
All this indicates a decline in the agricultural activity throughout many of the finest counties :* the province, and the western Ontario organization means to call a conference later in the year to discuss the facts and see what can be done to improve matters.
Everybody knows that western Ontario is a highly important part of the province and dominion, and everybody in western Ontario knows that the foundations of its prosperity are in its agriculture. The moving away of skilled farmers, the departure of the farmer's family for the city, the inability to secure useful farm help means at first idle fields and later idle farms, and a reduced and poorer countrvside.

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
It is time city people paid more heed than they have ever done to the warnings given in these columns that the province and dominion can have no real prosperity unless that prosperity begins with agriculture-the corner-stone of everything in this country.
From 1920 to 1924 the farmers of Manitoba, part of that great country which has been rightly called the granary of the empire, would have been better off financially had they allowed their farms to rest for three years, just raising sufficient for their own use. This period includes the year in, which there was a rusty crop which was not *worth the expense of handling; and from 1920 to 1924 the more the farmer raised the further he went behind, by reason of the high cost of production. It took two years before that calamity had reflected itself in the balance sheet of the eastern manufacturer. But it has got as far as eastern Canada; and it would be amusing were it not tragic to contemplate the different reasons assigned for the depression of trade conditions in this country. One of the real reasons for this depression is the fact that the prices of the products the farmer has to sell have been depreciated to pre-war level since 1920, while the prices of all the things he has to purchase have stayed at what they were during the war. Taken in bulk, everything the farmer purchases is twice as expensive now as it was in 1914, and it is small wonder he is making so few purchases on capital account. Very few farm implements have been purchased in these years of depression, and that condition has been reflected back to the makers of implements, who through lack of orders are unable to keep their factories going. This has resulted in unemployment. Very few buildings are being erected on the farms, and this means that the builders have had no employment; while building material has not been required and as a. natural consequence there has been no business for the lumber yards. This has been reflected back in the saw mills and further back to the bush cruise. Again, no nails have been required, nor has there been any need for general hardware, so that there is less business for the hardware stores, and this is reflected 'back to the wholesalers. Small wonder there is unemployment and the men are leaving this country and going elsew'here to get a chance to earn their daily bread. But they will come back as soon as conditions improve.
What is urgently needed in Canada above all else is a method to make agriculture profitable. In spite of all squirming and twisting, we will admit sooner or later that this basic truth remains, unshaken and undeniable, that the farmer's business must be made profitable or no one else's business is worth five cents.
And this should be kept squarely before us in any form of readjustment we may have 'in view. Nor do conditions relating to agriculture, such as I have described, obtain in Canada alone; the American farmer is in the same boat with his Canadian cousin. The Breeders' Gazette of December 4 last contained an editorial commenting on President Coolidge's remarks delivered at the Chicago stock yards. This article was written by Mr. Saunders, the editor of the Breeders' Gazette and president of the company, and it says in part:
We share in the President's sympathy with practical movements promising to give farmers a decent reward for their labours. The greatest single question before America to-day is how to make the farm pay. To the solution of the problems involved must be brought the best thought of the nation, and a disposition upon the part of all other industries to confess the great truth enunciated by the president in his down-town Chicago speech to city businessmen, to the effect that we must not and can not divest farming of the "human element" entering into it. His business must afford him a decent living for himself and family. In the language of the president, "He wants a fair show, and when he gets it he can be relied upon to take good care of himself and to contribute substantially towards taking care of the rest of us."
The question looms up larger than ever, how to make agriculture profitable. You cannot by any possibility raise the price of commodities on the markets of the world, and therefore the only thing is to lower production costs. The Montreal Gazette last fall had this to say about agri-1 am. cultural conditions, that it was neither the tariff nor high freight costs that hurt the west but the low world price for wheat. The same writer told the western farmers that they must look to the home markets because of the uncertain prospect of stability and economic recovery in Europe as a result of the adoption of the Dawes plan. I may say this about the home market for wheat:	With 7 bushels per capita
as the outside consumption, how is a population of 10.000,000 to consume an output which in 1923 amounted to 400,000,000 bushels and which in future years may easily exceed that? The Gazette's economist, out of a sense of patriotism and devotion to his economic views, might multiply, the consumption of wheat fivefold, but this would be beyond the capacity of the rest of our 10,000,000 people. This means that we shall have to sell our wheat to the British, the Germans, the Italians, the Japanese, the Chinese-to every nation under the sun which imports wheat; and to get into these markets we shall have to conform to world conditions. If the prices fixed 'by these conditions are so low at times as to wipe out the margin of profit,
The Budget-Mr. Lovie

the result will be stagnation, in the west with resultant hard times down east. The east is suffering to-day from a lack of purchasing power on the part of the western farmers; and until this revives there will be industrial depression.
Now, as to making agriculture profitable. It is no use at this time suggesting the home market as a remedy, because, although that might be a factor fifty years hence, relief from existing conditions must be given at once if agriculture and industry in Canada are going to be salvaged. The farmer had the value of all his stock and products depreciated in 1920 and 1921 to pre-war levels. He took his loss, and it was a heavy one, but he perforce had to take it and grin and bear. No other portion of the community have yet taken the loss and depreciation the farmer took in 1920 and 1921, and it is up to them to trim their sails and adjust their business to the conditions which now obtain. Manufacturers stated when deflation started there would be no reduction in prices of implements or machinery until implements manufactured from high priced material were sold at war prices, and this has militated against a return to normal as farm implements are almost twice the price they were in pre-wair days. Labour in Canada as a whole is 25 per cent better off in wages than it was in pre-war days, but the cost of living is high and rents are higher; consequently they will about break even. Freight rates are high, also express rates, and these last named play havoc with the marketing of produce, such as eggs, butter, cream and so on.
I do not know whether railroad wages are too high or not, but they are certainly out of line with the wages paid the men who are producing the freight for the railways to haul. Possibly the men on the farm are paid too low wages, I am inclined to think they are, but they are paid all the business of farming will afford. I will give a personal experience as to the difference between railway wages and farm wages. Last harvest I had stooking and threshing for me a Canadian Pacific fireman who was out of work. I was paying him $3.50 for stooking and $4 for threshing. He stayed with me until the weather became very wet, when he said, " I can get a job at railway firing and earn twice as much money as you are paying me." That is a far higher rate of wages than the farmer can afford to pay. Consequently I repeat, I do not know whether our farm men are paid enough, but they are paid all the business of farming will afford. Nine men out of every ten will tell you that because of the seasonal nature of railway work

in Canada high wages have to be paid to compensate the men for the season of the year when they are perforce idle. To find out just how seasonal railway employment is in Canada, I wrote the Dominion Statistician asking him to give me the number of men employed on Canadian railways month by month. On receiving his answer, I wrote him asking for the payroll of employees on Canadian railways month by month. I must say I was surprised, for the statistics certainly do not bear out the contention of seasonal employment and the consequent necessity for veiy high wages.
