The question of deficits on the Canadian National railway system should at once receive the attention of parliament. This subject has been taken up a good many times and I desire to mention it again in order to impress it on the House. No board cf directors can give their best service in the interests of a system that they know is in such a position financially, through over-capitalization, that it is impossible to earn operating expenses and pay interest on fixed charges. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) dealt with this question so fully that there is no need to go into it any further than to say that this proposal is not new; it has been brought before

The Budget-Mr. Lovie
the House and the country on several occasions, but it will have to be emphasized over and over again before the government will move in the matter. The government should, at as early a date as possible, write off the excess capitalization of the Canadian National Railways and add it to the national debt of the country. Give Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors a fair field with no favours and1 no political interference, and let them understand that if they cannot make the system pay under conditions extremely favourable, they must resign and make room for men who can accomplish the job. But, Mr. Speaker, I have faith enough in Sir Henry and his business ability to feel satisfied that he could accomplish the job successfully. The successful operation of the railways will not be accomplished by a raise in freight rates, as rates are now as high as the traffic will bear, and in some cases higher, but economy and good business management must be exercised, and duplication of service must be reduced to the minimum.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, to say a word on the coal situation. I am not familiar with the local conditions in Nova Scotia, but I am going to touch the coal question from a national and international standpoint. I am strenuously opposed to all duties on coal and seeing that the United States has no duty on coal, against any nation which allows American coal in free, I would strongly urge that American coal be allowed entry duty free, in other words, there should be reciprocity in coal. I have never been convinced that Alberta coal could be brought to Ontario, in fact I consider the proposition is not feasible commercially, and I am strenuously opposed to the taxpayers' money being paid out to assist impossible trade ventures. Winnipeg is as far east as Alberta coal can be drawn by rail as a commercial proposition, and even then it is worth 812 per ton, which is certainly its extreme value. With free trade in coal, Alberta mines could supply not only Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba but also North and South Dakota and Montana, which would give them quite a territory contiguous to their mines; Ontario would get its coal supply from Pennsylvania; and the Maritimes would supply the local market and the New England states. The fuel problem certainly looks simple when you wipe out the restrictions upon trade, imposed by man in his so-called wisdom and apply the law of geography and common sense, which is, that the shortest hauls possible should be utilized for heavy freight.
Our friends of the Conservative party are fond of throwing out the taunt to the government, "They are afraid to go to the country and submit their policy to the electors." Well, the life of the Canadian parliament is supposed to be five years, and personally I see no reason why general elections should be brought on oftener than is absolutely necessary. There is a certain amount of dislocation and unsettlement of business accompanying every general election, so the less of that unsettle-menit the country is subjected to the better for the country. While at my home in Manitoba during the Easter recess meeting my constituents, when the question of a general election was discussed the general expression of opinion was that these electors figured that they had done a pretty good stroke of business in 1921 in sending to parliament 65 members, all Progressives. These Progressive members owed allegiance to neither of the old political parties, were men and women who would vote on questions coming before parliament solely on the merits of the question at issue and in its reference to the good of the people of Canada as a whole, and with no consideration for party advantage. A record of the votes cast in this chamber during the sessions of 1922, 1923, 1924, and so far this session will show that so far the Progressive party have voted about as often with the official opposition as with the government, and sometimes the Progressive party have stood alone against the combined forces of the government and the official opposition. The men and women of western Canada who sent Progressive members to parliament in 1921 feel to-day that they played a very safe game in electing to the federal parliament members who thoroughly understand rural conditions, who are hampered by no party affiliations and to whom the lust for power or the spoils of office make no appeal, and these electors are quite prepared to repeat at the next federal election what they did in December 1921,
The policy proclaimed and preached by the Conservative party is anathema to a prairie farmer. He knows absolutely that no amount of protective tariff can assist him in any possible manner. Consequently he is not going to cast his vote to give the other fellow the privilege of taxing him in the so-called "interest of industry", as he well knows that the ability of any industry to establish and	sustain	itself	in	a free	field is
the	measure of its public utility.
A western farmer and those dependent upon him know absolutely that a vote cast for the Conservative party means a vote which, carried to its logical conclusion, will rivet more firmly than ever the fetters that have been hindering and handicapping him ever since the inauguration of the National Policy
The Budget-Mr. Louie

of protection The only party who will obtain support in the prairie provinces is the one who will absolutely stand squarely for equal rights to all, special privileges to none. If these manufacturers in Canada who clamour for protection would devote the same energy and expense to keeping their factories strictly up to date and keeping down production and distribution costs intead of maintaining an expensive lobby at Ottawa, they would enter the same class as the Brantford Cordage Company's binder twine factory at Brantford, Ontario, which claims to be doing veiy well under free trade conditions. I have an article here with regard to the conditions in connection with the Brantford Cordage Company: I will just read the last paragraph of it:
Regardless of political convictions, every Canadian must recognize in the Brantford Cordage Company a concrete denial of the oft-repeated doctrine that no Canadian company can battle unprotected against American competition. Here is a purely Canadian organization, created and operated with no governmental protection, possessing no peculiar advantages, which has succeeded, with constant progress, against the best efforts of the largest companies in the world through no means other than sheer courage, efficiency and hard work.
It would be unwise to generalize too freely from this instance to success. But the history of the Brantford company does indicate that where the necessity of selfreliance is accepted it is possible to substitute for tariff protection the independent defence of increased efficiency; that such necessity embodied in free trade conditions stimulates inventive effort and resourcefulness; that it tests courage and in testing it, strengthens it.
I wish to quote also a short paragraph from the Toronto Telegram of April 13, which is a report of a speech delivered by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris). Under the caption, "Canada needs Protection," the report quotes the hon. member as saying:
There was shipped into Canada from the United States 195,000 barrels of apples, 5,000,000 pounds of strawberries, 17,000,000 pounds of pears, 1,000,000 pounds of tomatoes, 27,000,000 bushels of potatoes and other farming produce which we grow ourselves. Let us protect ourselves against the men who can ship a month earlier than we can produce ready for market by a protective tariff and give our farmers a chance.
And at the bottom it adds:
Mr. Harris was received with great enthusiasm.
I may say just here that three years ago I was in a very southerly part of Ontario, on the 24th of May, and I went to see a gentleman there whom I knew. That particular country lying between Leamington and Windsor was a hive of industry: men and women were busy putting in all kinds of garden truck. The farms are small, but four or five men were employed on each one; in fact they were so busy at the time I was there that the people were unable to take in the

sports that were going on not half a mile away. I asked this gentleman where they found a market for all the garden truck that was being raised in that part of the country. He said: "We get all the market we want in Detroit." When I remarked about the duty, he said; "Oh, the duty does not bother us. The people come from Detroit with their motor trucks; they drive right into the fields and they take away all the stuff we can raise." Now, if the farmers in the Leamington district can find a market for all their garden truck in the city of Detroit, I cannot see that there is anything wrong with some of our people in Canada buying earlier fruit and vegetables from across the boundary.
It is the Liberal part of Ontario down there.

I do not know as to that. Let me quote the following with regard to shortage of British Columbia rhubarb:
The fruit and vegetable jobbing trade of Winnipeg are puzzled to understand why more British Columbia rhubarb is not reaching this city. So far, it was learned yesterday only one car of British Columbia rhubarb had arrived, while seven or eight cars have come in from the state of Washington. There is a large demand in Manitoba at this time of the year for this article of diet before the Manitoba product comes on the market, after which all outside shipments cease.
Note these last words: As soon as the home product comes on the market, all these outside shipments cease.
I wish to make some reference to the immigration problem, but I shall not say very much about it at this time, because the matter will come up later in the House, probably on the estimates. Moreover, the question has been discussed from every possible angle and I do not think I can throw very much light on it. We have had the open door advocated, and on tihe other hand there are some who are advocates of keeping out immigrants altogether. This is a tremendously big country- I have said, with 440,000,000 acres that are arable, only 110,000,000 are occupied, and
60,000,000 under cultivation; so that there is certainly room for a lot more people. I am not in- favour of the policy that was advocated by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) in his very able speech of the other day, to which we all listened' with so much interest-a policy of the open door for immigration. There are certain countries from which I think our immigrants should come. First and foremost, I would draw the Americans from the northern states, because they are already acquainted with conditions such as obtain in the Canadian west. As a rule when they decide to move to Canada they have farms to sell, and they bring their

The Budget-Mr. Bovie
outfits with them-horses, implements, and probably enough money to give them a start; they know the conditions and exactly how to go to work and make their work count. So I would take the American first. Second, I would take British born; third, Scandinavians and Icelanders, and, fourth, people from northern and central Europe. If we had about as many as we could assimilate every year from these two countries I think Canada would be on pretty safe ground so far as the question of immigration is concerned.
In the constituency of Macdonald, which I have the honour to represent in this House, particularly south of Glenboro, and Cypress river, there are a good many Icelanders, and these men are ideal farmers. They have splendid houses and foams and seem	to adapt	themselves	readily	to theconditions in that part of the country. The Icelanders and the Scandinavians seem to be very closely related, and I would say that from	either of	these countries, as	well asfrom Denmark, we can get the very best settlers. One thing I am entirely opposed to as regards immigration is allowing people who come	from other countries	and who	do notknow	the ways	of Canada	to settle	here in
colonies. That has always been a mistake. The first large immigration I remember in Manitoba was an immigration from the west highlands of Scotland, sent out under the auspices of Lady Gordon Cathcart. These men were fishers or crofters, but having settled in a colony near Pelican lake they did not do well and ultimately lost their land. But the young people who came from Scotland along with their families, who grew up and strayed around the country, were the nucleus of the very best settlers we have. I am very much in favour of allowing only those people to come to Canada who can be assimilated into our population, with whom we need not be ashamed to have our sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, intermarry-men and women whose descendants will grow up and be what we call the very best Canadians.
Those of us who are in this quarter of the House have been looking forward to having a measure to provide for the single transferable vote put on the statute book of this country. We were promised by the Prime Minister that that would be done at the last session, but it was not done and we have not heard a word of it this session. However, we still hope that a measure for the transferable vote will be enacted into legislation before the close of this session.
In .conclusion, so far as the amendment to the budget moved by the bon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) is concerned,
about the only comment I can make on that is one that I often heard made by a farmer in our part of the country, a very old man mow, but who in his early years lived in Mus-koka, later moving to Manitoba, where he made an ideal farmer, and he is now finishing his days in British Columbia. In commenting on patent medicines I often heard him say, "'They are just like a drink of water-little good, little harm." This amendment strikes me as a good deal like patent medicine-little good, little harm, and I for one am going to vote against it. As far as the budget itself is concerned, as I am an absolute believer in free trade, I cannot conscientiously myself, nor in the interests of my constituents, support this budget.
